A research team placed a 3 week old
kitten in front of a Rottweiler. The dog
had never encountered a cat before. It
had not been socialized with smaller
animals, but what the dog did next was
unexpected. The dog lowered its head and
it lay down and began licking the kitten
in slow, careful strokes. The kitten
crawled between its front legs and fell
asleep. So, does he know it's a baby?
So, they tried it again. This time with
a baby rabbit, then a duckling, then an
orphaned fawn. Every time results came
out the same. The dog relaxed its body,
softened its posture, and did something
gentle with a mouth that could kill in a
single reflex. The dog was not trained
to do this. It was not rewarded. The
question no one on the team could answer
clearly was how it knew. How a dog with
no exposure to any of these species
could look at each of them and arrive at
the same conclusion that it's a baby and
I should not hurt it. And here's the
explanation to this. Almost every
infantile feature looks the same across
every species, whether it's a puppy, a
human infant, or a baby seal. The eyes
sit too large for the head, the head too
large for the body, the forehead pushes
outward, and these proportions are not a
coincidence. They are signals. So,
what's actually going on inside the
brain when this happens? Researchers at
the University of Oxford put people
inside a brain scanner and showed them
photos of baby faces. Within 140
milliseconds before the person even
fully processed what they were seeing,
the reward center of the brain lit up.
The brain was treating baby faces like
something to move toward, protect, take
care of, and it was doing it before the
person had any say in the matter. The
decision to care was being made before
the subject was fully aware of what they
were looking at. And the key part, the
response didn't require the baby to be
human. The proportions alone were
enough. You can't put a wild leopard in
a brain scanner, but the way animals
behave is the same. This system isn't
just in us. It runs possibly in every
mammal alive. A female leopard in Kruger
National Park killed a baboon in a
marula tree. Normal hunt, but when the
body fell, something came with it. A
baboon infant, about 2 weeks old. A
safari guide named Ryan Sobey recorded
what happened next over several hours.
The leopard came down, walked to the
infant, and picked it up in her jaws,
but not the way she'd bite prey. She
used the carry bite, just enough
pressure to hold, not enough to break
skin. She carried the baboon infant into
a thicket, set it down, and began
grooming it, licking its fur in long,
slow strokes. The infant crawled toward
her belly and attempted to nurse. The
leopard allowed it. By morning, the
infant had died of exposure. Baboon
infants need near constant warmth in the
first weeks of life, and the leopard's
body couldn't give it that. But, she
stayed beside it through the night. When
hyenas came close, she picked it up and
moved it further away. This wasn't the
first time. Leopards in the greater
Kruger region have done this with baboon
infants on at least three separate
occasions. The baboon isn't her
offspring. It doesn't share her genes.
It can't return the favor. Every calorie
she spent protecting it was, by every
biological metric, wasted. And yet, she
keeps doing it. Something about the
infant, the way it moves, is hitting
something deep enough in the leopard's
brain to override the predator that was
working perfectly minutes earlier. It's
not just how babies look, it's also how
they sound. Baby distress cries across
mammal species are shockingly similar.
High-pitched, short, repeated bursts.
The pitch rises at the end. In 2014,
researchers at the University of
Winnipeg ran a simple test. They hid
speakers in the wild and played
recordings of baby cries, but not from
the species living there. They played
baby fur seal cries to deer, human baby
cries to marmots, animals that had never
heard these species in their lives.
Every time, the adults came to the
speaker. Every single time. They'd never
even encountered the species making the
cry, but something about the sound, the
pitch, the rhythm, the desperation in it
was close enough. The mammal brain isn't
asking, "Is this my baby?" It's just
asking, "Is this a baby?" But, listen to
this. Recognizing a baby and caring
about it are not the same thing. Now,
here's the disturbing part. Male langur
monkeys commit infanticide at rates that
have been documented across populations
in India for over 50 years. When a new
male takes over a group, he
systematically kills the existing
infants. Not because he fails to
recognize them as babies, because he
does. The infants are not his. As long
as they are alive and nursing, the
females are reproductively unavailable.
Killing the infants brings the females
back into estrus. The male can then sire
his own offspring. He knows exactly what
a baby is. He understands what killing
it means. The detection system is
working perfectly. The difference is
what happens after that recognition. In
the leopard, recognizing a baby triggers
protection. The animal becomes gentle,
careful, almost nurturing. But in the
male langur, that same recognition leads
somewhere completely different. It
triggers reproduction. Same recognition,
but opposite results. And it's not just
langurs that do this. Male lions have
been documented killing cubs after
taking over a pride. Dolphins have been
seen attacking and killing calves. Bears
do it, too. In some chimpanzee
populations, females have even been
observed killing and eating the infants
of rival females. This only works
because they can accurately recognize an
infant in the first place. But instead
of triggering care, that recognition can
also trigger competition. And here's
something even more interesting. A
primatologist named Jill Pruetz once
watched a group of chimpanzees in
Senegal take in a young chimp from a
completely different group. But they did
something different. They groomed him,
fed him, kept him close, almost like he
already belonged there. But he didn't.
He had no relation to any of them. He
came from another group entirely. And
yet, the females still accepted him. He
was too young to be a threat. Even
though nothing in their biology said he
should matter to them, something about
him still registered as baby. And they
responded to it anyway. There are even
documented cases of this happening
across completely different species.
We've seen dogs nursing kittens, cats
raising rabbits, and even hens
incubating duck eggs and caring for the
ducklings after they hatch. Every one of
these animals can tell the baby isn't
theirs, and they care for it anyway.
Part of that comes down to hormones. In
nursing mammals, baby-like features can
trigger a caregiving response almost
instantly. And then one animal learned
how to exploit all of it, the common
cuckoo. This bird sneaks its egg into
another bird's nest. When the chick
hatches, the first thing it does is push
the host's real eggs and babies out of
the nest, so it gets all the food for
itself. And it works. The host parent
keeps feeding it like nothing happened.
Day after day, the cuckoo grows. Within
a week or two, it's three or four times
bigger than the bird feeding it. It
looks nothing like the parent's own
young. There is no way to look at this
chick and think it belongs there. And
yet the parent bird keeps feeding it.
And the reason behind this is how they
cry. Researchers at Cambridge found that
a single cuckoo chick produces a begging
call that sounds like an entire nest
full of hungry chicks screaming at once.
The parent's brain is wired to respond
to how loud and desperate the begging
gets. The more intense it is, the more
food it brings. The cuckoo figured out
exactly how loud it needs to be. It
didn't trick the parent by looking
convincing. It found the exact point
where the parent's brain stops
questioning and starts caring. A safety
instinct turned into a weapon. Every
mammal carries this system. It reads the
face, the sound, the movement. It works
across species. It's older than most of
the animals running it. But all of this
leads to one question. Do they know it's
a baby? And yes, they know it's a baby.
What happens after depends on the
animal. Some see a baby from another
species and every instinct to protect it
kicks in. Others see the same thing and
exploit it. Same detection, completely
different response. It comes down to the
animal, its biology, and millions of
years of evolution shaping what it does
in that moment. So, yes, they know it's
a baby. The evidence is clear. They see
it, hear it, respond to it across
species lines in ways that cost them
something. The real question was never
whether they recognize it. It's what
they choose to do once they do. And
that, it turns out, looks a lot more
like us than we expected. And maybe
that's the most unsettling part of all
of this. We built entire philosophies
around the idea that compassion is
uniquely human. That empathy, that
instinct to protect something small and
helpless, was proof of something higher
in us, something special. But a leopard
sat in the dark next to a dying baboon
infant and never left. A dog with no
training, no reward, no reason, looked
at a duckling and went gentle. A bird's
brain gets hijacked so completely by a
cry that it feeds a creature three times
its size for weeks without stopping. A
predator goes gentle, A a competitor
goes protective. Something that should
trigger one response triggers the
opposite. The detection is reliable.
What follows it isn't. And that might be
the most honest thing the research has
produced so far. If you noticed a gold
coin with the face of Socrates hidden
somewhere in this video, drop the
timestamp in the comments. One random
person who gets it right wins a $20 gift
card. I'll announce the winner in the
next video. Thank you for watching.

Do Animals Know When Another Animal Is a Baby?

This video explores why — tracing the science behind one of the most consistent and unexplained behaviours in the animal kingdom. From a leopard in Kruger National Park who used her cub-carry bite on a baboon infant, to cross-species cry experiments in the wild, to the one bird that turned the entire system into a weapon. The answer goes deeper than instinct, older than most of the species running it, and ends somewhere no one on the research team expected.

All research and sources are linked below.

📚 RESEARCH & SOURCES:

▸ Konrad Lorenz — "Baby schema" (Kindchenschema) concept, originally published in:
"Die angeborenen Formen möglicher Erfahrung" (1943, Zeitschrift für Tierpsychologie)
https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1439-0310.1943.tb00655.x

▸ Morten Kringelbach et al. — Brain response to infant faces (University of Oxford)
"A specific and rapid neural signature for parental instinct" (2008, PLOS ONE)
https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0001664

▸ Susan Lingle & Tobias Riede — Cross-species baby cry study (University of Winnipeg, 2014)
"Deer Mothers Are Sensitive to Infant Distress Vocalizations of Diverse Mammalian Species"
(The American Naturalist, 2014)
https://doi.org/10.1086/677547

▸ Nick Davies et al. — Cuckoo begging call research (University of Cambridge)
"Cuckoo parasitism: a call to arms" and related studies on host manipulation
https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1253122

▸ Ryan Sobey — Safari guide, filmed the leopard and baboon infant encounter in Greater Kruger National Park, 2017. Multiple documented cases of leopards adopting baboon infants referenced in wildlife observation records from the Greater Kruger region.

▸ Langur monkey infanticide — foundational research:
Sarah Blaffer Hrdy — "The Langurs of Abu: Female and Male Strategies of Reproduction" (1977, Harvard University Press)
https://www.hup.harvard.edu/catalog.php?isbn=9780674512414

▸ Jill Pruetz — Primatologist, Iowa State University. Fieldwork on chimpanzees in Senegal (Fongoli Savanna Chimpanzee Project). Research on chimpanzee social behaviour and inter-group dynamics.
https://anthropology.iastate.edu/faculty/jill-pruetz

▸ Elephant empathy and brain structure — general reference:
Cynthia Moss — Amboseli Elephant Research Project
https://www.elephanttrust.org

PEOPLE MENTIONED IN THIS VIDEO:

▸ Konrad Lorenz — Austrian zoologist and ethologist. Winner of the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine (1973). Coined the term "Kindchenschema" (baby schema) in 1943 to describe the set of infantile features that trigger caregiving responses in adult animals. His work founded the modern field of ethology.

▸ Ryan Sobey — Safari guide in the Greater Kruger National Park, South Africa. Filmed and documented the female leopard's behaviour toward a live baboon infant following a hunt in 2017. The footage became one of the most widely referenced examples of cross-species caregiving in a wild predator.

▸ Susan Lingle — Wildlife biologist at the University of Winnipeg. Led the 2014 field study playing cross-species infant distress calls to wild animals. Her research demonstrated that mammalian adults respond to baby cries regardless of species origin, suggesting the response is tied to acoustic structure rather than species recognition.

▸ Nick Davies — Professor of Behavioural Ecology at the University of Cambridge. Leading researcher on cuckoo parasitism and host-parasite coevolution. His work identified how the cuckoo chick's begging call mimics an entire brood to override host parental behaviour.

▸ Sarah Blaffer Hrdy — Primatologist and anthropologist. Conducted foundational research on langur monkey infanticide in India. Author of "The Woman That Never Evolved" and "Mothers and Others." Her work established the reproductive logic behind male infanticide in primates.

▸ Jill Pruetz — Primatologist at Iowa State University. Directed the Fongoli Savanna Chimpanzee Project in Senegal. Documented cross-group infant adoption behaviour in wild chimpanzees, including cases where infants from outside groups were accepted and cared for by unrelated females.

description:
When did ancient humans start drinking alcohol? 
The answer goes back way further than you'd expect — not thousands, but millions of years. Our relationship with alcohol didn't begin with the invention of wine or the first brewery. It started on a forest floor in Africa, ten million years ago, when a small primate picked up a piece of fruit that had been sitting on the ground too long.

This video traces the full history of alcohol — from fermented fruit to the Natufian caves of Israel, the mysterious stone monuments of Göbekli Tepe in Turkey, the world's oldest recipe in ancient China, and the civilization-powering beer of ancient Egypt. By the end, you might start seeing your next drink a little differently.

All research and sources are linked below.

📚 RESEARCH & SOURCES:

▸ Patrick McGovern — "Fermented beverages of pre- and proto-historic China" (2004, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences) https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0407921102

▸ Patrick McGovern — "Uncorking the Past: The Quest for Wine, Beer, and Other Alcoholic Beverages" (UC Press) https://www.ucpress.edu/book/97805202...

▸ Göbekli Tepe — Archaeological evidence for fermented grain in large stone vessels at the site (German Archaeological Institute, Oliver Dietrich et al.)

Right now, you're probably drunk or
about to get drunk. And the last time
you had a drink, beer, wine, whatever,
you probably just drank it and forgot
about it. But what you did is one of the
oldest things a human being can do. It's
older than writing, older than farming.
It actually predates humans beings
entirely. Because our relationship with
alcohol doesn't start a few thousand
years ago with the invention of wine or
the first brewery. It starts about 10
million years ago on a forest floor in
Africa with a small primate picking up a
piece of fruit that had been sitting on
the ground for too long. In 2014, a
biologist at UC Berkeley named Robert
Dudley published a book called The
Drunken Monkey. His argument was simple.
When fruit falls from a tree and sits on
the ground, the natural sugars inside it
start breaking down. Yeast gets in,
fermentation begins, and the fruit
starts producing small amounts of
ethanol. And when primates ate that
fruit, the ethanol inside it made them
feel a little drunk. They had no idea
why, but it felt good. So, they kept
coming back for more. Over millions of
years, our ancestors didn't just
tolerate alcohol. They evolved to look
for it. So, by the time ancient humans
actually showed up, the taste for it was
already built in. It was there long
before anyone figured out how to make it
on purpose. The question is, when did
they figure that out? In 2018,
archaeologists were excavating a cave
near Haifa, Israel. The cave is called
Raqefet, and it was used by a group
called the Natufians about 13,000 years
ago. Inside, they found stone mortars
carved directly into the bedrock. When
they analyzed the residue left in those
mortars, they found traces of wheat and
barley that had been soaked, germinated,
and left to ferment. That's beer, brewed
in a cave 13,000 years ago. Now, here's
what makes that finding so important.
The Natufians were not farmers. They
hadn't invented agriculture yet. They
were still collecting wild grain by hand
and hunting animals for meat. They
didn't grow the barley, they found it.
But somehow, making beer was important
enough that they figured that out first.
Think about that. Because up until this
discovery, the story goes like this.
Humans settled down, started farming,
built villages, and then eventually
discovered fermentation and started
making drinks. Alcohol came after
civilization, but Roc de la Cave says
the opposite. These people were brewing
while they were still nomadic, and they
aren't the only ones. About a thousand
years later, someone in southeastern
Turkey built something enormous. At a
site called Göbekli Tepe, massive stone
pillars, some weighing over 10 tons,
were arranged in careful circles and
carved with images of animals. The whole
structure was deliberate and complex,
and it was built before farming, before
pottery, before anyone in the region had
a permanent home. These were still
hunter-gatherers. For years,
archaeologists couldn't explain why
nomadic people would organize the labor
needed to move 10-ton stones up a hill
and carve them with precision. What
would motivate that? Then they found
large stone vats at the site. When they
tested the insides, they found chemical
traces of fermented grain. People were
brewing at Göbekli Tepe, not small
amounts, enough for large gatherings.
The current theory is that this site
wasn't a home. It was a gathering place
for ritual and feasting. People traveled
from across the region, came together,
and drank. And this raises a question
that's been debated for decades. Why did
humans start farming? An archaeobotanist
named Patrick McGovern, the leading
expert on ancient alcohol in the world,
has spent decades arguing that humans
didn't start farming to make bread. They
started farming to make beer. And I
couldn't agree more. He says that bread
requires grinding, kneading, and baking.
It's a complex process. Beer is simpler.
You soak grain in water, leave it alone,
and fermentation happens by itself. And
the desire to drink would have been a
stronger motivator than the desire to
eat grain in a slightly different form.
If he's right, then alcohol isn't
something that showed up after humans
settled down. It might be the reason
they settled down in the first place. By
7000 BCE, the evidence gets more
precise. In a Neolithic village called
Jiahu in central China, archaeologists
found pottery jars containing residue
from a fermented drink made of rice,
honey, grapes, and hawthorn berries.
Chemical analysis confirmed the
ingredients and the fermentation
process. This is the oldest confirmed
recipe for alcohol anywhere in the
world, and it wasn't crude, it was a
blend. Multiple ingredients carefully
chosen and combined. Whoever made this
knew exactly what they were doing. From
there, it only grew. By the time ancient
Egypt came around, beer wasn't something
people made for fun. It was woven into
everything. Workers who built the
pyramids were paid in beer, about 4 to 5
L a day. That was their actual salary,
not coins, not grain, but beer. And it
made sense because the water from the
Nile was often contaminated and unsafe
to drink straight. But beer, because of
the brewing process, was cleaner. So it
kept people alive in a way water
couldn't. Honestly, if you were working
in the desert heat and someone gave you
a choice between a bag of coins or 5 L
of cold beer, what are you picking?
>> [clears throat]
>> Yeah, same. And on top of that, the
brewing process added calories and
nutrients. For a laborer dragging
limestone blocks in the desert heat,
those extra calories mattered. Beer
wasn't just a drink, it was lunch. And
then there was the religious side. The
Egyptians believed beer was created by
Osiris and given to humans as a gift. It
showed up in temple offerings, burial
rituals, and medical prescriptions.
Doctors would mix herbs into beer and
prescribe it for everything from stomach
problems to infections. So one single
drink was doing the job of a paycheck, a
water filter, a meal, a medicine, and a
prayer all from the same cup. So here's
the full picture. 10 million years ago,
your ancestors were drawn to fermented
fruit because it helped them find food.
13,000 years ago, they were deliberately
brewing in caves before they knew how to
farm. 12,000 years ago, they were
possibly building the first monuments in
human history just to have a place to
drink together. 9,000 years ago, they
had recipes. 5,000 years ago, entire
civilizations were running on it.
Alcohol didn't come after we built the
world we live in. There's a real
possibility that it's the reason we
built it at all. Every time you have a
drink, you're continuing something that
started before your species had a name
for itself. The process changed, the
ingredients improved, the cups got
fancier, but the impulse is the same one
that made a small primate reach for a
piece of overripe fruit on a forest
floor 10 million years ago. We just
learned how to make it on purpose. If
you want to dig deeper into any of this,
all the research is linked down in the
description.

actor_text:
When did ancient humans start drinking alcohol? 
The answer goes back way further than you'd expect — not thousands, but millions of years. Our relationship with alcohol didn't begin with the invention of wine or the first brewery. It started on a forest floor in Africa, ten million years ago, when a small primate picked up a piece of fruit that had been sitting on the ground too long.

This video traces the full history of alcohol — from fermented fruit to the Natufian caves of Israel, the mysterious stone monuments of Göbekli Tepe in Turkey, the world's oldest recipe in ancient China, and the civilization-powering beer of ancient Egypt. By the end, you might start seeing your next drink a little differently.

All research and sources are linked below.

————————————————————

📚 RESEARCH & SOURCES:

▸ Robert Dudley — "The Drunken Monkey: Why We Drink and Abuse Alcohol" (2014, UC Press) https://www.ucpress.edu/book/97805202...

▸ Raqefet Cave Discovery — "Fermented beverage and food storage in 13,000 y-old stone mortars at Raqefet Cave, Israel" (2018, Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports) https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jasrep.2018...

▸ Patrick McGovern — "Fermented beverages of pre- and proto-historic China" (2004, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences) https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0407921102

▸ Patrick McGovern — "Uncorking the Past: The Quest for Wine, Beer, and Other Alcoholic Beverages" (UC Press) https://www.ucpress.edu/book/97805202...

▸ Göbekli Tepe — Archaeological evidence for fermented grain in large stone vessels at the site (German Archaeological Institute, Oliver Dietrich et al.)

▸ Ancient Egypt — Beer rations for pyramid workers at Giza, archaeological evidence from excavations near the Giza Plateau

————————————————————

PEOPLE MENTIONED IN THIS VIDEO:

▸ Robert Dudley — Professor of Integrative Biology, University of California, Berkeley. Author of "The Drunken Monkey" hypothesis, which proposes that human attraction to alcohol evolved from our primate ancestors' preference for fermenting fruit.

▸ Patrick McGovern — Archaeochemist at the University of Pennsylvania Museum of Archaeology and Anthropology. Leading expert on ancient fermented beverages. Author of "Uncorking the Past" and "Ancient Brews." His research identified the world's oldest known alcohol recipe at Jiahu, China (7000 BCE) and he has long argued that humans began farming to make beer, not bread.

description:
Why Time Feels Faster As You Get Older. 
The Science Behind It

Have you ever wondered why childhood summers felt like they lasted forever, but entire years now disappear in what feels like weeks? You're not imagining it. There's real science behind why time seems to speed up as you age — and it has nothing to do with being busy.

In this video, we break down the two mechanisms inside your brain that control how you experience time — and why both of them start working against you the older you get.

What you'll learn:
→ Why a single summer at age 8 can feel longer than your entire 27th year
→ The "neural clock" theory and how your brain's processing speed changes over a lifetime
→ Adrian Bejan's 2019 Duke University research on neural signal transmission and aging
→ Why your brain consumes 66% of your body's calories at age 5
→ The proportional theory of time — and why it falls apart under scrutiny
→ How novelty and memory density reshape your perception of the past
→ The time paradox: why fun moments feel short but leave long memories
→ What you can actually do to slow time down

Research referenced in this video:

details, not what you ate or what shoes
you wore, but that feeling. June
stretched out ahead of you like an
ocean. Every single day had weight to
it. You could live an entire life
between breakfast and dinner. You
remember lying in the grass watching
clouds for what felt like hours, and it
still wasn't enough to fill the day. Now
you're an adult, and somehow yesterday
was March, and right now it's already
June. You blinked and an entire season
vanished. Whole months dissolve before
you even register they've started.
Everybody keeps saying this, "Where did
the time go?" The time didn't go
anywhere. Your brain did. The most
common explanation people give for this
is mathematical. It's called the
proportional theory. When you're 5 years
old, 1 year is 20% of your entire
existence. That's massive. A single
summer at that age makes up a
significant chunk of everything you've
ever experienced. But when you're 50, 1
year is just 2% of your life. So, each
year should feel proportionally smaller
compared to the growing total behind it.

Intuitively, it makes sense. A year does
mean more when you haven't lived many of
them. But the theory starts to collapse
when you push on it even slightly. If
you actually plot this out, 1 year as a
percentage of your life at every age,
and add up the total perceived time
underneath that curve, you'll find that
by age 6, half of your entire subjective
life is already gone, before you can
even read. No 6-year-old on Earth walks
around feeling like the best part is
behind them. The proportional theory
treats your brain like a calculator
running simple division. But your brain
doesn't do math with time. It does
something far more complicated. Your
brain has an internal clock. It's an
actual timing mechanism built from the
firing rate of your neurons, the speed
at which electrical signals travel
through your nervous system, and
neuroscientists have been measuring this
speed for decades. And what they found
is consistent. The firing of your
neurons peaks in childhood. Then it
begins to decline year after year for
the rest of your life. When you were
young, your neurons fired rapidly, which
meant your brain was capturing more
snapshots of the world per second. More
data points packed into every passing
moment. Your brain was essentially over
sampling reality. And because it was
processing more information per second,
each second felt fuller, heavier,
longer. As you age, the clock slows
down. Your neurons fire less frequently.
The same external hour passes, but your
brain captures fewer moments within it.
The world hasn't sped up. Your sampling
rate has dropped. In 2019, Adrian Bejan,
a professor of mechanical engineering at
Duke University, published a paper that
put hard physics behind this.
He measured how the speed of neural
signal transmission changes over a
lifetime and found something
straightforward. As we age, the pathways
those signals travel through become
longer and more complex. Each impulse
takes slightly more time to reach its
destination.

older brain processes fewer mental

outside keeps moving at the same pace it
always has, but the brain is sampling

The Science Behind It

Have you ever wondered why childhood summers felt like they lasted forever, but entire years now disappear in what feels like weeks? You're not imagining it. There's real science behind why time seems to speed up as you age — and it has nothing to do with being busy.

In this video, we break down the two mechanisms inside your brain that control how you experience time — and why both of them start working against you the older you get.

What you'll learn:
→ Why a single summer at age 8 can feel longer than your entire 27th year
→ The "neural clock" theory and how your brain's processing speed changes over a lifetime
→ Adrian Bejan's 2019 Duke University research on neural signal transmission and aging
→ Why your brain consumes 66% of your body's calories at age 5
→ The proportional theory of time — and why it falls apart under scrutiny
→ How novelty and memory density reshape your perception of the past
→ The time paradox: why fun moments feel short but leave long memories
→ What you can actually do to slow time down

description:
What did ancient humans do when they got sick—before hospitals, antibiotics, or modern medicine existed? In this fascinating deep dive, we explore how prehistoric humans, early civilizations, and ancient healers treated illness using nature, rituals, herbs, surgery, and survival instincts. From Stone Age remedies to Ancient Egyptian medicine, Ayurvedic healing, Chinese herbal practices, and tribal shamans, this video uncovers the surprising origins of healthcare and how early humans fought disease thousands of years ago.

The last time you got sick, you probably
did what everyone does. You opened Chat
GPT, searched your symptoms online. You
took something from the medicine
cabinet. Maybe you called a doctor.
Maybe you just spent three miserable
days on the couch rewatching something
you'd already seen before. But either
way, you understood what was happening
to you. You had some idea of what to do
next. For most of human history, you had
none of that. No name, no plan, no
medicine cabinet, no understanding of
what was happening inside your body.
Just pain, fever, weakness, and your
body failing in ways you couldn't
explain. And yet, people still survived.
They still raised children, built
communities, and eventually entire
civilizations. So, what did they
actually do when they got sick? The
answer is stranger, more creative, and
far more human than you'd expect. Let's
go back, way back. For the first 200,000
years of our existence, modern medicine
didn't exist. Humans had no idea that
invisible microscopic organisms were
responsible for making them feel like
they were dying. From their perspective,
illness appeared almost supernatural.
There was no visible wound, no predator,
no obvious cause. One day you were fine,
and the next your own body seemed to
turn against you from the inside. So,
ancient humans came to the only
conclusion that made sense to them. The
Sumerians believed illness was caused by
demons. Ancient Egyptians believed it
was punishment from the gods. Indigenous
cultures across every continent
developed similar ideas.
The body was seen as a vessel, sickness
as an intrusion, and healing as the
removal of whatever had entered inside.
At first, this sounds primitive, but
here's the fascinating part. They
weren't completely wrong. The
explanation was wrong, but the instinct
behind it was surprisingly close to the
truth. Ancient humans just didn't know
it was bacteria, viruses, or parasites.
It would take another 200,000 years for
us to finally understand what was
actually making people sick. But in the
meantime, humans got creative. The
earliest healers weren't doctors in the
modern sense. They were the people who
were the doctors of that era, who
believed they could communicate with
whatever force was causing the illness
and convince it to leave. Archaeological
evidence for this goes back at least
40,000 years. Burial sites from that era
show people with severe injuries and
disabilities that should have made
survival impossible alone. Crushed
bones, missing limbs, conditions that
would have prevented hunting or even
moving properly. And yet, many of those
injuries healed, which means those
people survived long after being
injured. Someone was feeding them,
protecting them, keeping them alive
while they recovered. Even before
medicine existed, humans were already
trying to heal each other. The oldest
surgical procedure we know of is
trepanation, drilling a hole in the
skull. We have skulls from 10,000 years
ago with clean, deliberate holes bored
through the bone. And here's the part
that stops you cold. The bone had healed
around the edges, meaning the patient
survived, meaning someone 10,000 years
ago cut open a human skull with a stone
tool, and the person lived long enough
afterward for their bone to start
growing back. We don't know exactly why
they performed trepanation. The most
common theory is that they believed
something was trapped inside the head.
Not because they understood neuroscience
or biology, but because humans are
incredibly persistent. They
experimented, improvised, and kept
trying things that should have been
impossible to survive. That's what
ancient humans did when they got sick.
They improvised on the edge of death.
But healing wasn't only spiritual, not
even close. Because while shamans
performed rituals and skulls were
drilled in desperate attempts to cure
suffering, something else was happening
quietly in the background. Something
less dramatic, but far more important in
the long run. Humans were observing,
remembering, passing knowledge from one
generation to the next. Not through
myths, but through experience. They
began noticing that certain plants
actually changed how sick bodies felt.
Some reduced pain, some lowered fevers,
some helped wounds heal. Ancient humans
discovered that certain plants did
specific things to sick bodies. Willow
bark reduced fever. We know this because
ancient Egyptian medical texts from 1500
BCE specifically recommended. Willow
bark contains salicin, which your body
converts into salicylic acid, which is
the active compound in aspirin. They
didn't understand the science behind it.
They just knew it worked. So, they kept
using it, passed it down, refined it,
and years later we extracted the
compound, synthesized it, put it in a
white tablet, and sold it in every
pharmacy on Earth. The molecule is the
same. The knowledge is 100,000 years
old. Turmeric, garlic, honey, ginger,
echinacea, every single one of these has
a long history of documented medical
use. Ancient humans were observing
outcomes, remembering what worked, and
passing that knowledge forward from
generation to generation. But, this is
where the story gets more complicated
because not everything ancient humans
did actually worked. And strangely,
those failures reveal just as much about
us as the successes do. When a fever
wouldn't break, when the plants failed,
when the ceremonies changed nothing,
people turned to something else. Ritual,
repetition, and community. They gathered
around the sick. They sang. They prayed.
They stayed awake through the night
beside them. They refused to let sick
people suffer alone. And without
realizing it, some of those actions were
genuinely affecting the body. Social
support can lower stress hormones.
Feeling cared for can reduce pain. Even
the belief that help is coming can
create measurable biological changes
inside the body. The placebo effect is
not imaginary. It is a real, documented,
consistently reproducible medical
phenomenon. And ancient humans had
discovered ways to trigger it tens of
thousands of years before anyone
understood what it was. Sometimes
healing came from medicine. Sometimes it
came from presence, ritual, and the
feeling that you weren't facing
suffering alone. Collective belief and
emotional support were creating real
effects inside the body, even if people
at the time had no scientific
explanation for it. And the truth is,
modern medicine never fully replaced
that. Modern medicine is extraordinary.
Antibiotics, surgery, vaccines, machines
that let us see inside the human body
without opening it. We have treatments
today that would have looked like
miracles to almost every human who lived
before the 20th century. But even with
all of that, one thing hasn't changed.
Research consistently shows that
patients who feel genuinely cared for
often recover better than those who
receive the same treatment but feel
ignored or unseen. Doctors who spend
more time with patients tend to get
better outcomes regardless of the
medication they prescribe, because
healing was never just about the
treatment itself. The care surrounding
it matters, too. Ancient humans
understood something we still keep
rediscovering today. Underneath all the
rituals, plant remedies, shamans, and
desperate medical experiments was one
simple idea. They refused to do nothing.
For 300,000 years, the human response to
illness was never just surrender. It was
resistance. People refused to sit back
and watch each other die without trying
something. Every culture in every era
created its own ways of fighting
disease. Some of those methods were
completely wrong, sometimes even
dangerous. But the impulse behind them
mattered, the refusal to accept that a
person should simply die from something
invisible and unexplained. That impulse
is the reason medicine exists at all.
Think about what your ancestors survived
without any of the things you rely on
today. No antibiotics, no vaccines, no
hospitals. People could literally trip,
get a small cut, and die a week later
from infection. A bad tooth could turn
into a death sentence. Childbirth was
terrifyingly dangerous. Even drinking
water from the wrong place could fill
your body with parasites or disease.
Measles, smallpox, cholera, the flu
alone wiped out millions. Humans spent
most of history surviving things that
sound almost ridiculous today. And the
only reason many of those diseases no
longer terrify us is because generation
after generation kept experimenting,
learning, and trying to heal each other
instead of giving up. And humanity
didn't even discover bacteria until the
1670s when Anthony Van Leeuwenhoek
looked through a microscope and saw
microscopic life for the first time.
Before that, humans had spent hundreds
of thousands of years fighting enemies
they literally couldn't see.
So, if all of those people hadn't kept
trying,
would you even be here today?

transcript_plaintext:
You've built something. Maybe it was a
bookshelf. Maybe it was a terrible
bookshelf with wobbly legs, one screw
left over that you still can't explain.
And yet the moment it was done,
you looked at it and thought, "That's
actually pretty good." That feeling that
you get has a name and it's quietly
controlling more of your life than you
realize. In 2011, three behavioral
scientists ran a study.
They gave one group of people an origami
frog to look at. They gave another group
the paper and instructions to fold one
themselves.
Then they asked both groups how much
they'd pay for it. The people who built
it valued it almost five times higher.
Same frog, same paper, completely
different price in their heads. They
called it the IKEA effect. The more
effort you put into something, the more
you love it. Not because it's better,
it's because you made it. Here's why
this happens. Your brain doesn't just
track what things are worth. It tracks
what things cost you.
Time, effort, frustration, focus. Your
brain treats all of that as investment.
And once you've invested, your mind does
something automatic. It starts
protecting that investment. It inflates
the value of what you made to justify
the effort you spent.
Just like this video. I made this myself
for you. To anyone else, it's just
another random video on the internet.
But because I invested my time, my
energy, my frustration into it, it means
something different to me.
I can't see it the way you see it.
That's just the IKEA effect running
silently in the background.
Psychologists call this effort
justification, and it runs deep. In the
1950s, researcher Elliot Aronson found
that people who went through a difficult
initiation to join a group rated that
group as significantly more valuable
than people who joined it easily.
Nothing about the group changed, only
the cost of getting in. Your brain
genuinely cannot separate effort from
worth. The harder something was, the
better it must be. That's not logic.
That's just how we're wired. And it's
everywhere once you see it. The student
who spends three weeks writing a thesis
believes it more deeply than one they
wrote overnight. The entrepreneur who
sacrifices for two years to build a
company can't see its flaws clearly. The
parent who struggles through a difficult
first year with a child forms a bond so
fierce, it borders on irrational. None
of that is a mistake. That's the IKEA
effect doing exactly what it was built
to do. Because here's the thing, for
most of human history, you had to make
everything yourself. Your food, your
shelter, your tools, your clothes. If
you made something badly, you didn't
romanticize it. You fixed it or you
died. The effort you put in was directly
tied to your survival.
So your brain evolved to reward that
effort with attachment, with pride, with
a value signal that said, "Protect this.
You worked for it." The problem is, we
live in 2025.
You don't need to make anything anymore.
Everything comes assembled, delivered,
instant. But your brain hasn't updated.
It still runs that old code. So when you
finally do build something with your
hands, even a flat-pack bookshelf with a
missing dowel, the ancient reward system
fires. And it doesn't care that IKEA did
90% of the work. You held the Allen key.
That's enough. But the IKEA effect has a
shadow side. Because the same mechanism
that makes you love what you build also
makes you blind to its flaws. The
researchers found that people who built
their origami frog rated it just as
highly as professionally made origami,
even when it was objectively worse.
Effort doesn't just inflate value, it
switches off your critical eye. This is
why founders can't kill bad products.
Why people stay in relationships they
built from something broken. Why
governments pour money into failing
projects they already spent billions on.
You don't just love the thing, you love
the version of yourself that made it.
There's a reason IKEA doesn't fully
assemble their furniture before shipping
it. It's not just cheaper, it's smarter.
They're selling you something more
valuable than a bookshelf.
They're selling you the feeling of
having built it.
And the moment you tighten that last
bolt and step back, that wobbly,
slightly uneven bookshelf becomes yours
in a way that no store-bought shelf ever
could. Not because it's better, because
part of you is in it now, and your brain
will never let you see it clearly again.

description:
The Real Reason Humans Started Wearing Clothes?

Tonight, when you look down at what you're wearing, you probably won't think twice about it. But clothing is one of the strangest things humans do — and for 99.9% of animal species on Earth, it makes absolutely no sense.
Every other creature survives naked. So why don't we?
The answer isn't warmth. It isn't modesty. And it definitely isn't what you learned in school.
In this video, we uncover the real reason humans started wearing clothes — and it reveals something deeply strange about what it means to be human.
We discuss:
The Lice Timeline: How scientists used parasite DNA to discover humans were wearing clothes 170,000 years ago — long before they needed to for warmth.
The Cognition Theory: Why archaeologist Ian Gilligan argues that clothing wasn't a survival tool — it was proof that the human brain had crossed a threshold no other animal ever has.
The Shame Discovery: The neurological reason we cover ourselves that has nothing to do with temperature, and everything to do with being seen.
The Social Technology: How clothing became the world's oldest communication system — telling strangers who you were before you ever spoke a word.
If you've ever felt anxiety about wearing the wrong thing to the wrong place, the truth is fascinating: that feeling isn't shallow — it's 170,000 years old.

probably didn't think about that
decision for more than a few seconds
this morning. Maybe you grabbed whatever
was closest. Maybe you checked the
weather. Either way, you put something
on before you walked out the door,
because that's what humans do. We cover
ourselves. Every culture on Earth, in
every climate, across every era of
recorded history, wears clothes. You
might think early humans started wearing
clothes for simple reasons: modesty,
protection, warmth. Except none of those
are the real reason we started covering
ourselves. And when you find out what
actually drove early humans to cover
their bodies, it changes how you think
about fashion, culture, language, and
what it means to be the kind of creature
that looks in a mirror and feels the
weight of being seen. Let's look at the
timeline. Anatomically modern humans
have been around for roughly 300,000
years, but when you look at the actual
evidence, you'll find things like bone
needles and hide scraping tools only
showing up around 120,000 years ago. And
even that estimate is generous. Most
textile historians place the widespread
adoption of clothing at around 75,000
years ago, which means for the first
half of our existence, we were mostly
naked under the same African sun,
dealing with thorns, insects, and cold
nights with nothing but our naked
bodies. Which immediately rules out the
most common explanation: warmth. Yes,
humans eventually moved into colder
climates where clothing became
essential. But clothing shows up before
that, while we were still in the
tropics. So warmth matters later. The
next explanation people reach for is
protection: thorns, rocks, insect bites.

the issue. If protection were the main
reason, clothing would have started on
the parts that actually took the most
damage: feet and hands. Instead, the
earliest clothing in almost every
culture covered the torso and groin
first, the areas least exposed. That's
not purely practical. It points to
something else. Then there's the lice
theory, and this one's actually
fascinating. Back in 2003, a group of
geneticists looked at something
unexpected: lice. Not just any lice, but
the split between head lice and body
lice. Head lice live in hair, body lice
live in clothing. They literally can't
survive without fabric. So, scientists
traced when these two types split from
each other, and that gives a clue about
when humans started wearing clothes
consistently enough for a whole new
species to depend on it. The answer,
approximately 170,000 years ago. That's
the oldest hard biological timestamp we
have for clothing. Not some bone needle
or a scraping tool, but because of a
parasite. And that gives a clue when
humans started wearing clothes, partly
because something evolved specifically
to live in them. But that date still
doesn't tell us why. It tells us when
the behavior was already established.
The actual origin goes back further than
we can currently measure. The reason
lies somewhere deeper than fabric and
needles and lice. Here's what
researchers have started to argue.
Clothing wasn't a practical invention,
it was a symbolic one. In 2009,
archaeologist Ian Gilligan published a
detailed analysis about clothing and how
we think. He suggested that choosing to
cover the body isn't just practical. It
reflects a deeper kind of thinking that
sets humans apart from other animals. To
wear clothing, you have to imagine a
future version of yourself. You look at
an animal hide, picture yourself wearing
it later, plan how to turn it into
something usable, and then actually do
it. That might sound simple, but it's
not. It involves memory, planning ahead,
and thinking about the future. The same
kind of mental ability we use to keep
promises, plan our days, or worry about
things that haven't even happened yet.
No other animal does this. A chimpanzee
doesn't look at a leaf and think about
how it could be useful tomorrow, but we
did. And the moment we started clothing
our bodies, we weren't just protecting
skin. We were demonstrating for the
first time that we could think ahead.

artifacts of the modern human mind. But
there's something even deeper underneath
that. Something most evolutionary
biologists don't talk about when this
topic comes up, which is shame. And not
in the religious sense. Shame in the
neurological sense. The awareness of
being perceived. The feeling that your
body is being observed and evaluated by
others. This is a uniquely human
experience. It requires what
psychologists call theory of mind, the
ability to step outside yourself and
imagine what you look like through
someone else's eyes. Dogs don't have
this. Crows don't have this. Even our
closest relatives, chimpanzees, barely
show traces of it. But somewhere along
the way, humans developed something
deeper, the ability to see ourselves
through other people's eyes, and once
that clicked, everything shifted. It
wasn't just about surviving anymore. It
became about how you looked, how you
were perceived, what you signaled to
others. From that point on, clothing
wasn't just about covering up. It became
a way to shape identity, a way to
control your image. The first person who
wrapped animal skin around themselves
wasn't just trying to stay warm. They
were, in a sense, choosing how they
wanted to be seen. And once that idea
took hold, it never really went away.
You can see it across cultures all over
the world, even in places where clothing
wasn't needed for warmth at all, like
parts of the Amazon or the Pacific
Islands. People still decorated
themselves. Beads, paint, feathers,
simple fibers, tattoos, something was
always there, because the body was never
just a body. Because researchers
studying clothing across different
cultures have found something
consistent. The impulse to dress seems
to accelerate during periods when human
social groups are becoming more complex.
As tribes grew larger, as hierarchies
formed, as strangers started interacting
with strangers, clothing became a social
technology, a system of instant
communication. Before you could speak to
someone, their clothing told you who
they were, what group they belonged to,
whether they were a threat or an ally,
whether they ranked above or below you.
Clothing is language, one of the oldest
forms we have. And here's the part that
should make you stop for a second,
because it applies to you right now. You
get dressed every morning without
thinking much about it, but your brain
is doing something ancient and deeply
social every time you do.
You're not just picking fabric. You're
constructing a version of yourself that
you want to project into the world.
You're negotiating between who you are,
who you want to be seen as, and what the
situation requires. That anxiety you
feel when you show up to something
overdressed or underdressed, or when you
realize you're wearing the wrong thing
for the moment, that's 170,000 years of
social cognition activating. That's your
brain running the same calculation your
ancestors ran around the fire. We solved
the basics, cold, survival, protection,
but we didn't stop. Our clothing became
more detailed, more intentional, because
it was never just about the body. It was
about the mind. The part of us that
knows we're being watched. Clothing
didn't just cover us, it created a
version of us. We didn't start wearing
clothes because we were cold. We started
because we became aware. Aware that
others could see us, and that never
stopped. Tomorrow you'll get dressed
like always, but underneath that routine
something ancient is still there. You're
not just picking clothes, you're
choosing how to be seen. The same
instinct humans have had for thousands
of years.

description:
Discover why white paint remains the standard for desert architecture to keep buildings cool in intense heat. This breakdown explains the science behind the practice.

We examine how the color of a structure impacts its interior temperature and why lighter surfaces are superior for heat reflection. By comparing the thermal efficiency of various building finishes, we show how simple, traditional methods effectively manage sunlight absorption without relying on modern electricity.

Understanding these techniques offers a clear look at how passive cooling relies on basic physics to create comfortable living environments. Whether you are interested in historical building methods or sustainable design, this analysis clarifies why this architectural choice persists in hot climates around the world.

blinding white. From the tumbling
cliffside towns of the Greek Islands to

pure radiant white, cascading down

most beautiful sights in the world and

white walls against a deep blue sky. But
here's the thing, these villages weren't

survival. Every one of those white walls
is the visible result of a whole set of
clever practical solutions to the brutal

people really painted everything white,

technology humans ever devised, hiding
in plain sight, disguised as a postcard.

when sunlight hits a surface. That
sunlight carries energy and when it
strikes something, that energy has to go
somewhere. A dark surface absorbs most
of that light energy and absorbed light
turns into heat. This is why a black car

shirt on a summer day makes you feel
like you're baking. Dark colors soak up
the sun's energy and heat up
dramatically, but a white surface does

energy away instead of absorbing it. And

regions, homes were originally built of
stone or mud brick, often dark,
heat-absorbing materials that turned

brilliant. They coated the outside of
their homes in white. And that white

before the heat could ever soak into the
walls. It was like giving every house a
shield against the sun. The difference
this makes is genuinely significant. A
white-painted building can stay
meaningfully cooler inside than a dark
one, purely because of the reflected
sunlight. In a world without electric
cooling, this wasn't a small luxury. It
was the difference between a home that
was livable in the summer heat and one
that was not. By painting their villages
white, these people were engineering
their entire environment to bounce the
sun's energy away and keep their homes
cool. Using nothing but a coat of
light-colored coating. It's passive
cooling in its purest, simplest form,
and it works so well that scientists
today are seriously exploring painting
roofs and even whole cities white or
reflective as a way to fight rising
temperatures. These ancient villages
figured it out thousands of years ago,
but here's where the story gets richer,

white paint. The traditional white
coating used in so many of these
villages was something specific,
something cheap, and something with
almost magical extra properties. It was

understanding what limewash actually is

mystery. Limewash is made from lime,

crucially, in many of these hot, dry
regions, limestone was abundant and
cheap, sometimes even a byproduct of
local quarrying. This mattered
enormously. These were often not wealthy
communities. They needed a way to
protect and coat their homes that
ordinary people could actually afford,
using materials that were locally
available. And limewash fit perfectly.

stone mixed with water, and it could be
applied by anyone, brushed onto walls
again and again. It was, in effect, the
perfect people's paint. Cheap,
accessible, easy to make, and easy to
use. That affordability is a huge part
of why entire villages, not just the
homes of the rich, ended up coated in
white. Everyone could afford limewash.

sun. It did something else, something
that turned out to be life-saving.

mildly antibacterial. When you coat your
walls in limewash, you're not just
painting them white. You're actually
sanitizing them, killing bacteria, and
helping to prevent the spread of
disease. And in the days before modern
medicine, before antibiotics and
hospitals, and our understanding of
germs, this was an enormous benefit,
even if people didn't fully understand
the science behind why it worked. This
disinfectant power became critically
important during outbreaks of disease.

people were desperate for anything that
might stop the spread. And whitewashing

cleansing the community and fighting
back against invisible killers. This is

white. It wasn't only about the heat, it
was about health, about survival against

real sense, a coat of protection against

beyond individual choice and became

in the 20th century, during a period of

country, especially in the island
villages, precisely because limewash was

could help control the disease. So, some
of the most famously white villages in

ordinary people could afford. And it

reinforced the others, and together they
made whitewashing an obvious,

regions of the world. When something is

healthy all at once, of course you're

there are a few other threads woven into

the white walls and the practice of
painting things white carried other

alongside the white, these villages
frequently feature accents of blue on

of this is practical and a part
cultural. The blue was sometimes made
from a cheap laundry blueing product
that households already had, mixed into

together became a beloved traditional

coat of white could take on many layers
of meaning. The core reasons though

part of the rhythm of life in these
villages. Limewash isn't permanent like
modern paint. It weathers and fades over
time, so it had to be reapplied
regularly, often once or several times a
year. And so whitewashing became a
ritual, a recurring communal act of
renewal. Families would refresh the
white on their homes, keeping the
village gleaming, maintaining both its
coolness and its cleanliness. Over
generations, this constant renewal kept
these places brilliantly, perpetually
white, and wove the color deep into the
identity and the yearly rhythm of the
community. The white wasn't a one-time
decision. It was a living practice,
renewed again and again by the hands of
the people who lived there. So when you
put it all together, you see that the
dazzling white of these sun-drenched
villages was never really about beauty,
at least not originally. It was one of
the most elegant survival strategies
humans ever devised, a convergence of
physics, economics, and medicine, all
expressed in a single coat of white. The
white reflected the punishing sun and
kept homes bearable in brutal heat
without any technology or energy at all.
It was made from cheap, abundant lime
that even the poorest families could
afford and apply themselves. It
disinfected homes and helped hold back
the deadly diseases that once swept
through these communities. And it
became, over time, a cherished tradition
renewed year after year until it grew
into the very identity of these places.
That's the beautiful irony at the heart
of this. The tourists who now flock to
these gleaming white villages, snapping
photographs of those perfect walls
against the blue sky, are admiring what
they see as pure aesthetic magic. But
what they're really looking at is
ancient survival technology. Every white
wall is a sun shield, a disinfectant, an
affordable solution born of hard
necessity. These communities didn't set
out to build some of the most beautiful
places on Earth. They set out to survive
the heat, to stop disease, and to
protect their families with the cheap
materials they had at hand. And in doing
so, almost by accident, they created a
beauty so striking that people travel
across the world just to witness it.
It's a perfect reminder that so much of
what we find beautiful in the world
began as something intensely practical.
Those white villages are what happens
when human ingenuity meets a harsh
environment. When people with almost
nothing find a clever way to reflect the
sun, fight disease, and endure. And the
stunning beauty we see today is simply
the visible signature of that ingenuity.
Thousands of walls painted white over
and over by generations of people who
were, more than anything, just trying to
keep cool, stay healthy, and survive
beneath a relentless sun. So, the next
time you see one of those breathtaking
white villages glowing under a hot blue
sky, look a little closer. You're not
just looking at something beautiful.

smartest survival tricks in human
history hiding in plain sight, disguised
as a postcard.

transcript_plaintext:
There was a killer in the trenches of
the First World War that took more men
out of the fight in some winters than
enemy bullets did. It didn't explode. It
made no sound. It crept up through the
soles of your boots while you slept, and
by the time you felt it, your feet were
already rotting on your legs. It could
cost you your toes, your feet, sometimes
your life. And the terrifying part was
that it struck when temperatures weren't
even at their worst, in cold that felt
merely miserable rather than deadly.
Millions of soldiers had to figure out
how to sleep night after night in
freezing, flooded, filthy trenches
without letting the cold quietly destroy
their bodies. How they did it is a grim,
brilliant, and genuinely surprising
story of survival. And it comes down to
a strange list of weapons including
grease made from whales, planks of wood,
and the feet of the man sleeping next to
you. To understand how they survived,
you first have to understand exactly
what they were fighting because it
wasn't only frostbite. There were two
cold enemies in that trench, and they
were different. Frostbite is the one
most people know. It strikes in genuine
freezing cold when the temperature drops
below freezing and the water inside a
person's flesh literally starts to turn
to ice, killing the tissue. In the
brutal winters on the Western Front,
especially the notoriously bitter winter
of 1916, temperatures plunged low enough
that soldiers' clothes froze solid and
frostbite claimed fingers, toes, ears,
and noses. But the second enemy was
sneakier and in many ways worse, and it
had a name born in that very war, trench
foot. And here's what made it so
dangerous. Trench foot didn't need
freezing temperatures at all. It struck
in conditions that were merely cold and
wet, above freezing but relentlessly
damp. When a soldier's feet stayed cold
and soaked inside his boots for hours
and days on end, unable to dry, the
blood vessels in his feet began to
constrict and the circulation shut down.
The foot would go numb, then swell, then
the skin would begin to break down. In
the worst cases, it turned to gangrene
and the foot had to be amputated. And
the cruelest part was that a soldier
often couldn't even feel it happening.
Men described how their feet were simply
cold and numb in the trench, giving no
warning. And it was only when they
finally got out of the line and pulled
off their boots that their feet would
swell up horribly and the agony would
begin. Some pulled off their boots to
find their feet ruined. So, the enemy
the soldiers were sleeping against every
night was this combination, the freezing
cold that could give them frostbite and
the endless cold soaking wet that could
give them trench foot. And they were
trying to sleep in the worst possible
place to fight either one. A trench was
often a ditch of freezing mud with water
pooling at the bottom, sometimes rising
to the knee, walls of cold wet earth on
either side, and the open sky above
raining and snowing down on them. Given
all that, the fact that any of them kept
their feet at all is a testament to a
whole system of survival tricks they
developed, sometimes at horrific cost
over the years of the war. The first and
most important battle was the fight to
stay dry because dampness was the real
killer, especially for trench foot. And
the single most important weapon in that
fight was a simple wooden plank.
Engineers built what were called
duckboards, slatted wooden walkways laid
along the bottom of the trench. These
raised the men up several inches above
the freezing water and mud pooling
below, giving them a slightly drier
surface to stand, walk, and rest on. To
manage the water itself, they dug
drainage channels and pits at the bottom
of the trench called sumps to collect
the water, and pumping stations were set
up to physically pump the flooding out
of the deeper positions. It was a
constant, losing, but essential battle
against the water. Every inch a man
could get above that freezing slop was
an inch of protection for his feet.
Soldiers learned to step carefully along
the duckboards because a single misstep
into a hole could plunge a foot back
into the icy water. But feet still got
wet, inevitably. And this is where one
of the strangest survival tools of the
war came in, whale oil. The greasy oil
rendered from whales became standard
issue for troops in the winter trenches,
and the soldiers were ordered to rub it
directly onto their feet before pulling
on their socks. Why? Because the grease
formed a water-resistant barrier over
the skin, helping to seal out the wet
and preserve the skin, keeping the feet
from breaking down as fast in the
constant damp. It sounds bizarre,
coating your feet in whale grease before
bed, but it genuinely helped protect
against trench foot. Soldiers went
through enormous quantities of the
stuff. Rubbing whale oil into your feet
became a nightly ritual of survival. And
then, there were the socks, which became
almost sacred. Keeping the feet dry
meant changing wet socks for dry ones as
often as possible. And soldiers were
constantly urged to do this. Dry socks
were precious, and men kept spare pairs
tucked inside their coats against their
bodies to keep them dry and warm with
body heat, ready to swap out. Families
back home knitted endless socks for the
troops precisely because dry socks saved
feet. A soldier might peel off a soaked
freezing sock, dry his foot as best he
could, rub in the whale oil, and pull on
a dry pair. And that simple act,
repeated whenever possible, was one of
the most effective defenses against
losing his feet. But here's the thing
about a numb, freezing foot. You often
can't feel that it's in danger. A man
alone might not notice his own feet
slowly dying. And so, the army came up
with one of the most clever and human
solutions of the entire war. They made
it someone else's job to check. Soldiers
were paired up, and each man was made
responsible for the feet of his partner.
This was the buddy system, and it was
mandatory. Your friend inspected your
feet, and you inspected his, looking for
the telltale signs of trench foot. The
numbness, the swelling, the
discoloration that you might miss or
ignore on your own. This simple idea,
making foot care a shared duty between
two men rather than leaving it to each
individual, turned out to be one of the
most effective measures of all. When
trench foot stopped being treated as
just a medical problem and became a
discipline that officers enforced and
buddies checked, the rates of it dropped
dramatically. The feet of the man next
to you were, quite literally, your
responsibility, and yours were his. So,
that was the fight for the feet. But, a
soldier trying to sleep also had to keep
the rest of his body from freezing. And
here, they layered every scrap of warmth
they could find. Men on woolen garments,
thick greatcoats, and wrapped scarves
tight around themselves. Wool was the
key material because wool has a
remarkable property. It can still trap
warmth and insulate even when it's damp,
unlike many other fabrics. Later in the
war, soldiers were issued sheepskin
coats and leather jerkins for extra
insulation against the biting cold. The
goal was to trap a layer of warm air
against the body, and layers of wool did
that better than anything else they had.
Even so, their clothing often soaked
through within hours, and staying warm
was a constant struggle. For actual
sleep, the safest place was below ground
in a dugout. These were shelters carved
into the walls or floor of the trench,
shored up with timber, and sometimes
roofed with corrugated iron. Dug into
the earth, a dugout was protected from
the wind, the rain, and the snow, and
the surrounding soil gave a little
insulation. This is where men would
retreat to eat and sleep when they
could. Inside, they might light a small
fire or a brazier, a metal container of
burning coke or charcoal, to create a
pocket of warmth underground. But, this
came with a deadly catch, the smoke. A
fire deep in a dugout could fill the
enclosed space with choking, poisonous
fumes, and the smoke rising from the
trench could also give away their
position to the enemy. So, warmth from
fire was a careful, limited, dangerous
luxury, not something they could rely on
freely. Far more reliable was the oldest
heat source of all, each other. Soldiers
huddled together for warmth, packing
close in the dugouts, sharing body heat
against the cold. Several men pressed
together generated and held far more
warmth than any of them could alone. In
the freezing dark, the heat of the man
beside you was often the difference
between a miserable night and a
dangerous one. Inside them, they fought
the cold with whatever warmth they could
put into their bodies. Hot food and hot
drinks were vital, not just for morale,
but for genuine warmth and energy. A hot
meal or a mug of hot tea could put real
heat back into a chilled body. And
famously, soldiers were often issued a
daily ration of rum, a shot of strong
spirit that gave a brief warming glow
and a moment of comfort, and helped
steady the nerves against the cold and
the fear. Warm food and drink from the
inside was another layer in the defense
against the cold. And underlying the
whole system was one final crucial
principle, rotation. No soldier was
meant to stay in the freezing front line
trench indefinitely. The armies rotated
their men, cycling them through the
front line for a period, often just days
at a time in the worst winter
conditions, and then pulling them back
to reserve and rear positions. Back
there, away from the front, they could
finally get warm, dry out their soaked
clothing and boots, properly tend to
their feet, rest, and recover before
rotating forward again. This rotation
was essential because no human body
could endure the freezing, wet front
line conditions endlessly without
breaking down. The chance to dry out and
warm up in the rear was often what
allowed a man's feet and body to recover
before the damage became permanent. So,
when you put it all together, the way
soldiers survived sleeping in those
freezing trenches wasn't one single
trick. It was an entire layered system,
built painfully through trial and error
and terrible suffering. They fought the
water with duckboards, drains, and

Understanding these medical challenges offers a deeper perspective on the daily struggles faced by infantry during the conflict. video_title: How Do Mongolian Nomads Survive Minus 40 Degree Winters in a Tent?
description:
On the open steppe of Mongolia winter temperatures plunge to minus forty degrees. No trees. No towns. No permanent buildings.

And the nomadic herders of Mongolia have lived out there for thousands of years. In a tent.

Inside that tent while it is minus forty outside it can be twenty-five degrees Celsius, warm enough for shirt sleeves.

Thick felt made from sheep's wool wrapping the entire frame, trapping air against the cold. A central iron stove fueled by dried animal dung — free, renewable, and slow-burning in a land with no forests. A perfectly circular shape that lets wind flow around it rather than battering it. A roof opening that handles smoke, ventilation, light, and timekeeping simultaneously.

And completely portable — packed up and moved in hours. A fully insulated home that follows the herds.

to block the wind, which howls unbroken
across a thousand miles of frozen
grassland. There are no towns nearby, no
permanent buildings, no shelter of any
kind out on that vast, empty, white
expanse. It is one of the harshest
inhabited climates on the entire planet,
a place where the cold can kill an
exposed human being with terrifying
speed. And the nomadic herders of

teeth of that cold, for thousands of
years. Not in stone houses, not in
heated buildings, in a tent, a round,
felt-covered tent called a ger, which
you may know by its Russian name, the
yurt. And here's the astonishing part:
inside that simple tent, while it's
minus 40 outside, it can be a cozy 25

comfortably in shirt sleeves. How is

the world's most brutal winters in what
is essentially a tent? The answer is one

huge portion of those are sheep. So wool

they wrap the entire wooden frame of the

superb natural insulator. The matted
wool fibers trap countless tiny pockets

burning day and night, a constant source

insulation and a stove would mean little

amount of living space inside, a round

fall of empires, and it's still in daily
use across Mongolia today, from the

gloves, and scarves, wrapping their

heart of one of the harshest winters on
Earth, even in a tent.
