transcript_plaintext:
I have a trade offer. You get $1 billion
but you also get the rarest diseases for
1 year. After that, you keep the money
and your body returns to normal. But
before you decide, these are the
diseases you're going to get. For
starters, you are now allergic to water.
You now have aquagenic urticaria or
water allergy. Any water contact on the
skin will cause small itchy welts that
last for 30 minutes to 2 hours. And not
just any specific area, either. The
whole body is now allergic to water. And
not just salt water, all water. Drinking
water, the rain, and even your tears and
sweat is now an allergic trigger. Water
is now your enemy. Spill drinking water
on your hands, that part is now itchy
for 2 hours. The room got too hot and
you're sweating, your whole body is now
itchy. The worst part is that we don't
even know why this happens. Allergic
reactions happen when your immune system
targets a specific foreign protein. For
example, peanut allergy happens when
peanut proteins, such as ARA H2, gets
targeted. But water is not protein.
That's why scientists believe is
reacting with something already sitting
in the skin, turning it into an allergen
on contact. And because we don't know
what it is, we have no cure for it. Only
a hundred documented cases worldwide.
The next disease can turn your body into
bone. Fibrodysplasia ossificans
progressiva or FOP is an extremely rare
genetic disorder that causes muscles,
tendons, ligaments, and other soft
tissues to gradually transform into
bone. It usually begins in early
childhood around the neck and shoulders
before spreading through the rest of the
body, slowly locking joints in place.
The condition is caused by a mutation in
the ACVR1 gene. Normally, this gene
helps regulate bone growth and repair.
But in people with FOP, the switch is
permanently stuck on. So, even minor
injuries like bumps, injections, or
surgery can trigger the growth of new
bone where it should never form. There
is no cure and treatment focuses on
preventing injuries and managing
symptoms as the body gradually becomes
trapped inside a second skeleton. FOP
affects only about 1 in 1.4 to 2 million
people worldwide. This one didn't come
from a lab or a mutation. It came from a
tradition. You're getting kuru, a fatal
brain disease that once spread among the
Fore people of Papua New Guinea through
a mortuary ritual where relatives
consumed the tissue of the deceased as
an act of mourning and respect. For the
next months, expect early tremors and
shakiness that gradually worsen into
loss of coordination, slurred speech,
and difficulty walking along with sudden
uncontrollable laughing fits, which is
exactly why it earned the nickname the
laughing sickness. It's caused by a
misfolded protein called a prion, the
same category of infectious agent behind
mad cow disease. And unlike a virus or
bacteria, it isn't alive at all. It just
forces normal proteins in the brain to
fold incorrectly and spread the damage
outward. In real cases, kuru attacks the
cerebellum specifically, the part of the
brain responsible for balance and
movement, which is why coordination is
usually the first thing to go. The
disease is almost extinct today since
the ritual that spread it ended in the
1950s and '60s. For this one, say
goodbye to sleep completely. Not
restless nights or tossing and turning,
an absolute inability to sleep at all.
You're getting fatal familial insomnia,
a prion disease that attacks the
thalamus, the part of your brain
responsible for regulating sleep cycles
and several automatic body functions.
Over the year, expect the insomnia to
progress through stages, starting with
mild trouble sleeping, then escalating
into complete sleeplessness, then vivid
panic-like hallucinations, and finally a
dementia-like mental decline, all while
your body simultaneously loses control
over things like heart rate, body
temperature, and sweating. This
eventually becomes fatal within about 18
months of the first symptoms because the
human brain and body cannot survive
indefinitely without any sleep at all.
It's caused by a mutation passed down
through families, and somewhere between
40 and 100 families worldwide are known
to carry it. This one fast-forwards your
body straight into old age while your
mind stays exactly where it is. You're
getting progeria, and over the next year
your body will begin aging at roughly
seven times the normal rate. Expect your
hair to thin and fall out, your skin to
grow thin and wrinkled, and your
cardiovascular system to start behaving
like someone decades older, all while
your thoughts, memory, and personality
remain completely unchanged. It's caused
by a mutation in a gene responsible for
producing a protein called lamin A,
which normally helps stabilize the
nucleus inside every one of your cells.
When that protein is faulty, the nucleus
becomes unstable, and cells age and
break down far faster than they should,
essentially aging your entire body from
the inside out. In real patients with
this condition, most don't survive past
their early teens due to heart attacks
or strokes, the same cardiovascular
problems normally seen in people in
their 80s and 90s. It occurs in roughly
one in four million births. This one
doesn't attack a single system, it
attacks nearly your whole body at once.
You're getting Alström syndrome, caused
by a mutation affecting tiny hair-like
structures called cilia that sit on
almost every cell in your body and help
cells communicate and function properly.
Expect your vision to blur and gradually
fade due to damage in the light-sensing
cells of your eyes, along with
progressive hearing loss, rapid weight
gain, and insulin resistance that pushes
your body toward diabetes. At the same
time, expect extra strain on your heart
and kidneys. This condition requires an
entire team of specialists working
together for life, since no single
doctor can manage vision, hearing,
metabolic, and organ complications all
happening simultaneously. Fewer than
1,000 cases have ever been confirmed
worldwide. You're getting ribose
5-phosphate isomerase deficiency, or
RPID, and for the next year your body
will struggle to properly process a
sugar called ribose-5-phosphate through
a pathway called the pentose phosphate
pathway. A process your cells normally
rely on to produce energy and protect
themselves from damage. This means your
cells would be very vulnerable and lack
energy, affecting your brain and nervous
system, potentially causing seizures,
muscle weakness, and cognitive fog as
nerve cells struggle to function
properly without that pathway working
correctly. Over nearly three decades of
modern medicine, only a handful of
cases, some sources say as few as one,
have ever been confirmed worldwide. That
means doctors still don't fully
understand how this disease behaves over
time, since there simply aren't enough
patients to study. Now, each of these
diseases is terrifying to have, but
combining them would be a completely
different level of hell and suffering.
Fatal familial insomnia makes you sweat
uncontrollably, but your sweat now
triggers your water allergy, leaving you
covered in itching hives whenever your
damaged nervous system loses control of
your temperature. Kuru and RPID destroy
your balance, weaken your muscles, and
trigger seizures. That makes you fall
repeatedly, and because you also have
FOP, every serious fall or muscle injury
could trigger more bone growth. As
Alström syndrome takes away your sight
and hearing, avoiding those falls
becomes almost impossible. Soon your
joints are stiffening from progeria
while FOP physically locks them together
with new bone. Your jaw and neck could
freeze in place just as the brain
diseases make swallowing and
coordination harder, turning eating,
drinking, and even clearing your throat
into a struggle. Then your chest begins
stiffening. FOP prevents it from
expanding normally. Alström syndrome
weakens the heart and progeria hardens
the arteries supplying it. Your lungs
cannot pull in enough air while your
heart becomes less capable of moving
that oxygen around your body. Even
treating you becomes dangerous. The
seizures, diabetes, heart problems,
kidney damage, and brain degeneration
demand constant medical intervention,
but injections, surgery, intubation, and
physical trauma could make the FOP
worse. Now knowing your fate, would you
still take the deal? Let me know in the
comments.
>> [music]
[music]

description:
How rare can a human really be?

In this video, we explore some of the rarest human traits ever documented, starting from the top of the body and working all the way down. From red hair and Uncombable Hair Syndrome to complete heterochromia, Anotia, Total Arhinia, ghost teeth, Rh null blood, Piebaldism, ambidexterity, Anonychia, and many more, you'll discover just how extraordinary the human body can be.

You'll also learn the science behind these rare conditions, how often they occur, what causes them, and why some of them have only been reported a handful of times in medical history.

Whether you're interested in genetics, anatomy, medicine, or simply fascinating facts about the human body, this video showcases some of the rarest traits known to science.

MedlinePlus Genetics. (n.d.). Uncombable hair syndrome. U.S. National Library of Medicine. https://medlineplus.gov/genetics/cond...

MedlinePlus Genetics. (n.d.). Congenital atrichia. U.S. National Library of Medicine.

MedlinePlus Genetics. (n.d.). Piebaldism. U.S. National Library of Medicine.

MedlinePlus Genetics. (n.d.). Situs inversus. U.S. National Library of Medicine.

National Organization for Rare Disorders. (n.d.). Rh deficiency syndrome (Rh-null syndrome).

Orphanet. (n.d.). Ectrodactyly. INSERM. 

Biesecker, L. G. (2002). Polydactyly: How many disorders and how many genes? American Journal of Medical Genetics, 112(3), 279–283.

This is the most average guy alive. He
has black hair, brown eyes, dark brown
skin. He is right-handed and about 5'5"
tall. His name is Muhammad and he is
Chinese. Has O positive blood and is
lactose intolerant. And most of you
watching right now have at least a few
traits in common with him. Maybe you
have black hair or are right-handed. But
what if we looked at the complete
opposite? What are the rarest human
traits a person can have? Let's start
our way from the top to the bottom,
starting with hair. For color, it's red.
Only about 1 to 2% of people are born
with naturally red hair. It is caused by
inherited variants in a gene called
MC1R.
Instead of producing mostly dark
eumelanin, people with these variants
produce more pheomelanin, the pigment
responsible for red and orange hues. But
even rarer is having uncombable hair
syndrome, a rare genetic condition that
causes a person's hair to grow dry,
frizzy, and stand out from the scalp in
every direction, making it nearly
impossible to comb flat. There are only
a few hundred recorded cases in the
world, and despite its unusual
appearance, it is completely harmless.
But what if you aren't born with hair?
While most babies go from bald to a head
full of hair in about 6 months, babies
who have congenital atrichia don't
develop hair or lose the little hair
they have shortly after birth and will
remain bald for life because their hair
follicles cannot produce normal hair.
Moving on to eyes, green is the rarest
natural eye color, which is about 2% of
the population. But what's rarer is
complete heterochromia, which is having
two completely different eye colors.
This occurs when melanin distribution is
asymmetrical and occurs in about 0.06%
of the population. However, including
mutations, the rarest would be pink or
red eyes and has a 1 in 100,000 chance
of occurrence since you need to have
albinism in order to have a chance to
get it. Moving on to ears, what if I
told you you could look like an elf?
Stahl's ear is a congenital condition
where an extra fold of cartilage gives
the ear a pointed or elf-like
appearance. But the rarest would be
anotia, an extremely rare birth defect
in which the external ear is completely
absent. Occurs in about 1 in 50,000
births. Moving down to your nose.
Unfortunately, the rarest is a medical
condition called total arhinia, which is
the total absence of an external nose.
Fewer than a few hundred cases have been
reported worldwide. Moving on to your
cheeks. Congenital cheek pit is the
rarest natural cheek trait, a small
permanent indentation on the cheek that
is present from birth and remains
visible even when the face is relaxed,
unlike a dimple that typically appears
only when smiling. It's so rare that I
haven't found any source stating its
probability. Moving on to the mouth.
Congenital bifid or split tongue could
give a person a snake-like tongue. This
occurs when the tongue is partially
split due to incomplete fusion during
fetal development. But again, the
absence of tongue or aglossia is rarer.
Fewer than 100 cases have been reported
worldwide in published medical reports.
Moving on, you could have ghost teeth or
regional odontodysplasia, an extremely
rare condition where one small area of
the mouth develops teeth that are weak
because they didn't form properly before
erupting. The enamel and dentin are thin
and poorly mineralized, so the teeth may
look yellow or brown, break easily, or
fail to come in completely. On X-rays,
these teeth appear faint and almost
transparent, like ghosts, which is how
the condition got its nickname. Only a
few hundred cases were reported. Your
lips have traits, too. Congenital double
upper lip is an extremely rare condition
where a person is born with an extra
fold of tissue on the inside of the
upper lip. It is usually not noticeable
when the face is relaxed, but becomes
visible when smiling. Fewer than 100
cases have been reported. Moving on to
your internal organs. Most people have
their heart, liver, and stomach on the
expected sides. But roughly 1 in 10,000
people have situs inversus, a condition
where the internal organs are a complete
mirror image of the normal layout. Many
people with it live their entire lives
without knowing, only finding out by
accident during an x-ray or surgery. But
rarer still is situs ambiguus, also
called heterotaxy, where the organs
aren't just flipped, they're scattered
in irregular, unpredictable positions.
It occurs in somewhere between 1 in
10,000 and 1 in 40,000 births, and often
comes with complex heart defects. Moving
on to blood type, AB negative is already
one of the rarest common types, found in
less than 1% of people. But the true
rarest blood type in the world is
Rh-null, nicknamed golden blood, because
it lacks all 61 possible antigens in the
Rh system. Fewer than 50 people on Earth
are known to have it, and it's so rare
that it can only be received from
another Rh-null donor, making it both
incredibly valuable to science and
incredibly risky for the people who
carry it. Since in an emergency, there
may be no compatible blood available
anywhere in the world. Moving on to
skin, albinism causes a near total lack
of melanin, resulting in very pale skin,
hair, and eyes, and affects about 1 in
20,000 people. But rarer is piebaldism,
a condition present from birth where
patches of skin and hair have no pigment
at all, creating permanent white
patches, most commonly a white forelock
that contrasts sharply against normal
pigmentation. Unlike vitiligo, which
develops later in life and can spread,
piebaldism patches are there from the
moment you're born, stay a fixed size
and shape for life, and come from a
mutation that stops pigment cells from
migrating to certain areas of skin
during development. Moving on to arms,
polydactyly of the hand is relatively
well known, but having an entire extra
arm is a different level of rare.
Polymelia is a congenital condition
where a person is born with one or more
supernumerary limbs, and it's so
exceptionally rare that only a handful
of documented cases exist worldwide. In
most cases, the extra limb is attached
near the shoulder or hip and has little
to no function. So, it's usually removed
surgically shortly after birth. In
extremely rare cases, however, the extra
limb is functional enough that the
person can move or even use it, which is
part of why these cases get so much
medical attention when they appear.
Moving on to hands and fingers,
polydactyly, being born with extra
fingers or toes, actually isn't that
rare, occurring in about 1 in 700 to
1,000 births. And in many cases, the
extra digit is just a small nub of skin
and cartilage with no bone. What's rarer
is ectrodactyly, sometimes called
lobster claw syndrome, where the central
fingers or toes are missing, splitting
the hand or foot into two claw-like
parts. It occurs in roughly 1 in 90,000
people and can affect one or all four
limbs. Moving on to handedness, about
10% of the population is left-handed.
But true ambidexterity, having equal
skill and preference in both hands
rather than one dominant side, is
estimated at around 1%, making it rarer
than being left-handed. Genuine
ambidexterity is actually linked to a
more symmetrical brain, since handedness
is normally tied to one hemisphere being
dominant for motor control. Some studies
have found naturally ambidextrous people
are slightly more likely to experience
issues with memory and attention. On the
upside, true ambidexterity is common
among elite fencers, boxers, and
baseball switch-hitters, since being
able to switch hands seamlessly removes
an entire category of predictability
that opponents rely on. Moving on to
nails, most people take a full set of
fingernails for granted. But anonychia
is a rare genetic condition where a
person is born with partial or complete
absence of nails on the fingers or toes.
It stems from a mutation in a gene
involved in nail bed development and can
appear entirely on on own or alongside
other limb abnormalities like
underdeveloped fingers. Since nails
normally protect the sensitive tips of
fingers and toes, people with anonychia
are often more prone to injury and
infection in those areas over a
lifetime. Moving on to joints. Being
double-jointed or having hypermobile
joints is fairly common and often
harmless, letting some people bend their
thumbs back to their wrists or
hyperextend their elbows.

How rare can a human really be?

In this video, we explore some of the rarest human traits ever documented, starting from the top of the body and working all the way down. From red hair and Uncombable Hair Syndrome to complete heterochromia, Anotia, Total Arhinia, ghost teeth, Rh null blood, Piebaldism, ambidexterity, Anonychia, and many more, you'll discover just how extraordinary the human body can be.

video_title: What Made Vikings So Terrifying
description:
Why were the Vikings so terrifying? It was not just because of axes, swords, or legendary warriors. Their strength came from a combination of physical endurance, clever tactics, advanced shipbuilding, and psychological warfare that allowed them to overwhelm communities across medieval Europe.

In this video, we explore what really made Viking raiders so successful, from the infamous attack on Lindisfarne in 793 AD to the powerful longships that carried them across oceans and rivers. We also examine how their diet and lifestyle built formidable warriors, why they carefully chose vulnerable targets, and the enduring mystery surrounding the legendary berserkers.

Drawing on archaeology, historical records, and modern research, this video separates myth from reality and reveals why the Vikings earned a reputation that spread fear across Europe for centuries.

If you enjoy history, archaeology, and the science behind famous civilizations, be sure to like the video, subscribe to the channel, and turn on notifications for more content.

Sources:

Brink, S., & Price, N. (Eds.). (2008). The Viking world. Routledge.
Price, N. (2020). Children of ash and elm: A history of the Vikings. Basic Books.
Sawyer, P. H. (2001). The Oxford illustrated history of the Vikings. Oxford University Press.
Williams, G., Pentz, P., & Wemhoff, M. (Eds.). (2014). Vikings: Life and legend. British Museum Press.
Winroth, A. (2014). The age of the Vikings. Princeton University Press.
Jesch, J. (2015). The Viking diaspora. Routledge.

transcript_plaintext:
It's 793 AD and you are a monk at
Lindisfarne. Life is good in serving the
Lord, but then you see something in the
distance. A ship? Lots of ships?
Merchants perhaps? Nope, Vikings.
The ships glided out of the fog low and
fast and suddenly life is not so good
anymore. Within hours the monastery was
burning and your fellow monks were
either slain, drowned or captured as
slaves. Priceless holy relics were
pillaged and the church desecrated and
this was just the beginning. Vikings
would raid settlements along coasts for
centuries with little opposition. But
why is that? What allowed Viking raiders
to overwhelm so many communities? The
answer is not just shields and swords,
but on the physiology of these warriors.
Vikings were not the giants often shown
in movies. Skeletal remains show the
average Viking man stood around 5'7"
close to the average height for that era
in Europe. But what set them apart was
not size, but raw functional strength.
Their diet played a big role.
Archaeological digs at sites like Birka
and Hedeby reveal a menu built for hard
labor. Barley and rye formed the base
eaten as bread and porridge. Fish such
as herring and cod were everyday staples
alongside meat from cattle, sheep and
pigs. Dairy foods like skyr, a thick
yogurt-like food and cheese added extra
protein. This calorie-dense,
protein-rich diet fueled bodies that
worked hard from a young age and that
work never stopped. Farming, felling
timber for ships, blacksmithing and
above all rowing built serious muscle.
Rowing a longship for hours demanded
constant effort from the back, shoulders
and core. Bone analysis from Viking age
skeletons shows thickened muscle
attachment points, a clear sign of
bodies shaped by years of repetitive
heavy physical work. That physical power
explains half the story. The other half
is what was happening in people's minds.
Vikings understood something modern
armies still study today. The element of
surprise can be more powerful than
numbers. That's why Viking raids happen
at early dawn. This is when most people
are still asleep and there is enough
light to see where you're going. This is
also the time where night watch or
lookouts are getting sleepy and they are
also an organized force. They would send
scouts days and hours before the raid to
find landing sites and take note of
defenses. The attacking force is divided
in war bands which is based on personal
loyalty. This means a war band consists
of family members and friends that know
each other well and therefore fought
together as a unit. Vikings fought smart
as well. Most of them carried arrows and
fire volleys before resulting in an
all-out brawl. Larger raid parties also
formed shield walls with the strongest
warriors on the front while spears and
arrows were launched from behind and
they choose targets carefully. They
avoided large fortified settlements and
clustered towns where help can arrive
fast. They targeted small isolated
communities and these were often
monasteries and churches. These sites
held gold, silver, and religious
treasures and they were guarded by monks
not soldiers. The raid on Lindisfarne
was recorded by a scholar named Alcuin
who described the horror in letters that
spread across Christian Europe and word
of mouth did the rest. The English had
learned to fear the Vikings and so
before a Viking ship reached a new
coastline, its reputation often arrived
first. Speed made this fear possible. A
raiding party could appear, strike, and
vanish before soldiers could organize a
defense. Entire regions felt permanently
exposed never knowing when or where the
next raid would happen. That uncertainty
was its own kind of psychological
warfare. But none of this would have
worked without one piece of technology.
The longship was the real secret weapon.
Built using overlapping wooden planks in
a method called clinker construction, it
was light, flexible, and fast. Its
shallow draft meant it could cross open
ocean then turn and glide up shallow
rivers that most other ships could never
reach. Vikings could strike deep inland
far from any coastal defense, then
vanish back out to sea. Weapons were
simple but effective. Axes were common
because they were cheap to make and
doubled as everyday tools. Swords were
more expensive and often passed down as
status symbols. Wealthier warriors wore
mail shirts, but most fighters relied on
thick leather padded clothing and round
wooden shields reinforced with iron. All
of this explains the raids, but one part
of Viking warfare remains genuinely
mysterious. Norse sagas describe a type
of warrior called a berserker, said to
fight in a wild trance-like fury.
Enemies described them as almost
impossible to stop. What caused this
state is still debated by historians.
Some point to self-induced psychological
rituals or group hysteria before battle.
A popular theory suggests they consumed
hallucinogenic mushrooms. The truth is
we still do not fully know, and that
mystery is part of what keeps the
berserker legend alive. So, how does all
of this add up? Modern archaeology
paints a fuller picture than the old
image of mindless raiders. Many Vikings
were farmers, traders, and settlers who
built trade networks stretching from
North America to Baghdad. The reason we
remember them mainly as terrifying
attackers is partly because their
victims, mostly literate monks, were the
ones writing the history. Even so, the
fear was real. Strong, well-fed bodies.
Ships that could strike almost anywhere.
A culture that rewarded boldness and
risk. A reputation that spread faster
than any single raid ever could. Put
together, these are the real reasons
Vikings became one of the most feared
forces in medieval history.

[music]

video_title: Why Humans are Scared of the Ocean
description:
What makes the deep ocean so terrifying?

We know more about the surface of Mars than we do about much of our own ocean floor. In this video, we explore why the deep sea has fascinated and frightened humanity for centuries.

From the psychology of thalassophobia and the crushing pressure of the abyss to ancient sea monster legends, mysterious disappearances, forgotten shipwrecks, and the incredible creatures that actually live in the darkest parts of the ocean, this is a journey into one of Earth's last great frontiers.

Discover the science behind our fear, the history that shaped it, and why the unknown depths continue to capture our imagination even today.

If you enjoy videos about science, history, mysteries, and the unknown, subscribe for more explorations into the world's most fascinating topics.

What deep sea creature do you find the most unsettling? Let us know in the comments.

Sources:

National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. (n.d.). How much of the ocean have we explored? 

National Geographic Society. (2023). Deep sea. 

Jamieson, A. J. (2015). The hadal zone: Life in the deepest oceans. Cambridge University Press.

Ellis, R. (1998). The search for the giant squid. Lyons Press.

Tyack, P. L. (2008). Implications for marine mammals of large scale changes in the marine acoustic environment. Journal of Mammalogy, 89(3), 549–558.

transcript_plaintext:
We have better maps of the surface of
Mars than we do of our own ocean floor.
Think about that for a second. We know
more about a dead frozen planet millions
of miles away than we know about what
lies a few kilometers beneath the waves
on our own planet. And maybe that's
exactly what makes the ocean different.
It's familiar enough to forget and
unknown enough to fear. So why does
something so close feel so unknown and
so unsettling? Let us start with the
body. Fear of the deep ocean is not just
cultural. It is wired into us.
Psychologists call it thalassophobia, an
intense fear of large bodies of water,
especially deep or dark water. But the
roots of that fear go back much further
than any phobia label. Humans are visual
creatures. Around 80% of how we
understand our environment comes through
sight. In the deep ocean, past about
1,000 m, sunlight disappears almost
completely. This is called the aphotic
zone, the region of darkness. When our
primary sense is taken away, our brain
fills the void with worst-case
scenarios. This is the same reason a
dark bedroom feels more threatening than
a lit one. Except in the ocean, that
darkness extends for miles in every
direction with genuinely unknown things
swimming through it. There is also the
matter of scale. The deep ocean is the
largest habitable space on Earth, yet
humans have physically explored less
than 5% of it. Our brains are
pattern-seeking machines. We fear what
we cannot predict, and nothing resists
prediction quite like an environment we
have barely mapped. There is also a
physiological layer to this fear. As you
descend, water pressure increases
roughly one atmosphere for every 10 m.
By the time you reach 1,000 m, the
pressure is enough to crush an
unprotected human body almost instantly.
Some researchers believe humans carry an
unconscious, almost instinctive
awareness of this crushing force even
without ever learning the physics behind
it. Add to this the eerie behavior of
sound underwater. Sound travels about
four times is in water than in air, and
low-frequency noises like whale calls or
shifting ice can travel for thousands of
kilometers. During the Cold War,
hydrophone networks built to track
Soviet submarines picked up a mysterious
sound nicknamed the Bloop. So massive in
scale that scientists initially wondered
if something enormous and unknown was
making it. It was later attributed to
icequakes, but for years it fed public
imagination about what might be living
in the deep. History had a role, too.
Long before submarines and research
vessels, sailors had only their eyes,
their instincts, and their imaginations.
Ancient Greek sailors spoke of Scylla
and Charybdis, monstrous forces waiting
in narrow straits to destroy ships.
Norse legends told of the Kraken, a
colossal beast said to drag entire
vessels beneath the waves. Medieval maps
often marked unexplored waters with the
phrase here be dragons, a warning that
beyond the known coastline anything was
possible. Part of this came from real
encounters. Sailors did see giant squid
or fish and other deep sea creatures
that occasionally surfaced or washed
ashore, often dying or already dead.
Without context, a 100-ft long oarfish
looks exactly like a sea serpent. Add to
this the very real dangers of early
ocean travel, storms, shipwrecks,
scurvy, and ships that simply vanished
without explanation. The ocean did not
need embellishment to be terrifying, it
was already killing people. This is
evident in the thousands of shipwrecks
throughout history. A notable one being
off the coast of Greece, near the island
of Antikythera, where divers in 1900
discovered a shipwreck containing the
Antikythera mechanism, an ancient bronze
device so complex it is often called the
world's first analog computer. It had
been sitting at the bottom of the sea
for roughly 2,000 years. Similarly, the
Baltic Sea has preserved shipwrecks in
astonishing condition because its cold,
low-oxygen, low-salinity water slows
decay dramatically. Some wooden warships
from the 17th century like the Swedish
ship Vasa have been recovered almost
fully intact after centuries underwater.
Divers exploring these wrecks often
describe an unsettling stillness. Ships
frozen in time sitting exactly as they
sank. Then there are the disappearances
that were never explained. The USS
Cyclops, a US Navy ship carrying over
300 people vanished in 1918 somewhere in
the Atlantic without a single distress
signal or piece of wreckage ever found.
This fed directly into legends like the
Bermuda Triangle, a stretch of ocean
blamed for dozens of disappearances. As
exploration advanced the myths did not
disappear. They evolved. In 1960 the
bathyscaphe Trieste descended nearly
11,000 m into the Mariana Trench, the
deepest known point in our ocean. It
proved humans could conquer the crushing
pressure of the deep, but also that life
existed even there in total darkness and
extreme pressure. We discovered
creatures like the anglerfish using a
glowing lure to draw prey into a
mouthful of needle-like teeth. We found
giant isopods, tube worms living near
boiling hydrothermal vents, and gulper
eels that can swallow prey larger than
themselves. For centuries giant squid
were considered legend blamed for the
kraken stories of Norse sailors. It was
not until 2004 that scientists captured
the first photographs of a live giant
squid in its natural habitat and not
until 2012 that one was filmed on camera
in the deep sea for the first time. A
creature that inspired centuries of
monster stories turned out to be real
all along simply living far beyond where
humans could easily see it. Even now
with satellites, submarines, and remote
operated vehicles our fear has not gone
away. If anything films and media keep
it alive. Movies about deep sea
disasters, viral photos of bizarre
creatures, and documentaries about
shipwrecks all reinforce a very old idea
that the deep ocean is a place that does
not belong to us. And in a strange way,
it reminds us that this is one of the
last truly wild places on Earth. A place
we have not tamed, mapped, or fully
understood. So, the next time you're
swimming and your feet can no longer
touch the bottom, and that flicker of
unease creeps in, know that you are
experiencing something ancient.
>> [music]
[music]

of Antikythera, where divers in 1900

been sitting at the bottom of the sea

frozen in time sitting exactly as they
sank. Then there are the disappearances

experiencing something ancient.

video_title: The Perfect Urban Animal
description:
Every year, human cities unintentionally kill countless animals through glass buildings, roads, power lines, pollution, and constant environmental change. Yet while most wildlife struggles to survive in urban environments, some species are already adapting in remarkable ways.

In this video, we explore a fascinating question. If evolution were to design the perfect animal for city life, what would it look like?

Drawing inspiration from real animals, we combine the intelligence of crows, the curiosity of magpies, the adaptability of rats, the agility of stone martens, the climbing ability of palm civets, the camouflage of tawny owls, the stealth of foxes, the resilience of urban blackbirds, the reproductive strategy of city coyotes, and the incredible immune system of the Virginia opossum to imagine the ultimate urban survivor.

The result is a creature perfectly suited for the concrete jungle, one that thrives not despite cities, but because of them.

The most surprising part is that this animal may not be as fictional as it seems. Evolution is already laying the groundwork in the wildlife living alongside us every day.

transcript_plaintext:
Every year more than a billion birds die
due to collisions with man-made
structures. May it be towering glass
buildings, communication towers,
windmills, or power lines. These
structures kill millions every day. In
the United States alone, an estimated 1
million animals are killed every day due
to vehicle-related incidents. In 2011,
after heavy rainfall overwhelmed
London's combined sewer system, about
450,000 tons of raw sewage entered the
river. The resulting drop in oxygen
levels killed tens of thousands of fish.
It's clear that the world we built is
not built for the natural world. And it
seems that where humans thrive, animals
suffer. But what if that's not the case?
What if there's an animal that is
perfect for the urban jungle we have
built? To understand what that animal
would need, we first have to understand
what makes cities so brutal for
wildlife. Cities are loud, bright,
toxic, and dense. Food comes in
packages, water sits in gutters,
predators are replaced by cars, and the
biggest threat of all is
unpredictability. A forest changes
slowly over decades, but a city block
can change in a weekend. Most animals
are hardwired for consistency, and
cities offer none of that. So, our
perfect urban animal needs to be built
for chaos. Let's start with what sits at
the very top of survival in any
environment, the brain. In 2009,
researchers at the University of
Washington ran a study where they wore
masks while trapping crows on campus.
Months later, the crows that had been
caught would dive-bomb and scold anyone
wearing that specific face. And they
taught their flockmates to do the same.
They held grudges, communicated threat
information socially, and adjusted their
behavior based on experience rather than
instinct. Our animal needs exactly that,
the ability to learn, remember, and pass
knowledge along because the city is
always changing. That intelligence
connects directly to curiosity, and here
the magpie is the clearest example.
Magpies are one of the only non-mammal
species to pass the mirror
self-recognition test, meaning they
understand that what they see in a
reflection is themselves. They
investigate new objects deliberately,
probe unfamiliar environments, and show
genuine problem-solving behavior when
food is hidden or blocked. In a city
full of constantly shifting
infrastructure, new packaging, new
routines, and new obstacles, that
instinct to explore rather than flee is
the difference between finding food and
starving next to it. From curiosity, we
move to diet because a clever animal
still dies if it cannot eat what the
city offers. The species to look at here
is the brown rat. Studies tracking urban
rat populations have found them
consuming everything from curry and
pizza grease to soap, candle wax, and
electrical cable insulation when nothing
else is available. Their digestive
systems produce enzymes flexible enough
to break down foods that would cause
organ failure in most mammals. They also
build up tolerance to toxins over
generations with many urban populations
now showing resistance to poisons
specifically designed to kill them. Our
animal carries that same biochemical
flexibility, a gut that treats the
contents of any dumpster as a balanced
meal. Now the body itself, and this is
where the marten becomes the reference
point. Stone martens, which have
colonized European cities over the last
few decades, are famous for being found
inside car engines, behind wall panels,
and inside roof insulation. They are
roughly cat sized, extremely flexible in
their spine, and able to compress their
bodies through gaps that look impossibly
small. They also move fast and change
direction sharply, which on a city
street crowded with obstacles is exactly
the kind of locomotion that keeps an
animal alive. Our animal is built along
those same lines, compact, low profile,
and able to treat infrastructure as a
natural habitat rather than an obstacle.
But cities are not just horizontal, they
are vertical. Rooftops, fire escapes,
drainage pipes, ledges, cable strung
between buildings. The animal that can
use that vertical space has access to a
highway that almost nothing else can
travel. The closest real-world model is
the common palm civet, a small mammal
found increasingly in Asian cities that
moves along rooftops and building edges
with almost unsettling ease. Its ankles
can rotate nearly 180°,
letting it descend vertical surfaces
headfirst and grip at angles that would
send most animals falling. It uses the
high ground not just for safety, but for
navigation, reading the city from above
before dropping down to forage. Our
animal has that same relationship with
height. Back at ground level, camouflage
shifts entirely when the environment is
made of concrete. The tawny owl is a
useful reference here, not for cities
specifically, but for how effective
tonal matching to your actual
environment can be. Its mottled
gray-brown plumage makes it nearly
invisible against tree bark. Our
animal's coat does exactly that,
patterned in the specific grays and
dusty browns of urban surfaces. That
invisibility extends to sound. Studies
on urban fox behavior have shown that
city foxes move significantly more
quietly than their rural counterparts,
with softer paw placement and far less
vocalization in populated areas. They
learned behaviorally to turn their
volume down. Our animal goes further. It
communicates in ultrasonic ranges, the
same frequency range bats use,
completely outside human hearing. Cities
can be loud and busy, which brings us to
stress tolerance. A 2013 study on urban
versus rural blackbirds found that city
blackbirds had measurably lower stress
hormone responses to human presence
compared to their forest-dwelling
relatives. They had essentially
recalibrated their threat response over
generations of living around people. Our
animal takes this to its logical
conclusion. Humans do not register as a
threat at all. It can move through a
crowded market, across a busy sidewalk,
past a group of people talking outside a
restaurant. That flat calm response
means zero wasted energy and zero fatal
panicked dashes into traffic. Now we
move to reproduction. Urban coyote
research out of Ohio State found that
city coyotes adjust their litter sizes
based on available resources far more
precisely than rural populations,
essentially reading the environment and
deciding how many young they can support
before committing. They also raise young
communally in some cases with older
siblings helping care for newer litters.
Our animal does the same. It reproduces
fast and intelligently, matching its
population to what the city can actually
sustain at any given moment. And holding
everything together is an immune system
modeled closest on the Virginia opossum,
an animal so biochemically unusual that
it is immune to the venom of most North
American snakes, resistant to rabies,
and able to consume rotting food that
would hospitalize a human. Researchers
studying opossums have found proteins in
their blood that actively neutralize a
wide range of toxins. In a city full of
chemical runoff, treated water,
processed food residue, and heavy metal
contamination, that kind of internal
defense system is a requirement. To
recap, our animal has the intelligence
of a crow, the curiosity of a magpie,
the digestive flexibility of a brown
rat, the flexible body of a stone
marten, the vertical mobility of a palm
civet, a camouflaged fur inspired by the
tawny owl, quiet as a fox, and the
silent communication of a bat, the
stress tolerance of an urban blackbird,
the adaptive reproduction of a city
coyote, and the immune system of a
Virginia opossum. Put all of that
together and you get something genuinely
remarkable. A sleek, intelligent,
dexterous, fearless creature that scales
buildings like a ghost, eats whatever
the city throws at it, and moves through
human civilization completely
unbothered. A true urban apex survivor.
Not because it is powerful in the
traditional sense, but because it is
perfectly tuned to a world that we built
for ourselves and accidentally made into
the harshest habitat on Earth. The funny
thing is, this animal is not entirely
fictional. Look closely at a raccoon
opening trash bins. Watch a brown rat
navigate a subway system it knows better
than most commuters. Watch a peregrine
falcon hunt from a skyscraper it has
adopted as a cliff face. These animals
are already partway there. They are the
rough drafts. What we just described is
the finished version, but given enough
time and enough pressure, the city might
just build it on its own.
>> [music]
[music]

and inside roof insulation. They are
roughly cat sized, extremely flexible in
their spine, and able to compress their
bodies through gaps that look impossibly
small. They also move fast and change
direction sharply, which on a city
street crowded with obstacles is exactly
the kind of locomotion that keeps an
animal alive. Our animal is built along
those same lines, compact, low profile,
and able to treat infrastructure as a
natural habitat rather than an obstacle.
But cities are not just horizontal, they
are vertical. Rooftops, fire escapes,
drainage pipes, ledges, cable strung
between buildings. The animal that can
use that vertical space has access to a
highway that almost nothing else can
travel. The closest real-world model is
the common palm civet, a small mammal
found increasingly in Asian cities that
moves along rooftops and building edges
with almost unsettling ease. Its ankles
can rotate nearly 180°,
letting it descend vertical surfaces
headfirst and grip at angles that would
send most animals falling. It uses the
high ground not just for safety, but for
navigation, reading the city from above
before dropping down to forage. Our
animal has that same relationship with
height. Back at ground level, camouflage
shifts entirely when the environment is
made of concrete. The tawny owl is a
useful reference here, not for cities
specifically, but for how effective
tonal matching to your actual
environment can be. Its mottled
gray-brown plumage makes it nearly
invisible against tree bark. Our
animal's coat does exactly that,
patterned in the specific grays and
dusty browns of urban surfaces. That
invisibility extends to sound. Studies
on urban fox behavior have shown that
city foxes move significantly more
quietly than their rural counterparts,
with softer paw placement and far less
vocalization in populated areas. They
learned behaviorally to turn their
volume down. Our animal goes further. It
communicates in ultrasonic ranges, the
same frequency range bats use,
completely outside human hearing. Cities
can be loud and busy, which brings us to

hormone responses to human presence
compared to their forest-dwelling
relatives. They had essentially
recalibrated their threat response over
generations of living around people. Our
animal takes this to its logical
conclusion. Humans do not register as a
threat at all. It can move through a
crowded market, across a busy sidewalk,
past a group of people talking outside a
restaurant. That flat calm response
means zero wasted energy and zero fatal
panicked dashes into traffic. Now we
move to reproduction. Urban coyote
research out of Ohio State found that
city coyotes adjust their litter sizes
based on available resources far more
precisely than rural populations,
essentially reading the environment and
deciding how many young they can support
before committing. They also raise young
communally in some cases with older
siblings helping care for newer litters.
Our animal does the same. It reproduces
fast and intelligently, matching its
population to what the city can actually
sustain at any given moment. And holding
everything together is an immune system
modeled closest on the Virginia opossum,
an animal so biochemically unusual that
it is immune to the venom of most North
American snakes, resistant to rabies,
and able to consume rotting food that
would hospitalize a human. Researchers
studying opossums have found proteins in
their blood that actively neutralize a
wide range of toxins. In a city full of
chemical runoff, treated water,
processed food residue, and heavy metal
contamination, that kind of internal
defense system is a requirement. To
recap, our animal has the intelligence
of a crow, the curiosity of a magpie,
the digestive flexibility of a brown
rat, the flexible body of a stone
marten, the vertical mobility of a palm
civet, a camouflaged fur inspired by the
tawny owl, quiet as a fox, and the
silent communication of a bat, the
stress tolerance of an urban blackbird,
the adaptive reproduction of a city
coyote, and the immune system of a
Virginia opossum. Put all of that
together and you get something genuinely
remarkable. A sleek, intelligent,
dexterous, fearless creature that scales
buildings like a ghost, eats whatever
the city throws at it, and moves through
human civilization completely

traditional sense, but because it is
perfectly tuned to a world that we built
for ourselves and accidentally made into
the harshest habitat on Earth. The funny
thing is, this animal is not entirely
fictional. Look closely at a raccoon
opening trash bins. Watch a brown rat
navigate a subway system it knows better
than most commuters. Watch a peregrine
falcon hunt from a skyscraper it has
adopted as a cliff face. These animals
are already partway there. They are the
rough drafts. What we just described is
the finished version, but given enough
time and enough pressure, the city might
just build it on its own.

Every year, human cities unintentionally kill countless animals through glass buildings, roads, power lines, pollution, and constant environmental change. Yet while most wildlife struggles to survive in urban environments, some species are already adapting in remarkable ways.

In this video, we explore a fascinating question. If evolution were to design the perfect animal for city life, what would it look like?

Drawing inspiration from real animals, we combine the intelligence of crows, the curiosity of magpies, the adaptability of rats, the agility of stone martens, the climbing ability of palm civets, the camouflage of tawny owls, the stealth of foxes, the resilience of urban blackbirds, the reproductive strategy of city coyotes, and the incredible immune system of the Virginia opossum to imagine the ultimate urban survivor.

The result is a creature perfectly suited for the concrete jungle, one that thrives not despite cities, but because of them.

The most surprising part is that this animal may not be as fictional as it seems. Evolution is already laying the groundwork in the wildlife living alongside us every day.

description:
Rabies is one of the oldest and most terrifying diseases in human history.

For over 4,000 years, civilizations from Mesopotamia, Egypt, Greece, Rome, India, and medieval Europe documented the same horrifying pattern: a bite from an animal, a period of apparent normality, and then a descent into madness, aggression, hydrophobia, and death.

In this video, we explore the complete history of rabies, from its earliest appearance in ancient law codes to its influence on mythology, folklore, and the werewolf legends of medieval Europe. We examine how ancient physicians recognized the disease long before microscopes existed, why rabies became associated with possession and transformation, and how generations lived in fear of a disease that was almost always fatal.

We also follow the scientific breakthrough that finally changed everything, culminating in Louis Pasteur's revolutionary vaccine and the survival of Joseph Meister in 1885.

Rabies shaped laws, inspired myths, created monsters, and remained undefeated for thousands of years. This is the story of humanity's longest battle against one of nature's most ruthless killers.

Sources and script research include historical records from Mesopotamia, Ancient Greece, Rome, India, China, medieval Europe, and modern medical literature on rabies.

If you enjoyed this video, consider liking, subscribing, and sharing it with others interested in history, medicine, mythology, and the darker side of the human past.

Sources: 

Jackson, A. C. (2013). Rabies: Scientific basis of the disease and its management (3rd ed.). Academic Press.

Rupprecht, C. E., Fooks, A. R., & Abela-Ridder, B. (Eds.). (2018). Laboratory techniques in rabies (5th ed.). World Health Organization.

World Health Organization. (2018). WHO expert consultation on rabies: Third report (WHO Technical Report Series No. 1012). World Health Organization.

Baer, G. M. (Ed.). (1991). The natural history of rabies (2nd ed.). CRC Press.

Steele, J. H., & Fernandez, P. J. (1991). History of rabies and global aspects. In G. M. Baer (Ed.), The natural history of rabies (2nd ed., pp. 1–24). CRC Press.

Levinson, W. (2023). Review of medical microbiology and immunology (17th ed.). McGraw Hill Education.

Aristotle. (1910). Historia animalium (D. W. Thompson, Trans.). Clarendon Press. (Original work published ca. 350 BCE)

This is Maximus. He is a good boy. He
likes belly rubs, chasing cats, and
protecting the Roman Empire. Speaking of
which, you are on patrol with him now.
Just you and Maximus at a peaceful
route. Or is it? You hear rustling in a
bush. A wolf emerges, growling, its
mouth foaming. It looks enraged. Maximus
takes a defensive stance, then the wolf
pounces and a brawl ensues. Luckily,
Maximus drove it away and smiles at you
like nothing happened. A month later,
something feels wrong. Maximus is
restless. He won't eat. He won't drink.
He stumbles when he walks and the floor
around him is strangely wet with drool.
And he becomes completely aggressive to
everyone. You approach him, but he
growls at you like you are a stranger.
And then he bites your hand and you
realized that is not your best friend
anymore. Something has taken over his
mind. A few days later, Maximus dies.
You grieve the death of your friend, but
the bite he gave you won't stop itching.
Then it starts burning. Your head hurts.
You can't sleep. Every sound gets on
your nerves. You feel thirsty, but when
you try to drink, your throat locks up.
Then you go mad. The people around have
no choice but to restrain you. You
scream. You bite. You fight people who
try to help. You lose control of your
own mind. A few days later, you're dead.
A terrifying way to die. And cases like
this have been recorded throughout
history. The Eshnunna Code, a
Mesopotamian legal text written around
4,000 years ago, contains the earliest
written mention of rabies. It includes a
law stating that if a dog bites a person
and that person dies as a result, the
dog's owner must pay a fine. Scholars
believe this implies the community
already understood that certain dog
bites could lead to fatal illness. They
had seen it happen enough times to build
it into their legal system. Laws do not
get written about hypothetical
situations. The people of Eshnunna had
clearly been watching this happen for
generations. Ancient Egyptian texts from
roughly the same era reference a
condition caused by dog bites that sent
people into states of uncontrollable
terror and madness. The god Sirius was
sometimes invoked in connection with
dog-related illness, and some historians
believe early Egyptian mythology around
mad dogs and divine punishment may have
been shaped in part by repeated
encounters with rabies. Moving into
ancient Greece, the Greeks called the
condition lyssa, meaning frenzy or rage.
The playwright Euripides used it as a
dramatic device. Demosthenes referenced
it in speeches, and Aristotle made an
observation that was centuries ahead of
his time. He correctly identified that
rabies spread through the saliva of
infected animals, commonly dogs, and
that it was invariably fatal in humans
once symptoms appeared. He had no
understanding of viruses. He had no
microscope, no germ theory, and yet he
had correctly identified the
transmission mechanism purely through
careful observation of patterns. Rome
absorbed Greek medical knowledge and
added its own. Roman writers, including
Virgil, Ovid, and Pliny the Elder, all
wrote about rabid animals, and Roman
physicians developed some of the
earliest formal treatment protocols for
bite wounds. Celsus, writing in the 1st
century, recommended aggressively
cutting out the bitten flesh and
cauterizing the wound with a hot iron
immediately after exposure. This was not
entirely wrong. Heat applied quickly
enough to a fresh wound can destroy the
virus before it reaches nerve tissue.
So, what is actually happening inside
the body? When the rabies virus enters
the body through a bite, it does
something almost sinister in its
patience. Rather than spreading through
the bloodstream like most pathogens, it
hijacks the peripheral nervous system
and travels slowly from the wound toward
the spinal cord and then up into the
brain. This journey can take weeks or
even months, which is why the incubation
period is so unusually long and
variable. Once it reaches the brain, it
targets the limbic system, the region
governing emotion, memory, and behavior.
The result is the unmistakable
progression of aggression, confusion,
and that extraordinary aversion to water
where the simple act of swallowing
triggers violent muscle spasms. The
virus also drives heavy salivation,
which is not incidental. It is the
mechanism by which the virus gets
transmitted. The disease has essentially
engineered its own spread through the
behavior of its host. Once symptoms
appear, survival is nearly impossible.
In all of recorded medical history,
there have been fewer than 20 documented
human survivors, nearly all involving
prior vaccination. The long silent
incubation followed by rapid and total
neurological collapse is exactly what
made rabies so terrifying to ancient and
medieval observers. In countries where
the natural world was understood through
divine will and supernatural forces,
rabies fit almost too neatly into
existing frameworks of punishment,
possession, and transformation. In
ancient India, texts from the
Atharvaveda, written around 3,000 years
ago, describe a dog bite illness with
symptoms matching rabies and attribute
it to a demon called Kandu. The
prescribed treatment involved ritual
purification, specific herbs, and
prayers to Indra. In ancient China,
records from as early as 556 BC describe
what appears to be rabies in dogs and
the madness that followed human bites.
Chinese physicians developed their own
bite wound treatments and, like the
Romans, eventually landed on
cauterization as one of the more
effective options. Medieval Europe had
no shortage of exposure to rabid
animals. Wolves were a real and
persistent threat across the continent,
and wolf attacks on villages were not
uncommon. When a wolf attacked and bit
several people in a single incident, and
then weeks later those people began
exhibiting violent, erratic behavior,
flinching from water, foaming at the
mouth, the community had no framework
for understanding what they were
witnessing. The werewolf myth, in its
most persistent medieval form, maps with
uncomfortable precision onto a rabies
outbreak. A person is bitten by a wolf.
After a period of apparent normalcy,
they begin to change. They become
aggressive, unpredictable. They lose the
ability to behave like a person. They
may growl, bite, attack those closest to
them. They die, and no one can explain
what happened. For most of history, from
Mesopotamia through Greece, Rome, and
the medieval world, there was no
effective treatment for rabies once
symptoms appeared. People could only
manage the wound and hope. Different
cultures developed their own remedies.
Romans placed hair from the attacking
dog into the wound, while medieval
physicians prescribed poultices,
prayers, and pilgrimages. In Europe,
many rabies victims traveled to the
shrine of Saint Hubert of Belgium,
patron saint of rabies sufferers. Some
communities even pressed a heated metal
key associated with the saint into bite
wounds. The heat may have provided some
real benefit, though no one understood
why. In the 16th century, the Italian
physician Girolamo Fracastoro proposed
that diseases spread through invisible
particles passed between people and
animals. He cited rabies as an example,
observing that something in the saliva
of infected animals entered through
wounds. Then, in 1885, everything
changed. Louis Pasteur, already famous
for his work on germ theory and
vaccination, turned his attention to
rabies. Unable to see the virus itself,
he developed an attenuated vaccine from
infected animal tissue and tested it in
dogs. On July 6th, 1885, a 9-year-old
boy named Joseph Meister was brought to
Pasteur after being severely bitten by a
rabid dog. With no other options
available, Pasteur administered his
experimental vaccine over 13 days.
Meister survived. For the first time in
4,000 years of recorded history,
medicine had a real defense against
rabies. Meister went on to live a full
life and later worked as a gatekeeper at
the Pasteur Institute, the very place
where his life had been saved. Rabies is
one of the oldest diseases in the human
record. It shaped our myths, our laws,
our monsters. It gave medieval Europe
its werewolves and gave ancient
physicians some of their first lessons
in the relationship between animal
behavior and human death. It killed
without mercy or exception for 40
centuries before a single person
survived it. The virus is still out
there in bats, in foxes, in dogs across
Africa and Asia where it still kills
roughly 59,000 people a year, most of
them children. The same pathogen, the
same progression, the same ending. What
changed is not the disease. What changed
is that we finally understood it and
maybe someday we could develop a cure
for it.
>> [music]

mouth foaming. It looks enraged. Maximus
takes a defensive stance, then the wolf
pounces and a brawl ensues. Luckily,
Maximus drove it away and smiles at you
like nothing happened. A month later,
something feels wrong. Maximus is
restless. He won't eat. He won't drink.
He stumbles when he walks and the floor
around him is strangely wet with drool.
And he becomes completely aggressive to
everyone. You approach him, but he
growls at you like you are a stranger.
And then he bites your hand and you
realized that is not your best friend
anymore. Something has taken over his
mind. A few days later, Maximus dies.
You grieve the death of your friend, but
the bite he gave you won't stop itching.
Then it starts burning. Your head hurts.
You can't sleep. Every sound gets on
your nerves. You feel thirsty, but when
you try to drink, your throat locks up.
Then you go mad. The people around have
no choice but to restrain you. You
scream. You bite. You fight people who
try to help. You lose control of your
own mind. A few days later, you're dead.
A terrifying way to die. And cases like
this have been recorded throughout
history. The Eshnunna Code, a
Mesopotamian legal text written around
4,000 years ago, contains the earliest
written mention of rabies. It includes a
law stating that if a dog bites a person
and that person dies as a result, the
dog's owner must pay a fine. Scholars
believe this implies the community
already understood that certain dog
bites could lead to fatal illness. They
had seen it happen enough times to build
it into their legal system. Laws do not
get written about hypothetical
situations. The people of Eshnunna had
clearly been watching this happen for
generations. Ancient Egyptian texts from
roughly the same era reference a
condition caused by dog bites that sent
people into states of uncontrollable
terror and madness. The god Sirius was
sometimes invoked in connection with
dog-related illness, and some historians
believe early Egyptian mythology around
mad dogs and divine punishment may have
been shaped in part by repeated
encounters with rabies. Moving into
ancient Greece, the Greeks called the
condition lyssa, meaning frenzy or rage.
The playwright Euripides used it as a
dramatic device. Demosthenes referenced
it in speeches, and Aristotle made an
observation that was centuries ahead of
his time. He correctly identified that
rabies spread through the saliva of
infected animals, commonly dogs, and
that it was invariably fatal in humans
once symptoms appeared. He had no
understanding of viruses. He had no
microscope, no germ theory, and yet he
had correctly identified the
transmission mechanism purely through
careful observation of patterns. Rome
absorbed Greek medical knowledge and
added its own. Roman writers, including
Virgil, Ovid, and Pliny the Elder, all
wrote about rabid animals, and Roman
physicians developed some of the
earliest formal treatment protocols for
bite wounds. Celsus, writing in the 1st
century, recommended aggressively
cutting out the bitten flesh and
cauterizing the wound with a hot iron
immediately after exposure. This was not
entirely wrong. Heat applied quickly
enough to a fresh wound can destroy the
virus before it reaches nerve tissue.
So, what is actually happening inside
the body? When the rabies virus enters
the body through a bite, it does
something almost sinister in its
patience. Rather than spreading through
the bloodstream like most pathogens, it
hijacks the peripheral nervous system
and travels slowly from the wound toward
the spinal cord and then up into the
brain. This journey can take weeks or
even months, which is why the incubation
period is so unusually long and
variable. Once it reaches the brain, it
targets the limbic system, the region
governing emotion, memory, and behavior.
The result is the unmistakable
progression of aggression, confusion,
and that extraordinary aversion to water
where the simple act of swallowing
triggers violent muscle spasms. The
virus also drives heavy salivation,
which is not incidental. It is the
mechanism by which the virus gets
transmitted. The disease has essentially
engineered its own spread through the
behavior of its host. Once symptoms
appear, survival is nearly impossible.
In all of recorded medical history,
there have been fewer than 20 documented
human survivors, nearly all involving
prior vaccination. The long silent
incubation followed by rapid and total
neurological collapse is exactly what
made rabies so terrifying to ancient and
medieval observers. In countries where
the natural world was understood through
divine will and supernatural forces,
rabies fit almost too neatly into
existing frameworks of punishment,
possession, and transformation. In
ancient India, texts from the
Atharvaveda, written around 3,000 years
ago, describe a dog bite illness with
symptoms matching rabies and attribute
it to a demon called Kandu. The
prescribed treatment involved ritual
purification, specific herbs, and
prayers to Indra. In ancient China,
records from as early as 556 BC describe
what appears to be rabies in dogs and
the madness that followed human bites.
Chinese physicians developed their own
bite wound treatments and, like the
Romans, eventually landed on
cauterization as one of the more
effective options. Medieval Europe had
no shortage of exposure to rabid
animals. Wolves were a real and
persistent threat across the continent,
and wolf attacks on villages were not
uncommon. When a wolf attacked and bit
several people in a single incident, and
then weeks later those people began
exhibiting violent, erratic behavior,
flinching from water, foaming at the
mouth, the community had no framework
for understanding what they were
witnessing. The werewolf myth, in its
most persistent medieval form, maps with
uncomfortable precision onto a rabies
outbreak. A person is bitten by a wolf.
After a period of apparent normalcy,
they begin to change. They become
aggressive, unpredictable. They lose the
ability to behave like a person. They
may growl, bite, attack those closest to
them. They die, and no one can explain
what happened. For most of history, from
Mesopotamia through Greece, Rome, and
the medieval world, there was no
effective treatment for rabies once
symptoms appeared. People could only
manage the wound and hope. Different
cultures developed their own remedies.
Romans placed hair from the attacking
dog into the wound, while medieval
physicians prescribed poultices,
prayers, and pilgrimages. In Europe,
many rabies victims traveled to the
shrine of Saint Hubert of Belgium,
patron saint of rabies sufferers. Some
communities even pressed a heated metal
key associated with the saint into bite
wounds. The heat may have provided some
real benefit, though no one understood
why. In the 16th century, the Italian
physician Girolamo Fracastoro proposed
that diseases spread through invisible
particles passed between people and
animals. He cited rabies as an example,
observing that something in the saliva
of infected animals entered through
wounds. Then, in 1885, everything
changed. Louis Pasteur, already famous
for his work on germ theory and
vaccination, turned his attention to
rabies. Unable to see the virus itself,
he developed an attenuated vaccine from
infected animal tissue and tested it in
dogs. On July 6th, 1885, a 9-year-old
boy named Joseph Meister was brought to
Pasteur after being severely bitten by a
rabid dog. With no other options
available, Pasteur administered his
experimental vaccine over 13 days.
Meister survived. For the first time in
4,000 years of recorded history,
medicine had a real defense against
rabies. Meister went on to live a full
life and later worked as a gatekeeper at
the Pasteur Institute, the very place
where his life had been saved. Rabies is
one of the oldest diseases in the human
record. It shaped our myths, our laws,
our monsters. It gave medieval Europe
its werewolves and gave ancient
physicians some of their first lessons
in the relationship between animal
behavior and human death. It killed
without mercy or exception for 40
centuries before a single person
survived it. The virus is still out
there in bats, in foxes, in dogs across
Africa and Asia where it still kills
roughly 59,000 people a year, most of
them children. The same pathogen, the
same progression, the same ending. What
changed is not the disease. What changed
is that we finally understood it and
maybe someday we could develop a cure
for it.

actor_text:
Rabies is one of the oldest and most terrifying diseases in human history.

For over 4,000 years, civilizations from Mesopotamia, Egypt, Greece, Rome, India, and medieval Europe documented the same horrifying pattern: a bite from an animal, a period of apparent normality, and then a descent into madness, aggression, hydrophobia, and death.

In this video, we explore the complete history of rabies, from its earliest appearance in ancient law codes to its influence on mythology, folklore, and the werewolf legends of medieval Europe. We examine how ancient physicians recognized the disease long before microscopes existed, why rabies became associated with possession and transformation, and how generations lived in fear of a disease that was almost always fatal.

We also follow the scientific breakthrough that finally changed everything, culminating in Louis Pasteur's revolutionary vaccine and the survival of Joseph Meister in 1885.

Rabies shaped laws, inspired myths, created monsters, and remained undefeated for thousands of years. This is the story of humanity's longest battle against one of nature's most ruthless killers.

Sources and script research include historical records from Mesopotamia, Ancient Greece, Rome, India, China, medieval Europe, and modern medical literature on rabies.

If you enjoyed this video, consider liking, subscribing, and sharing it with others interested in history, medicine, mythology, and the darker side of the human past.

description:
What is the rarest possible person on Earth?

This video explores a fascinating question: if we combined some of the rarest human traits known to science, what would the rarest human being look like?

From extremely small ethnic groups and albinism to complete heterochromia, left handedness, tetrachromacy, and hyperthymesia, we calculate the odds step by step and discover just how astronomically unlikely one person can be.

Along the way, you'll learn about genetics, human diversity, rare neurological conditions, and the incredible uniqueness hidden within every individual.

By the end, you'll see why the chances of being exactly who you are may be far smaller than you ever imagined.

If you enjoyed the video, consider liking, subscribing, and sharing it with someone who appreciates strange statistics and fascinating facts about humanity.

transcript_plaintext:
You are sitting in a park one afternoon,
when a woman walks by and sits beside
you. She is white as snow. Her hair is
silver and curly. Her eyes are blue. You
are captivated, so you ask her name. She
says Abarash, and she adds she's from a
tribe in sub-Saharan Africa. And then
you realize she is a black woman with
albinism. You ask for her number. She
takes your phone and types with her left
hand. You go on dates and she is
brilliant. You have fallen in love, and
luckily she becomes your girlfriend. And
then your alarm goes off. It was just a
dream. You just lay there heart racing
and dumbfounded, and you ask yourself,
"Does a person like that actually exist?
Statistically?" Yes. But that raises a
more interesting question. Out of the 8
billion people alive today, what would
the rarest possible person look like? To
answer that, we need to break humanity
down trait by trait, starting with where
our person comes from. There are roughly
7,000 distinct ethnic groups on Earth.
Most of humanity is concentrated in a
relatively small number of large ethnic
populations. Han Chinese alone account
for about 18% of the global population.
That is more than 1.4 billion people
from a single ethnic group. But on the
other end of that scale, sit some of the
smallest ethnic groups alive. The
Sentinelese of the Andaman Islands are
estimated at between 50 and 400 people.
The Kawahiva of the Brazilian Amazon are
thought to be fewer than 30 individuals.
The Spinifex people of Australia
numbered only around 200 at their last
count. For our rarest human, we place
their ethnic origin in one of these
groups. We will use a conservative
population of 500 people within a global
population of 8 billion. That is 500
divided by 8 billion, or 1 in 16
million. Our person has now a
0.0000000625%
chance of existing. Now we give this
person albinism. Albinism is a genetic
condition caused by mutations
in genes responsible for melanin
production. Melanin is the pigment that
determines the color of skin, hair, and
eyes. In a person with complete
albinism, this production pathway is
either severely reduced or entirely
absent. The result is white or
near-white skin, very light or silver
hair, and eyes that range from light
blue to gray to pink depending on how
light interacts with the unpigmented
iris. Globally, albinism occurs in
approximately 1 in 20,000 people.
Combining both probability, our person
has now a 1 in 320 billion chance of
existing. Now, the eyes. Green eyes are
the rarest color with a probability of 1
in 50 people. But, this is not the
rarest eye mutation. Complete
heterochromia is a rare condition in
which a person has two completely
different eye colors, such as one blue
eye and one brown eye. It is usually
present from birth and results from
differences in the amount or
distribution of melanin. In most cases,
it is harmless and does not affect
vision. The chance of having this eye
trait is about 0.06%
or 1 in 1,667
people. Now, let's make this person
left-handed. Handedness is partly
heritable, but no single gene determines
it. Even identical twins who share
nearly identical DNA differ in
handedness about 20% of the time. Brain
lateralization also plays a key role.
Most right-handed people process
language mainly in the left hemisphere,
while left-handed people often show more
bilateral organization with both
hemispheres sharing the load. In many
traditional communities, social pressure
encourages children to use their right
hand, which may lead to underreporting
of natural left-handedness. While the
true rate could be somewhat higher, a
conservative estimate remains about 10%
or 1 in 10 people. Now, combining
ethnicity, albinism, eye color, and
handedness, our person has now a 1 in
5.33 quadrillion chance of existing.
Now, most humans see color through three
types of cone cells in the retina,
sensitive roughly to blue, green, and
red wavelengths. The brain combines
signals from these cones to create the
roughly 1 million colors visible to
normal human vision. Tetrachromats have
a fourth cone type, sensitive to
wavelengths between red and green. This
can provide color information most
people cannot see, allowing some
tetrachromats to distinguish up to 100
million colors. Tetrachromacy is almost
exclusively found in women because it is
linked to the X chromosome. Women can
inherit both a standard and a mutated
version of the relevant gene,
potentially creating a fourth cone type,
while men generally cannot. About 12% of
women carry the mutation, but only a
small fraction develop functional
tetrachromacy. Researchers estimate it
occurs in roughly 1 in 40,000 women, or
1 in 80,000 people overall. Our rarest
human remembers everything.
Hyperthymesia, or highly superior
autobiographical memory, is the ability
to recall nearly every day of one's life
in extraordinary detail. Not just major
events, but ordinary days,
conversations, and experiences. The
condition was first formally identified
in 2006 by neuroscientist James McGaugh
after Jill Price described to stop
remembering her past. She likened it to
a continuous involuntary replay of her
life. Fewer than 100 confirmed cases
have been identified worldwide. Even
generous estimates that include
undiagnosed individuals place the total
at only a few hundred people globally,
making hyperthymesia one of the rarest
known memory traits. Conservatively, we
place the probability at 500 out of 8
billion, which is 1 in 16 million. To
recap, the rarest human we created so
far is from an ethnicity of 500 people,
has albinism, has complete
heterochromia, is left-handed, has
tetrachromacy, and has hyperthymesia. In
other words, this person. That brings
the total probability of that person
existing to 1 in 6.83 septillion. To put
that into perspective, the number of
stars in the observable universe is
roughly at most 1 septillion. If you
count all the grains of sand on Earth,
you would need to have 910,000
Earths to to to that number. And this is
not even the rarest person you can make.
There are still so many traits that hold
countless possibilities. Rare blood
types, body mutations, intelligence
level, etc. Too many to add to the
video. The point is that all of us are
unique and have beaten unbelievable odds
to exist as who we are. It's true that
there are plenty of fish in the sea, but
no one is as cool as you. So, keep on
swimming.
>> [music]

actor_text:
What is the rarest possible person on Earth?

This video explores a fascinating question: if we combined some of the rarest human traits known to science, what would the rarest human being look like?

From extremely small ethnic groups and albinism to complete heterochromia, left handedness, tetrachromacy, and hyperthymesia, we calculate the odds step by step and discover just how astronomically unlikely one person can be.

Along the way, you'll learn about genetics, human diversity, rare neurological conditions, and the incredible uniqueness hidden within every individual.

By the end, you'll see why the chances of being exactly who you are may be far smaller than you ever imagined.

If you enjoyed the video, consider liking, subscribing, and sharing it with someone who appreciates strange statistics and fascinating facts about humanity.
