video_title: Did Ancient Humans get Cancer?
description:
In this video, we explore the remarkable evidence showing that cancer has existed for millions of years. From a 1.7 million year old fossilized bone discovered in South Africa to tumors found in ancient Egyptian mummies, the story of cancer stretches deep into our evolutionary past.

Discover how ancient humans experienced cancer long before modern lifestyles, why scientists have found evidence of tumors in fossils and mummies, and how civilizations thousands of years ago documented this devastating disease. Learn why cancer is an unavoidable consequence of multicellular life, why longer lifespans make it more common today, and how researchers are studying nature itself for clues that could help us fight it.

Cancer is not just a medical challenge. It is one of the oldest evolutionary battles ever faced by our species. And for the first time in that long history, humanity has the tools to understand it and push back.

Sources: 

Armelagos, G. J., Brown, P. J., & Turner, B. (2005). Evolutionary, historical and political economic perspectives on health and disease. *Social Science & Medicine, 61*(4), 755–765. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.socscimed.2...

David, A. R., Zimmerman, M. R., & Aufderheide, A. C. (2010). Cancer: An old disease, a new disease or something in between? *Nature Reviews Cancer, 10*(10), 728–733. https://doi.org/10.1038/nrc2914

Hippocrates. (1923). Aphorisms (W. H. S. Jones, Trans.). Harvard University Press. (Original work published ca. 400 BCE)

Odes, E. J., Randolph Quinney, P. S., Alqahtani, S. J., & Hublin, J. J. (2016). Earliest hominin cancer: 1.7 million year old osteosarcoma from Swartkrans Cave, South Africa. *South African Journal of Science, 112*(7/8), 1–5. https://doi.org/10.17159/sajs.2016/20...

Zimmerman, M. R. (2010). Paleopathology of cancer: North American perspective. *Human Pathology, 41*(7), 1007–1014. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.humpath.200...

Breivik, J. (2015). The evolutionary origin of genetic instability in cancer development. *Seminars in Cancer Biology, 35*, S92–S97. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.semcancer.2...

transcript_plaintext:
Cancer is brutal. It just starts
quietly. Somewhere deep inside the body,
a single cell goes wrong. Then another,
then another. And then one day a doctor
sits across from you and says the words,
"You have cancer." It steals years. It
steals people. It hollows out families.
It takes the young. It takes the old. It
does not care who you are or how much
you have to live for. Cancer is one of
the most savage things that exists in
nature. And the worst part? It's been
here since the beginning. Most people
think cancer is a modern disease. We
blame processed food, pollution, and our
sedentary lifestyles. And while those
things definitely play a role, the truth
is far older. In 2016, inside a cave in
South Africa, they found a foot bone
from a human ancestor. The bone belonged
to a species called Australopithecus or
early Homo. It was approximately 1.7
million years old, and it showed clear
signs of osteosarcoma, a malignant bone
cancer. This was not a crack or an
injury. The bone had a tumor. Growing in
a creature that walked the earth before
our species even existed. The same study
also found a benign spinal tumor in a
skeleton from roughly the same time
period. Scientists call these types of
growths neoplasms, and finding them in
fossils from nearly 2 million years ago
tells us something profound. Cancer is
not new. Cancer is ancient. Cancer
mostly affects soft tissue, organs,
skin, blood. Soft tissue does not
fossilize. It disappears over centuries
and millennia. What survives is bone.
So, what we find in the fossil record is
only a tiny fraction of the cancers that
actually existed. Scientists call this a
preservation bias. We are only seeing
the cancers that left a mark on hard
tissue. That is why mummies have been so
valuable. Mummies preserve soft tissue.
And mummies have told us a great deal.
Researchers using CT scans and advanced
imaging have found tumors in Egyptian
mummies that are thousands of years old.
One study scanned 137 mummies and found
evidence of cancer in several of them.
So, the fossil and mummy record together
paint a consistent picture. Ancient
humans got cancer regularly, but we do
not have to rely only on bones and
mummies. Ancient people wrote about
cancer, too. The Edwin Smith Papyrus
from ancient Egypt dates back to around
1600 BCE. It describes bulging tumors of
the breast. The text notes they have no
treatment. That is a frank and
devastating acknowledgement from a
physician writing nearly 4,000 years
ago. The Greek physician Hippocrates,
who lived around 400 BCE, gave cancer
its name. He used the word karkinos.
That is the Greek word for crab. He
thought the swollen veins around a tumor
looked like crab legs reaching outward.
The Roman physician Celsus later
translated that word into the Latin word
cancer. That is the word we still use
today. So, for thousands of years across
multiple civilizations, people observed
cancer, documented it, and tried to
understand it. They just did not know
what was causing it. To understand why
cancer is ancient, we need to understand
what cancer actually is. Cancer begins
when a cell gets a mutation. The DNA
inside the cell gets damaged or copied
incorrectly. Most of the time, the body
catches and fixes these errors, but
sometimes a mutated cell escapes that
correction system. It starts dividing
uncontrollably. It builds up into a
mass. It invades surrounding tissue.
Mutations happen naturally. They can
happen every time a cell divides. They
are part of life itself. The more cells
you have and the longer you live, the
more chances there are for a mutation to
slip through. Every living organism with
cells that divide carries this risk.
Dinosaurs got cancer, ancient fish got
cancer, even trees can get cancer. So,
did ancient humans actually get cancer
less frequently than we do today? The
honest answer is probably yes, but not
for the reasons people usually think.
The biggest reason is lifespan. Most
ancient humans died young. They died
from infection, injury, predators, and
famine. The average life expectancy for
a prehistoric human was roughly 25 to 35
years. Cancer takes time. Most cancers
develop after the age of 50. If you die
at 30 from a lion attack or a tooth
infection, cancer never has a chance to
develop. Ancient humans also had
different risk factors. They did not
smoke tobacco. They were not exposed to
industrial chemicals. They ate whole
foods. They moved their bodies
constantly. All of these things reduced
certain cancer risks. But, they had
their own risks, too. Smoke from cooking
fires caused lung irritation. Parasitic
infections and chronic inflammation can
promote certain cancers. Sunlight
exposure without protection raises skin
cancer risk. They were not living in a
cancer-free paradise. They were just
dying of other things first. So, why
does it seem like cancer is everywhere
today? Part of the answer is that we
live longer. Modern medicine has
eliminated or reduced many of the things
that killed people young. So, we now
have millions of people reaching their
60s, 70s, and 80s. That is the prime
window for cancer to develop and be
detected. Another part of the answer is
detection. We have technologies now that
can find a tumor the size of a
fingernail inside the body. Ancient
physicians could only see what was
visible or felt on the surface. Most
internal cancers went completely
undetected. And yes, modern lifestyle
factors do increase certain cancer
risks. Tobacco is directly linked to
lung, throat, and mouth cancer.
Processed red meat is linked to
colorectal cancer. Obesity is connected
to over a dozen cancer types. UV
radiation causes skin cancer.
Understanding that cancer is ancient
actually helps scientists today. If
cancer has been with us for millions of
years, it means it is woven deep into
the fabric of multicellular life.
Researchers are now studying why some
ancient animals seem to have had lower
cancer rates. Elephants, for example,
carry extra copies of a
cancer-suppressing gene called TP53.
Scientists are studying those genes to
see if they can create human cancer
treatment. The fossil record also helps
us track how cancer rates change over
time. By comparing ancient bone tumors
to modern ones, researchers can study
how certain cancers evolve and which
conditions seem to trigger them. Cancer
is not just a medical problem. It is an
evolutionary puzzle, and understanding
its deep history is part of solving it.
A 1.7 million-year-old bone, a tumor, a
creature that lived before language,
before fire, before civilization. Cancer
was there. It is one of the oldest
adversaries the human lineage has ever
faced. And for the first time in that
long history, we actually have the tools
to fight back.
>> [music]

In this video, we explore the remarkable evidence showing that cancer has existed for millions of years. From a 1.7 million year old fossilized bone discovered in South Africa to tumors found in ancient Egyptian mummies, the story of cancer stretches deep into our evolutionary past.

Discover how ancient humans experienced cancer long before modern lifestyles, why scientists have found evidence of tumors in fossils and mummies, and how civilizations thousands of years ago documented this devastating disease. Learn why cancer is an unavoidable consequence of multicellular life, why longer lifespans make it more common today, and how researchers are studying nature itself for clues that could help us fight it.

Cancer is not just a medical challenge. It is one of the oldest evolutionary battles ever faced by our species. And for the first time in that long history, humanity has the tools to understand it and push back.

video_title: Why are Humans Scared of Spiders
description:
Why are so many people terrified of spiders, even though most spiders are completely harmless?

In this video, we explore the fascinating science behind arachnophobia, one of the most common fears in the world. From the role of the amygdala and the fight or flight response to groundbreaking studies involving infants, psychologists, and evolutionary biology, you'll discover why spiders seem to have a unique ability to trigger fear in humans.

Learn how millions of years of evolution may have hardwired our brains to detect spiders faster than other threats, why babies react to spider images before they can learn fear from others, and how disgust and fear work together to make arachnophobia so powerful.

Whether you love spiders, fear them, or are simply curious about human psychology, this video reveals the surprising reasons behind one of humanity's oldest and most widespread fears.

If you enjoy science, psychology, evolution, and fascinating facts about human behavior, be sure to like, subscribe, and turn on notifications for more videos.

Sources:

Hoehl, S., Hellmer, K., Johansson, M., & Gredebäck, G. (2017). Itsy bitsy spider...: Infants react with increased arousal to spiders and snakes. *Frontiers in Psychology, 8*, 1710. [https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.01710]

New, J., Cosmides, L., & Tooby, J. (2007). Category specific attention for animals reflects ancestral priorities, not expertise. *Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 104*(42), 16598–16603. [https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0703913104]

New, J., & German, T. C. (2015). Spiders at the cocktail party: An ancestral threat that surmounts inattentional blindness. *Evolution and Human Behavior, 36*(3), 165–173. [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.evolhumbeha...]

Polák, J., Sedláčková, K., Nácar, D., Landová, E., & Frynta, D. (2021). Fear, disgust, and aesthetic responses to live arthropods. *Scientific Reports, 11*, 22022. [https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-021-01...]

Öhman, A., & Mineka, S. (2001). Fears, phobias, and preparedness: Toward an evolved module of fear and fear learning. *Psychological Review, 108*(3), 483–522. [https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.108...](https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.108...)
transcript_plaintext:
You walk into a room and you see
something small skitters across the
wall. You look closer, it's a spider and
before your brain has formed a single
thought, your heart is already pounding.
You may have screamed, you may have
grabbed a shoe, but the spider was
probably harmless. So, what is actually
going on? Why does a creature that has
never wronged you and in most cases
couldn't even hurt you trigger one of
the most powerful fear responses a human
being can have? The answer is woven into
your DNA, your evolutionary history and
some genuinely fascinating science.
First, the numbers. Arachnophobia is one
of the most common specific phobias on
Earth. Roughly 1/3 of women and 1/4 of
men experience measurable spider fear
and for many of them it is severe enough
to affect daily life. Studies in the UK
estimate around 4% of the population
meets the clinical threshold for
arachnophobia. And here is the thing
that should puzzle you. Of the roughly
45,000 known spider species, only a tiny
fraction are genuinely dangerous to
humans. The fear is wildly out of
proportion to the actual threat. And
that disproportionality is exactly what
makes it so scientifically interesting.
When you see a spider, the response does
not start consciously. It starts in the
amygdala, a small almond-shaped
structure deep in your brain that
functions as your threat detection
alarm. The amygdala processes incoming
sensory data at extraordinary speed and
can launch a full stress response before
your rational, conscious mind has even
been consulted. Adrenaline floods your
system, your pupils dilate, your muscles
tense. You are already in fight or
flight before you have consciously
registered what you are looking at. This
is not a design flaw, it is a survival
feature. The question is why spiders
specifically seem to have a dedicated
fast lane into that system. To answer
that, you have to go back to the East
African savanna tens of thousands of
years ago where our earliest ancestors
were emerging. Researchers from Columbia
University, including psychologist
Joshua New and his colleague Tamson
German, proposed that the human visual
system retains what they called
ancestral mechanisms uniquely dedicated
to the rapid detection of immediate and
specific threats that persistently
recurred throughout evolutionary time.
In that early environment, many spiders
were venomous. With no antivenom and no
medicine, a bite could be fatal. Natural
selection heavily favored individuals
whose nervous systems detected and
avoided spiders fastest because those
individuals survived, reproduced, and
passed on their genes. Over hundreds of
thousands of years, the alarm became
hardwired. The fear was not learned, it
was inherited, and it is still sitting
in your genome. The most compelling
evidence for this came from the Max
Planck Institute for human cognitive and
brain sciences in Germany.
Neuroscientist Stephanie Hoehl's team
worked with 48 infants who were only 6
months old. These babies had not seen
horror movies, had not heard a parent
scream, had not absorbed any cultural
messaging about spiders. They were a
clean slate. Using an infrared eye
tracker to measure pupil dilation, the
researchers showed the infants images of
spiders and images of flowers as a
comparison. When shown spiders, the
infants' pupils dilated to an average of
0.14 mm. For flowers, just 0.03
mm. Nearly five times the response in
babies with no reason to consciously
fear anything. Hoehl concluded that the
fear of spiders appears to be deeply
embedded in our evolutionary heritage,
present from birth, not built from
experience. New and German's Columbia
research confirmed something else
remarkable. The human brain appears to
have a preloaded spider template it is
constantly and subconsciously scanning
for. In their experiment, 252 volunteers
viewed computer screens filled with
abstract shapes and various images
including distorted spiders, hypodermic
needles, and houseflies. Participants
detected spider images faster and more
reliably than any other image. Even a
broken, unnatural spider image beat out
a clear image of a needle or a fly.
There is one more piece of science worth
knowing. Fear and disgust are separate
but reinforcing systems. A 2021 study in
Scientific Reports analyzed emotional
responses to live arthropods and found
that spiders and scorpions triggered the
highest combined levels of both fear and
disgust. Disgust evolved as a pathogen
avoidance mechanism. Things associated
with contamination, decay, and hidden
dark spaces trigger it automatically.
Spiders with their unpredictable
movement and their tendency to lurk in
corners near dead things register as
both a physical threat and a
contamination risk. Both signals fire at
once, which is part of why the aversion
is so intense and so stubbornly
resistant to logic. So, the next time a
spider sends you scrambling, know that
you are not being irrational. You are
responding to a signal carved into your
nervous system by millions of years of
survival on a dangerous planet. Your
ancestors who felt that alarm and acted
on it lived. You are the product of
their caution. But, you also live in a
world where that caution is almost never
necessary anymore. The spider in your
bathroom corner is not hunting you. It
is eating the mosquitoes and bugs that
pests you. So, don't squash them.
They're your friends.

Why are so many people terrified of spiders, even though most spiders are completely harmless?

In this video, we explore the fascinating science behind arachnophobia, one of the most common fears in the world. From the role of the amygdala and the fight or flight response to groundbreaking studies involving infants, psychologists, and evolutionary biology, you'll discover why spiders seem to have a unique ability to trigger fear in humans.

Learn how millions of years of evolution may have hardwired our brains to detect spiders faster than other threats, why babies react to spider images before they can learn fear from others, and how disgust and fear work together to make arachnophobia so powerful.

Whether you love spiders, fear them, or are simply curious about human psychology, this video reveals the surprising reasons behind one of humanity's oldest and most widespread fears.

description:
Why do we eat three meals a day? Breakfast, lunch, and dinner feel like a natural part of life—but this daily routine is far more recent than most people realize.

In this video, we explore the surprising history of the three-meal day, from prehistoric hunter-gatherers and ancient civilizations to the British Royal Navy, the Industrial Revolution, and the rise of the breakfast industry. Along the way, we'll uncover how agriculture, religion, factory schedules, commerce, and human biology helped shape the way we eat today.

You'll also discover what modern science says about meal timing, metabolism, and whether our bodies are actually designed to eat three times a day.

The story behind breakfast, lunch, and dinner is much more fascinating than you might think.

transcript_plaintext:
You woke up this morning and ate
breakfast. Around noon, you probably
grabbed lunch. And tonight, you will sit
down for dinner. You did not question
it. You never have. It just feels like
the natural order of things. But, here
is what almost no one talks about.
Nobody decided this for you based on
biology. No doctor prescribed it. No
ancient wisdom handed it down. Three
meals a day is not a law of nature. It
is a story. And it is one of the most
fascinating stories in all of human
history.
Let us go back. Way back. Around 23,000
years ago, on the shores of what is now
the Sea of Galilee in Israel, there was
a place called Ohalo II. Archaeologists
found the remains of small brush-walled
dwellings there, each one built around a
hearth. Scattered near those hearths was
evidence of over 140 types of seeds and
nuts. There were bones, too, from birds,
fish, and small mammals. The people who
lived here were hunter-gatherers. They
ate whenever food was available. Not
three times a day, not twice. Just
whenever. There were no meal times
because there was no guaranteed food
supply. Some days they feasted, some
days they went hungry. The very concept
of a structured daily eating schedule
would have meant nothing to them. Eating
was not a routine. It was a result. The
result of a successful hunt or a lucky
morning of foraging. Then something
happened that changed everything.
Around 10,000 BCE, agriculture took hold
in the Fertile Crescent, across parts of
modern-day Iraq, Iran, and Turkey. For
the first time, people had a reliable
food supply. They did not need to chase
food anymore. Food stayed put, so people
stayed put, too. Permanent settlements
formed. Cooking grew more complex. Meals
became more communal. But even then,
three structured meals a day did not
exist. What people ate and when still
depended entirely on culture, geography,
and daylight. Ancient Egypt gives us one
of the earliest pictures of structured
eating. Egyptians typically ate two
meals, a light morning meal of bread and
beer, and a heavier evening meal with
vegetables, lentils, and whatever
protein was available. Two meals, not
three. The ancient Greeks were a little
closer to what we would recognize today.
They had a small morning meal called
akratisma, which was basically bread
dipped in wine. Then came ariston, a
midday meal. And finally deipnon, a more
substantial evening gathering. But not
everyone ate all three. These were not
fixed time locked events. The Romans are
perhaps the most surprising case of all.
The Roman Empire was one of the most
organized civilizations the world had
ever seen. You might expect them to have
had a strict meal schedule. They did
not. The Romans were deeply suspicious
of eating more than once a day.
Historian Caroline Yeldham explains that
they were obsessed with digestion and
believed that eating multiple meals was
simply a form of gluttony. Their primary
meal was called cena, eaten around
midday. A small morning snack called
ientaculum existed, but it was barely
treated as a real meal. This one meal
model stayed dominant across much of
Europe for centuries. Then came the
moment when European settlers arrived in
the Americas. They were genuinely
shocked by how Native Americans ate.
According to historian Abigail Carroll,
author of Three Squares, the settlers
watched indigenous people eat in ways
that seemed chaotic to them. Native
Americans fasted when necessary,
adjusted their food intake with the
seasons, and followed no fixed daily
schedule. The Europeans called this
uncivilized. That bias would eventually
help spread three meals a day across the
entire world. So, where exactly did the
three meal structure actually come from?
The answer takes us to 16th century
Europe and a world that was beginning to
organize itself around the clock. The
British Royal Navy was one of the first
large institutions to formalize three
meals a day. Since at least the 1500s,
the Navy served sailors three set meals
built around the shipboard routine. A
simple breakfast of ship's biscuits and
salted meat, a midday lunch as the main
meal, and a lighter dinner in the
evening. The reasoning was entirely
practical. Sailors needed fuel at
predictable intervals. Physical naval
work was relentless and the schedule had
to match it. But what truly locked three
meals into the lives of ordinary people
was the Industrial Revolution. Starting
around 1760 in Britain and spreading
across Europe and North America over the
following century, the Industrial
Revolution changed how people related to
time itself. For the first time, large
numbers of people were not working in
fields with loose seasonal rhythms. They
were working in factories with rigid
standardized hours. You clocked in and
out at a fixed time. You had one break
in the middle of the day. Breakfast
before work, lunch at midday, dinner
after the shift, it mapped perfectly
onto the new industrial schedule. Three
meals a day was not a discovery. It was
a solution, an organizational answer to
the demands of factory life. As cities
grew and people moved away from farms,
the morning meal became increasingly
important. The word breakfast literally
means to break the fast of the night
before. In medieval Christian Europe,
eating before morning mass was often
discouraged. So, breakfast as a regular
full meal was slow to catch on. But
skipping a morning meal while working a
10- or 12-hour industrial shift was not
a spiritual discipline. It was a health
hazard. The morning meal became
essential. Dinner shifted, too. Before
industrialization, the main meal was
eaten at midday when natural light was
at its strongest. But as artificial
lighting improved and factories kept
workers busy well into the afternoon,
the main meal migrated to the evening.
By the mid-1800s,
dinner after work had become the daily
anchor for most people in Europe and the
United States. Then in the early 20th
century, the final piece fell into
place. Someone you might not expect
helped cement breakfast as a daily
ritual, a serial entrepreneur named John
Harvey Kellogg. Kellogg invented
cornflakes as a health food and through
aggressive marketing campaigns in the
1920s and 1930s, the idea that breakfast
was the most important meal of the day
spread everywhere. It was not pure
science. It was also commerce. Cereal
companies needed people eating breakfast
every single morning, and it worked.
Now, here is the most important question
of all. Does your biology actually want
you to eat three times a day? The answer
might surprise you. Inside every human
being is a circadian rhythm, your body's
internal 24-hour clock. Research
published in Current Biology shows that
the timing of your meals affects blood
glucose, insulin sensitivity,
metabolism, and even the behavior of fat
cells at a cellular level. In the
morning, cortisol rises, and your body
becomes remarkably efficient at
processing food. Insulin sensitivity is
near its peak, meaning carbohydrates and
sugars are more likely to be converted
into usable energy instead of stored
fat. Eat that exact same meal late at
night, and the outcome changes
dramatically. Blood sugar rises higher,
sleep quality worsens, fat storage
increases. Your hunger hormones, ghrelin
and leptin, follow this rhythm, too. In
fact, your body begins preparing for
meals before you even take the first
bite. Scientists call this physiological
food anticipation. Your biology is not
passive. It learns your habits, predicts
your routines, and adjusts itself around
them. And that reveals something
important. What matters most is not
necessarily the number of meals you eat,
but when you eat them. Two meals, three
meals, or even four can all work
reasonably well as long as most food is
consumed during daylight hours when the
body is metabolically prepared for it.
But biology is only part of the story.
For more than 23,000 years, humans have
gathered around food not just to
survive, but to connect. Long before
factories, office schedules, or cereal
advertisements existed, shared meals
were how communities built trust,
strengthened relationships, and signaled
safety. Research in social psychology
consistently finds that people who eat
regularly with others report greater
happiness, stronger social bonds, and a
deeper sense of belonging. Three meals a
day, whatever its historical origins,
gives us three recurring opportunities
to do something profoundly human. So,
why do we eat three meals a day? Because
sailors needed schedules, because
factory workers needed predictable
breaks, because medieval Christians
could not eat before mass, because
industrial society reorganized life
around the clock, because cereal
companies turned breakfast into a
business opportunity, and because
underneath all of that history, human
biology already operated on rhythms that
happened to align with it. Three meals a
day is not a biological law, but it is
not a meaningless invention, either. It
is the result of centuries of religion,
agriculture, industry, commerce, and
human physiology gradually shaping one
another over time. Tonight, you will
probably sit down for dinner like
billions of people before you. And now,
you will know why.

companies needed people eating breakfast
every single morning, and it worked.

you to eat three times a day? The answer
might surprise you. Inside every human

internal 24-hour clock. Research

metabolism, and even the behavior of fat

near its peak, meaning carbohydrates and
sugars are more likely to be converted

deeper sense of belonging. Three meals a
day, whatever its historical origins,
gives us three recurring opportunities
to do something profoundly human. So,
why do we eat three meals a day? Because
sailors needed schedules, because
factory workers needed predictable
breaks, because medieval Christians

industrial society reorganized life

Why do we eat three meals a day? Breakfast, lunch, and dinner feel like a natural part of life—but this daily routine is far more recent than most people realize.

In this video, we explore the surprising history of the three-meal day, from prehistoric hunter-gatherers and ancient civilizations to the British Royal Navy, the Industrial Revolution, and the rise of the breakfast industry. Along the way, we'll uncover how agriculture, religion, factory schedules, commerce, and human biology helped shape the way we eat today.

You'll also discover what modern science says about meal timing, metabolism, and whether our bodies are actually designed to eat three times a day.

The story behind breakfast, lunch, and dinner is much more fascinating than you might think.

description:
Why does food feel incomplete without a video playing in the background?

For millions of people, eating and watching have become inseparable. Breakfast with YouTube. Lunch with TikTok. Dinner with Netflix. But this habit isn’t just a smartphone-era addiction.

It turns out humans have been pairing food with stories, entertainment, and companionship for thousands of years.

In this video, we explore the neuroscience, psychology, history, and culture behind why eating alone feels strange — and why screens have quietly become part of the modern meal.

This video covers:

🍽️ Why food + videos feel unusually satisfying (dopamine & sensory synergy)
🧠 The “distraction-eating paradox” and what happens in your brain while watching
👥 How screens replace social connection during solo meals
🏛️ Ancient Roman banquets, medieval feasts, radio dinners, and the history of eating with entertainment
📺 TV dinners, streaming platforms, autoplay, and why algorithms love your mealtime attention
🇰🇷 Mukbang, ASMR eating, and the psychology of not wanting to eat alone
⚖️ Whether eating while watching is actually bad for you

Humans were never really designed to eat alone in silence. We just replaced the banquet hall with a screen.

probably eating something. Breakfast,
lunch, dinner, it almost doesn't matter
anymore. Eating has quietly become
paired with watching. Before taking the
first bite, we open YouTube, TikTok, or
whatever platform we use, scrolling
until we find the perfect video that
somehow makes the meal feel more
enjoyable. For a lot of people, food no
longer feels complete on its own. A
screen has become part of the
experience. At first, it seems like a
modern habit created by smartphones and
endless content, but this behavior
actually goes much deeper than that. The
urge to pair eating with stimulation is
tied to something much older. Let's
start with your brain because something
genuinely strange happens when you
combine eating and entertainment. Eating
activates your brain's reward system,
specifically the mesolimbic dopamine
pathway. That's the same system that
lights up when you fall in love or win a
game or scroll through social media.
Food triggers dopamine. It's one of the
most fundamental reward signals in your
entire nervous system. When you add
something visually stimulating, a video,
a show, a movie, you're stacking a
second dopamine source on top of the
first. Two reward streams firing
simultaneously. Neuroscientists call
this sensory synergy, which is partly
why your cereal tastes fine, but your
cereal with a YouTube video tastes
weirdly satisfying. But, there's a flip
side. This same effect suppresses what
researchers call interoceptive
awareness, your brain's ability to
listen to your body's internal signals,
like your stomach saying, "Hey, I'm
actually full now." A 2006 study in the
American Journal of Clinical Nutrition
found that people eating while
distracted consumed significantly more
food and reported feeling less satisfied
afterward, even though they'd eaten
more. You ate more, enjoyed it less, and
felt hungry sooner. That's the
distraction eating paradox. Your brain
is so busy processing the screen that it
misses the memo from your stomach. But,
neuroscience is only half the story. The
psychology here goes deeper. Eating
alone is honestly a modern problem. For
most of human history, meals were
communal. You gathered with your tribe,
your family, your village. Eating
together wasn't just about food. It was
bonding. It was safety. It was social
glue. When we eat alone today, which
millions of people do every single day,
something feels off. Evolutionarily, a
solitary meal might have meant you were
isolated, left out, maybe even in
danger. Screens fill that void. When you
watch a show while eating, your brain
partially simulates the experience of
eating with company. The voices, the
faces, the narrative tension, it
activates similar social processing
circuits. Psychologists call this a
parasocial relationship, a one-sided
social bond where you feel connected to
people on screen who don't know you
exist. Friends, The Office, anime, true
crime podcasts, these aren't just
entertainment. During mealtime, they're
surrogate companions. There's also what
psychologists call hedonic escapism,
using pleasurable distraction to avoid
being present with your own thoughts.

uncomfortable quiet. A video immediately
fills that space with novelty,
narrative, humor, drama. Your brain
finds this enormously relieving. Here's
where things get really interesting,
because eating with entertainment is not
new, not even remotely. In ancient Rome,
wealthy citizens held convivia,
elaborate dinner parties where food was
literally accompanied by performances.
Poets recited verse, musicians played,
jugglers juggled. The whole point was
that the meal and the entertainment were
inseparable. You weren't just feeding
your body, you were feeding your mind
and your status. Ancient Greek symposia,
which literally means drinking together,
followed the same logic. Wine, food,
philosophical debate, flute players, it
was all one experience. In medieval
Europe, great halls had minstrels
performing during feasts. The lord of
the manor eating in silence would have
been considered strange, even sad. By
the Victorian era, dinner parties were
elaborate performances in themselves.
Conversation was an art form, and a meal
without good talk was considered a
failure of hospitality. Then in the
1920s and 30s, something shifted. The
radio entered the home. Suddenly, for
the first time, ordinary families, not
just the wealthy, could have
entertainment while they ate. Families
gathered around the kitchen table with
the radio on. It became a ritual.
Then television arrived, and the TV
dinner, Swanson invented them in 1953,
was literally designed to be eaten in
front of a screen. The tray even
mimicked a television set shape. And
then came streaming, and then
smartphones, and now we carry infinite
entertainment in our pockets, available
the moment we sit down to eat. So, this
isn't a new behavior your generation
invented. It's a very old human impulse,
eating with stimulation, with company,
with story. Now available to everyone,
anytime, anywhere.
There's a cultural layer, too, and it's
fascinating. In South Korea, the mukbang
phenomenon took this idea and flipped it
inside out. Instead of watching
entertainment while you eat, you watch
someone else eat, often massive
quantities of food, with immersive sound
design, while you eat your own meal.

Because eating with other people is so
deeply wired into us that watching a
stranger eat on a screen genuinely
reduces the feeling of eating alone.

measurable reductions in loneliness
during meals. The ASMR eating genre does
something similar. It recreates the
sensory intimacy of a shared meal
through sound alone. In Japan, there's a
parallel tradition called hitorigoto,
talking to yourself while eating alone,
which was common long before smartphones
existed. It served the same purpose,
filling the silence, creating the
feeling of company through sound. These
aren't weird internet subcultures.
They're modern solutions to a very
ancient problem. Humans aren't designed
to eat alone in silence.
Here's something a little unsettling.
Streaming platforms and YouTube don't
just benefit from your mealtime habits.
They're actively designed around them.
The average lunch break is 30 minutes.
The average sitcom episode 22 minutes.

television executives figured this out
decades ago and modern platforms have
refined it to a science. Netflix's
autoplay feature, YouTube's endless
queue, TikTok's infinite scroll. These
are all engineered to eliminate the
moment of decision where you might put
the phone down. They call it reducing
friction and meal times are prime real
estate for this because you're already
seated, already in a low effort mode,
and your hands are literally occupied
with a fork. You're a captive audience
in the most literal sense. Food requires
just enough attention to keep you from
doing real work, but not enough to stop
you from watching. The algorithm figured
that out long before you did.

eating in front of a screen? Honestly,
it depends. The research does
consistently show that distracted eating
leads to higher calorie intake and lower
satisfaction. If you're trying to be
healthier, eating mindfully without
screens makes a real measurable
difference. But the psychological
benefits are real, too. For people who
live alone or are dealing with
loneliness, eating with a show on isn't
a moral failure. It's a coping mechanism
and not all coping mechanisms are bad.
The sweet spot most nutritionists
suggest, be intentional about it. Pick
something. Don't just doom scroll. Give
yourself the first few bites to actually
taste your food. And occasionally, not
always, just occasionally, try eating in
actual silence. You might find it more
comfortable than you expect. So, the
next time you automatically reach for
your phone before taking a bite, you're
not just a screen addicted millennial or
Gen Z zombie. You're a deeply social
primate who's hardwired to connect
stories, company, and food into a single
experience. You're doing something
Romans did it banquets, something
medieval lords did in their great halls,
something your grandparents did around
the radio on a Tuesday night. You're
just doing it with better resolution. If
you found this interesting, there's a
video on why we binge watch right here.
The psychology behind that is equally
fascinating. And subscribe if you want
more deep dives into the science behind
things you do every day without really
knowing why.

enjoyable. For a lot of people, food no

screen has become part of the
experience. At first, it seems like a
modern habit created by smartphones and
endless content, but this behavior
actually goes much deeper than that. The
urge to pair eating with stimulation is
tied to something much older. Let's
start with your brain because something
genuinely strange happens when you
combine eating and entertainment. Eating
activates your brain's reward system,
specifically the mesolimbic dopamine
pathway. That's the same system that
lights up when you fall in love or win a
game or scroll through social media.
Food triggers dopamine. It's one of the
most fundamental reward signals in your
entire nervous system. When you add
something visually stimulating, a video,
a show, a movie, you're stacking a
second dopamine source on top of the
first. Two reward streams firing
simultaneously. Neuroscientists call
this sensory synergy, which is partly
why your cereal tastes fine, but your
cereal with a YouTube video tastes
weirdly satisfying. But, there's a flip

awareness, your brain's ability to
listen to your body's internal signals,
like your stomach saying, "Hey, I'm
actually full now." A 2006 study in the
American Journal of Clinical Nutrition
found that people eating while
distracted consumed significantly more
food and reported feeling less satisfied
afterward, even though they'd eaten
more. You ate more, enjoyed it less, and
felt hungry sooner. That's the
distraction eating paradox. Your brain
is so busy processing the screen that it
misses the memo from your stomach. But,
neuroscience is only half the story. The
psychology here goes deeper. Eating
alone is honestly a modern problem. For

communal. You gathered with your tribe,

together wasn't just about food. It was

partially simulates the experience of
eating with company. The voices, the
faces, the narrative tension, it
activates similar social processing
circuits. Psychologists call this a
parasocial relationship, a one-sided
social bond where you feel connected to
people on screen who don't know you
exist. Friends, The Office, anime, true
crime podcasts, these aren't just
entertainment. During mealtime, they're
surrogate companions. There's also what
psychologists call hedonic escapism,
using pleasurable distraction to avoid
being present with your own thoughts.

uncomfortable quiet. A video immediately
fills that space with novelty,
narrative, humor, drama. Your brain
finds this enormously relieving. Here's

because eating with entertainment is not
new, not even remotely. In ancient Rome,
wealthy citizens held convivia,
elaborate dinner parties where food was
literally accompanied by performances.

followed the same logic. Wine, food,

Europe, great halls had minstrels
performing during feasts. The lord of
the manor eating in silence would have
been considered strange, even sad. By
the Victorian era, dinner parties were
elaborate performances in themselves.

without good talk was considered a
failure of hospitality. Then in the
1920s and 30s, something shifted. The

just the wealthy, could have
entertainment while they ate. Families

actor_text:
Why does food feel incomplete without a video playing in the background?

For millions of people, eating and watching have become inseparable. Breakfast with YouTube. Lunch with TikTok. Dinner with Netflix. But this habit isn’t just a smartphone-era addiction.

It turns out humans have been pairing food with stories, entertainment, and companionship for thousands of years.

In this video, we explore the neuroscience, psychology, history, and culture behind why eating alone feels strange — and why screens have quietly become part of the modern meal.

This video covers:

🍽️ Why food + videos feel unusually satisfying (dopamine & sensory synergy)
🧠 The “distraction-eating paradox” and what happens in your brain while watching
👥 How screens replace social connection during solo meals
🏛️ Ancient Roman banquets, medieval feasts, radio dinners, and the history of eating with entertainment
📺 TV dinners, streaming platforms, autoplay, and why algorithms love your mealtime attention
🇰🇷 Mukbang, ASMR eating, and the psychology of not wanting to eat alone
⚖️ Whether eating while watching is actually bad for you

Humans were never really designed to eat alone in silence. We just replaced the banquet hall with a screen.

video_title: How Ancient Humans reacted to Eclipses (Lunar and Solar Eclipses)
description:
What would you do if the Sun suddenly disappeared in the middle of the day… and you had no idea why?

Long before modern science, eclipses terrified ancient civilizations across the world. A blood red Moon could mean the death of a king. A blackened Sun could signal the anger of the gods. Entire cities panicked, armies feared disaster, and rulers believed the heavens themselves were sending warnings.

In this video, we explore the terrifying history of solar and lunar eclipses and how ancient people reacted when the sky suddenly went dark.

Discover:
Ancient Babylon’s deadly “substitute king” ritual
The blood moon that terrified Constantinople before its fall
How Christopher Columbus used a lunar eclipse to manipulate an entire population
Chinese legends of dragons devouring the Sun
Why eclipses were seen as omens of war, death, and catastrophe

From collapsing empires to frightened armies and desperate prayers, this is the story of humanity’s fear of eclipses before science explained the heavens.

Sources: 

1. Graff, S. (2017, August 30). The solar eclipse and the substitute king. The Metropolitan Museum of Art. The Metropolitan Museum of Art article
2. Casazza, R., & Gangui, A. (2013). The explanation of eclipses in Greco Roman antiquity. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/1304.7297
3. Encyclopaedia Britannica. (2025). 9 celestial omens. Britannica. Britannica celestial omens article
4. European Space Agency. (n.d.). The eclipse in history. ESA Science & Technology. ESA eclipse history article
5. Jones, C. W. (2021). Power and elite competition in the Neo Assyrian Empire 745–612 BC. Columbia University. Referenced in the discussion of substitute king rituals and eclipse omens.
6. Guillermier, P., & Koutchmy, S. (1999). Total eclipses: Science, observations, myths and legends. Springer. Referenced in discussions of eclipse myths and the 1453 Constantinople eclipse.

Now imagine you're a farmer in ancient
Babylon. It's midday. The sun burns
overhead as you work beneath a clear
sky. And then it dims suddenly. You look
up and the sun itself is being swallowed
whole right in front of your eyes.
Within minutes, daylight drains from the
world. The sky turns a deep unnatural
blue. Stars appear at noon. Birds stop
singing. Animals panic. The temperature
drops. No one warned you. No one could
warn you. There's no science, no
astronomy textbook, no NASA live stream
explaining what's happening. As far as
you know, the world might actually be
ending. You think to yourself, I am
going to die. Well, that is a valid
reaction and you're not alone on that.
Ancient people did absolutely lose their
minds. So today we're diving into how
ancient civilizations reacted to solar
and lunar eclipses. Let's begin. The
blood moon. Imagine being a servant in
ancient Babylonia. One day your master
calls you out. Congratulations, you're
the new king. Well, at least
temporarily.
You see ancient Mesopotamians,
especially Assyrians and Babylonians,
believed lunar eclipses could foretell
disaster or death for a king. When court
astrologers predicted a dangerous
eclipse, a blood moon, they sometimes
performed a substitute king ritual
installing a temporary stand-in while
the real king withdrew from public life.
The substitute would symbolically absorb
the evil omen until the danger period
passed and the real king could safely
return.
I mean sure you are a human shield for
an omen, but who believes in that
anyway? But being a king for a few days,
endless food, servants waiting on you,
an entire kingdom at your command. Not
bad, right? Well, not exactly. You
didn't actually wield real political
power. You were treated well, but not
true king well. And when the ritual
period ended, there was a very real
chance you would be executed ensuring
the omen died with you instead of
transferring back to the real king.
So, they can predict eclipses? Well,
some civilizations could. In fact, there
are old prophecies tied to lunar
eclipses. One of these was of
Constantinople.
By 1453, the Byzantine Empire was dying.
Its capital, Constantinople, had stood
for over a thousand years. Massive walls
protected the city, and many believed it
was chosen by God himself. But, this was
all about to change. Constantinople was
under siege by the Ottoman Empire. The
city had been surrounded by tens of
thousands of soldiers led by the young
Sultan Mehmed the second.
Giant cannons pounded the ancient walls
day and night. Food was running low.
Fear spread through the streets. Inside
churches, people prayed constantly,
hoping God would save their city.
But, that night something changed. The
moon slowly darkened. Then, it turned
deep red. A blood moon hanging over the
city.
Many citizens believed ancient
prophecies had predicted that
Constantinople would fall after signs
appeared in the heavens. To them, the
blood-red moon was proof that disaster
was coming. Some believed God had
abandoned the city completely. Panic
spread through Constantinople. Churches
filled with desperate prayers. Religious
processions marched through the streets
carrying candles and holy icons. Some
people wept openly. Others prepared for
death. And outside the walls, the
Ottoman army waited. On May 29th, the
final attack began. The walls were
finally breached, and soldiers flooded
into the city. Emperor Constantine the
11th Palaiologos disappeared during the
fighting and was never seen again. And
within hours, the city fell.
The blood moon seemed to mark the end of
a thousand-year empire.
But, what happens when you are able to
predict a lunar eclipse? During his
fourth voyage in 1503, Christopher
Columbus and his crew became stranded in
Jamaica after their ships were badly
damaged by storms and shipworms. With no
way home, they were forced to live on
the island for months. At first, the
local Taino people helped them survive
by supplying food and resources, but as
time passed, relations deteriorated.
Some of Columbus' men stole from locals
and abused their hospitality, causing
many islanders to stop bringing food
altogether.
Columbus and his crew were now starving,
stranded, and desperate. Fortunately for
Columbus, he owned an astronomical
almanac that predicted an upcoming total
lunar eclipse on February 29th, 1504.
Seeing an opportunity, he warned local
leaders that his God was angry with them
for refusing to help his men and would
soon make the moon disappear in
punishment. The locals didn't believe
him at first, but then the eclipse
began. The full moon slowly darkened
before turning a deep red in the night
sky, a blood moon. Many islanders were
terrified and begged Columbus to restore
it. Columbus secluded himself,
pretending to pray while secretly timing
the eclipse using his almanac. Near the
end of the eclipse, he emerged and
announced that God had forgiven them.
Soon after, the moon gradually returned
to normal, seemingly proving Columbus'
power. Food supplies resumed, helping
Columbus and his crew survive until
rescue ships finally arrived months
later.
The black sun. In 2134 BC in ancient
China, two royal astronomers, Xi and He,
failed to predict a solar eclipse and
were executed for their negligence.
Eclipses were considered politically and
spiritually important because they were
seen as signs connected to the mandate
and stability of the emperor. Chinese
mythology often described eclipses as a
celestial dragon devouring the sun or
moon. During eclipses, people would beat
drums, bang pots, shoot arrows into the
sky, and make as much noise as possible
to scare the dragon away. So, imagine
the emperor's reaction when he saw the
sun being devoured and the drums weren't
ready.
But, China wasn't the only civilization
terrified by eclipses. Another empire
would see the darkening sky as a warning
of disaster.
In 480 BCE, Xerxes the first led one of
the largest armies in history toward
Greece. The Persian king was confident
he would conquer the Greek world. His
massive army crossed into Europe while
thousands of soldiers marched behind
him. But, as the invasion began, strange
signs appeared in the sky. According to
Herodotus, celestial omens surrounded
Xerxes' campaign. They were believed to
be messages from the gods about the fate
of kings and empires. Persian priests
and Magi studied these signs carefully.
So, when the sky darkened, many may have
feared it was a warning that Xerxes'
invasion would fail.
Imagine being a Persian soldier. You are
marching with the most powerful army on
Earth. Then suddenly, the heavens
themselves seem disturbed. To ancient
people, an eclipse could mean the gods
were angry, a king was doomed, or a
great disaster was coming. Despite
Persia's enormous power, Xerxes failed
to conquer Greece. His forces suffered
devastating defeats at the Battle of
Salamis and other battles, forcing the
Persian army to retreat. To many people
at the time, the darkened sky had been a
warning all along.
Today, we understand eclipses through
science. They are just instances of
alignment between the sun, moon, and
Earth. But, for ancient civilizations,
eclipses were terrifying. A blood-red
moon could mean the death of a king. A
blackened sun could signal the anger of
the gods. Entire cities panicked. Kings
hid. Armies feared the sky itself.
And honestly, even today, eclipses still
feel unsettling.
The sudden darkness, the silence, the
cold air.
For a moment, the world feels wrong.
Maybe that's why humans have feared and
obsessed over eclipses for thousands of
years. Because no matter how much
science explains them, seeing the sky go
dark still feels deeply unnatural.

What would you do if the Sun suddenly disappeared in the middle of the day… and you had no idea why?

Long before modern science, eclipses terrified ancient civilizations across the world. A blood red Moon could mean the death of a king. A blackened Sun could signal the anger of the gods. Entire cities panicked, armies feared disaster, and rulers believed the heavens themselves were sending warnings.

In this video, we explore the terrifying history of solar and lunar eclipses and how ancient people reacted when the sky suddenly went dark.

Discover:
Ancient Babylon’s deadly “substitute king” ritual
The blood moon that terrified Constantinople before its fall
How Christopher Columbus used a lunar eclipse to manipulate an entire population
Chinese legends of dragons devouring the Sun
Why eclipses were seen as omens of war, death, and catastrophe

From collapsing empires to frightened armies and desperate prayers, this is the story of humanity’s fear of eclipses before science explained the heavens.

Sources: 

1. Graff, S. (2017, August 30). The solar eclipse and the substitute king. The Metropolitan Museum of Art. The Metropolitan Museum of Art article
2. Casazza, R., & Gangui, A. (2013). The explanation of eclipses in Greco Roman antiquity. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/1304.7297
3. Encyclopaedia Britannica. (2025). 9 celestial omens. Britannica. Britannica celestial omens article
4. European Space Agency. (n.d.). The eclipse in history. ESA Science & Technology. ESA eclipse history article
5. Jones, C. W. (2021). Power and elite competition in the Neo Assyrian Empire 745–612 BC. Columbia University. Referenced in the discussion of substitute king rituals and eclipse omens.
6. Guillermier, P., & Koutchmy, S. (1999). Total eclipses: Science, observations, myths and legends. Springer. Referenced in discussions of eclipse myths and the 1453 Constantinople eclipse.

description:
For most of human history, obesity was rare. Humans evolved in a world shaped by hunger, constant movement, and limited food supplies. Survival depended on endurance, physical labor, and the ability to store energy whenever food was available.

So how did humanity go from scarcity to a world where over a billion people are overweight or obese?

This documentary explores the history of obesity across thousands of years, from Stone Age hunter-gatherers and ancient civilizations to medieval kings, the Industrial Revolution, and the rise of modern fast food and ultra-processed diets. Along the way, we examine how agriculture, sugar, industrialization, and modern convenience transformed the human body and the way we eat.

Featuring the Venus of Willendorf, ancient Rome, Henry VIII, William Banting, and the modern obesity epidemic, this is the story of how ancient biology collided with a world humans were never designed to live in. 

Sources:

1. The foundational science on obesity as a modern epidemic
Flegal, K. M., Carroll, M. D., Kit, B. K., & Ogden, C. L. (2012). Prevalence of obesity and trends in the distribution of body mass index among US adults, 1999–2010. JAMA, 307(5), 491–497. https: //doi.org/10.1001/jama.2012.39

2. The evolutionary mismatch argument — why ancient bodies fail in modern environments
Lieberman, D. E. (2013). The story of the human body: Evolution, health, and disease. Pantheon Books.

3. The Venus figurines and what prehistoric body ideals reveal

4. The agricultural revolution and the emergence of metabolic disease
Cordain, L., Eaton, S. B., Sebastian, A., Mann, N., Lindeberg, S., Watkins, B. A., O'Keefe, J. H., & Brand-Miller, J. (2005). Origins and evolution of the Western diet: Health implications for the 21st century. American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, 81(2), 341–354. https: //doi.org/10.1093/ajcn.81.2.341

5. Hippocrates and the first recorded medical thinking on obesity

6. Sugar consumption and the rise of metabolic disease in the Early Modern period
Mintz, S. W. (1985). Sweetness and power: The place of sugar in modern history. Viking Penguin.

7. William Banting and the first popular weight loss movement

transcript_plaintext:
Humans evolved in a world of hunger. For
hundreds of thousands of years, survival
depended on movement, endurance, and the
ability to secure scarce calories.
Obesity existed, but it was rare. Today,
over a billion people are overweight or
obese. In just a few generations, the
human body found itself trapped in an
environment it was never designed for.
According to the World Health
Organization, global obesity has nearly
tripled since 1975. In 2022, they
reported that 16% of adults worldwide
were obese. In the United States, the
Centers for Disease Control and
Prevention reported adult obesity
prevalence at 40.3% between 2021 and
2023. That's two out of every five
people.
But what exactly is obesity? Obesity is
generally defined as having an excessive
amount of body fat that increases the
risk of serious health problems. In
medicine, the most common screening tool
is the body mass index or BMI. BMI is
measured by dividing your weight in
kilograms by the square of your height
in meters. To be considered obese, a
person must have a BMI of 30 or above.
Say you are 5 ft 6 in tall or about 168
cm. You would need to weigh around 186
lb or 84.4 kg to fall into the obese
category. It is clear that obesity is
increasing at a rapid rate, but was it
as common back then as it is today?
Let's look at obesity throughout human
history and find out what went wrong.
The Stone Age. This is where we begin.
Your earliest ancestors lived in a world
that demanded constant movement.
Hunting, gathering, climbing, carrying,
and walking long distances were all part
of survival, burning far more calories
each day than the average modern person.
The idea of a Stone Age human with
excess body fat is almost biologically
impossible on a population level. The
food wasn't there. The rest wasn't
there. But here's where it gets strange.
In 1908, in a cave in Austria,
archaeologists found a small figurine
carved from limestone. She is about 11
cm tall. She has enormous breasts, a
wide rounded stomach, heavy thighs, and
no face. She is called the Venus of
Willendorf. She is approximately 25,000
years old, and she is not alone. Across
Europe, archaeologists have found dozens
of similar figures. The Venus of
Lespugue, the Venus of Dolní Věstonice,
the Venus of Laussel. All of them share
the same proportions, large, round, what
a modern person would describe as obese.
But nobody knows exactly what they
meant. Fertility symbols is the most
common theory. Representations of
abundance, possibly goddesses, possibly
idealized female forms in a world where
fat meant survival, where a woman with
body fat reserves was more likely to
survive winter, more likely to carry a
pregnancy to term, more likely to keep a
child alive. In the Stone Age, the human
body didn't produce obesity at scale.
But the human mind was already treating
fatness as something worth carving into
stone and keeping.
The Bronze Age. Agriculture changed
everything. When humans settled into
farming communities, the calorie
equation shifted. For the first time in
history, societies could produce more
food than they immediately needed. They
could store it, protect it, and build
entire civilizations around it. Grain
became the foundation of daily life.
Bread, beer, porridge. Diets
increasingly centered around
concentrated carbohydrates instead of
the wide variety of wild foods humans
had eaten before. And for the first
time, archaeologists begin seeing clear
signs of dietary change in the human
body. Studies of Bronze Age skeletal
remains across the Middle East and
Europe show rising rates of dental
decay, nutritional deficiencies, and
other markers linked to grain-heavy
diets. Obesity itself leaves almost no
trace in bone. Fat does not fossilize,
but changes in health and diet do. The
Bronze Age did not produce obesity on a
modern scale. Most people still lived
physically exhausting lives, farming by
hand, carrying water, grinding grain,
working from sunrise to sunset. But for
the first time in human history, a small
layer of society didn't have to. Rulers,
priests, elites who controlled food
instead of laboring for it. And in many
early civilizations, excess body fat
slowly became associated with wealth,
abundance, and power.
The Iron Age. The Iron Age accelerated
many of the changes the Bronze Age
began. Better tools improved farming,
improved farming created larger food
surpluses, and those surpluses helped
build larger cities, more powerful
states, and sharper divisions between
social classes. By the classical world,
Greek and Roman writers were beginning
to describe something new. Individuals
whose body size stood out enough to be
recorded, not always with admiration,
often with discomfort, mockery, or
suspicion. Physical fitness was deeply
tied to status, discipline, and military
strength. In Sparta, citizens were
expected to maintain strong athletic
bodies, and excess weight was associated
with weakness and lack of self-control.
The Celtic peoples were described
similarly by outside observers. The
Greek geographer Strabo claimed that
some Celtic societies criticized men
whose wastes grew too large for standard
belts, though historians still debate
how literal these accounts really were.
These stories suggest something
important. Obesity was still uncommon.
Most people continued to live physically
demanding lives with limited and
unpredictable food supplies. But for the
first time, excess body fat had become
visible enough to attract social
attention, even if that attention was
negative.
The Ancient Age.
Around 400 BC, the Greek physician
Hippocrates described excessive fatness
as a medical problem. He observed that
heavier individuals were more likely to
die younger and suffer sudden illness.
He even warned that excess fat around
the body could be dangerous. He was
remarkably close to the truth. He just
did not yet understand the biology
behind it. Rome took the relationship
between food and status in a very
different direction. Elite Roman
banquets were famously extravagant.
Wealthy Romans consumed imported
delicacies, exotic animals, enormous
quantities of wine, and multi-course
feasts that could last for hours. Eating
had become more than survival. It had
become a performance. Roman writers and
physicians increasingly described the
health consequences of excess. Wealthy
individuals weakened by overeating,
inactivity, and luxury. The Roman
emperor Maximinus Thrax, who ruled
during the 3rd century AD, was described
by ancient sources as a man of enormous
size and appetite. Some accounts even
claimed he stood nearly 8 ft tall,
though modern historians believe these
descriptions were heavily exaggerated.
But, the exaggeration itself reveals
something important. In the ancient
world, unusual size and enormous
appetites had become associated with
power, wealth, and authority. For the
elite, food was no longer simply
survival. It was proof that you had more
than everyone else.
The Middle Ages.
After the fall of the Roman Empire,
Europe's complex food systems collapsed.
Most people lived with constant food
insecurity. In medieval Europe, famine
and starvation were far more common than
obesity. Disasters like the Great Famine
of 1315 to 1322 killed millions. The
wealthy elite, however, lived very
differently. Kings and nobles used
excessive eating and drinking to display
power, wealth, and status. Stories like
King Henry I First allegedly dying from
overeating lampreys reflected how
indulgence had become associated with
royalty. Henry VIII became the clearest
example. Once athletic and fit, he grew
severely obese later in life, likely
suffering from complications such as
type 2 diabetes. His condition
symbolized a broader pattern among
medieval elites, whose wealth was
expressed through excess consumption.
For ordinary people, thinness was not a
lifestyle choice. It was the unavoidable
result of scarcity, hunger, and hard
survival.
The early modern age. The early modern
period is where the story starts to look
familiar. Global trade expanded rapidly.
Sugar arrived in Europe from Caribbean
plantations in quantities never seen
before. Chocolate, coffee, refined
flour, and rum, once rare luxuries,
became increasingly common among the
wealthy. In England, sugar consumption
rose from around 4 lb per person per
year in 1700 to roughly 18 lb by 1800. A
massive increase in a single century.
Physicians also began documenting
illnesses linked to richer diets and
increasing body weight more frequently
than before. Not simply people who
overate during feasts, but individuals
whose bodies slowly accumulated fat
through years of excess and reduced
physical labor. Portraits from the era
tell part of the story as well. Dutch
Golden Age merchants and English
aristocrats often appear noticeably
heavier and softer than figures in
earlier medieval art. The English
physician Thomas Venner described
corpulency as an increasing problem
among the wealthy. More than a century
later, Thomas Short argued that
excessive weight was becoming more
common and was no longer limited to the
upper class. For the first time, obesity
was beginning to move beyond the elite.
The industrial age.
For the first time in human history,
food became cheaper while daily movement
began to decline at the same time.
Factory labor was still exhausting, but
it was a different kind of exhaustion
from farming. The work was repetitive,
confined, and increasingly mechanized.
Many workers stood in one place for
hours, repeating the same motions
instead of walking long distances or
performing varied physical labor
outdoors. And when they returned home,
the food available to them was changing,
too. White bread, refined sugar, lard,
tinned meat, cheap calorie-dense foods
produced on an industrial scale.
The early industrial age was still
marked by widespread poverty and
malnutrition. For many families, getting
enough food remained the main struggle.
But as industrial economies expanded and
wages slowly rose, obesity became
increasingly visible outside the upper
classes. One man captured this
transition perfectly. William Banting
was a London undertaker in the 1860s who
became so overweight that he struggled
to tie his shoes and walk downstairs
comfortably. Under medical advice, he
cut back on bread, sugar, beer, and
other carbohydrates. He lost a
significant amount of weight and
published a pamphlet describing the
experience. The pamphlet became
enormously popular. In parts of Europe,
Banting even became a verb meaning to
diet. By the early 20th century,
American insurance companies were
compiling large-scale mortality tables
linking excess body weight to higher
death rates. The statistics were
beginning to confirm what physicians had
been observing for decades. The modern
obesity era had begun. The modern age.
Post-war prosperity transformed daily
life. Suburban expansion reduced the
amount of walking built into everyday
routines. Highways spread across entire
countries. Cars became the primary mode
of transportation for millions of
people. Fast-food chains expanded
rapidly in the 1950s, offering meals
that were cheap, convenient, highly
palatable, and available almost
everywhere. In the 1970s, high-fructose
corn syrup entered the American food
supply on a massive scale.
Ultra-processed foods, products
engineered to maximize flavor, shelf
life, and convenience, became
increasingly dominant in modern diets.
In 1960, roughly 13% of American adults
were classified as obese. By 2020, that
number had risen to more than 42%.
Not overweight, obese.
In just a few generations, obesity
shifted from being relatively uncommon
to becoming one of the defining health
problems of the modern world. Here's
what all of this actually means. For
most of human history, obesity was
probably rare. Food was uncertain. Life
demanded constant movement. The human
body evolved in conditions defined more
by scarcity than abundance. Then, in
only a few centuries, a blink in
evolutionary time, that scarcity began
to disappear. But human biology did not
change nearly as fast as human
civilization did. The same instincts
that once helped our ancestors survive,
craving calorie-dense foods rich in fat,
sugar, and salt whenever they were
available, now operate in a world where
those foods are cheap, constant, and
engineered for overconsumption. Modern
obesity is not simply a failure of
discipline or willpower. It is the
result of ancient biology colliding with
an environment unlike anything humans
evolved to handle. And that tension may
explain why larger bodies appear again
and again throughout human history, from
ancient rulers to the Venus of
Willendorf, carved more than 25,000
years ago by people living in a world
where stored body fat may have
symbolized fertility, survival, or
abundance. We cannot know exactly what
her creators intended, but the figure
survived. And across thousands of years
of human history, one idea appears again
and again. In a world shaped by hunger,
body fat could represent safety. The
problem is that the world changed faster
than the human body did.

For most of human history, obesity was rare. Humans evolved in a world shaped by hunger, constant movement, and limited food supplies. Survival depended on endurance, physical labor, and the ability to store energy whenever food was available.

So how did humanity go from scarcity to a world where over a billion people are overweight or obese?

This documentary explores the history of obesity across thousands of years, from Stone Age hunter-gatherers and ancient civilizations to medieval kings, the Industrial Revolution, and the rise of modern fast food and ultra-processed diets. Along the way, we examine how agriculture, sugar, industrialization, and modern convenience transformed the human body and the way we eat.

Featuring the Venus of Willendorf, ancient Rome, Henry VIII, William Banting, and the modern obesity epidemic, this is the story of how ancient biology collided with a world humans were never designed to live in.

1. The foundational science on obesity as a modern epidemic
Flegal, K. M., Carroll, M. D., Kit, B. K., & Ogden, C. L. (2012). Prevalence of obesity and trends in the distribution of body mass index among US adults, 1999–2010. JAMA, 307(5), 491–497. https: //doi.org/10.1001/jama.2012.39

2. The evolutionary mismatch argument — why ancient bodies fail in modern environments
Lieberman, D. E. (2013). The story of the human body: Evolution, health, and disease. Pantheon Books.

3. The Venus figurines and what prehistoric body ideals reveal
Nowell, A., & Chang, M. L. (2014). Science, the media, and interpretations of Upper Paleolithic figurines. American Anthropologist, 116(3), 562–577. https: //doi.org/10.1111/aman.12121

4. The agricultural revolution and the emergence of metabolic disease
Cordain, L., Eaton, S. B., Sebastian, A., Mann, N., Lindeberg, S., Watkins, B. A., O'Keefe, J. H., & Brand-Miller, J. (2005). Origins and evolution of the Western diet: Health implications for the 21st century. American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, 81(2), 341–354. https: //doi.org/10.1093/ajcn.81.2.341

5. Hippocrates and the first recorded medical thinking on obesity
Eknoyan, G. (2006). A history of obesity, or how what was good became ugly and then bad. Advances in Chronic Kidney Disease, 13(4), 421–427. https: //doi.org/10.1053/j.ackd.2006.07.002

6. Sugar consumption and the rise of metabolic disease in the Early Modern period
Mintz, S. W. (1985). Sweetness and power: The place of sugar in modern history. Viking Penguin.

7. William Banting and the first popular weight loss movement
Banting, W. (1863). Letter on corpulence, addressed to the public. Harrison.

description:
Why do humans love cheese even though it is basically milk left to rot 🧀

In this video, we explore the strange and fascinating story behind one of the world’s most beloved foods. From its accidental discovery thousands of years ago to the science of how it affects your brain, cheese is more than just a snack. It is biology, history, and evolution in one bite.

You will learn how ancient humans turned spoiled milk into survival food, why aged cheese can feel almost addictive, and how your brain is wired to crave it. What seems disgusting at first glance turns out to be one of the most powerful foods ever created.

Watch until the end. You might never look at cheese the same way again.
