of tunnel, then a hard left turn. Above
ground, Vietnam is loud. Underground,
there's nothing. Just your breathing and
your heartbeat, amplified by the clay
walls until it sounds like someone else
is breathing with you. Tunnel rats call
this the black echo. You reach a
vertical drop to the second level. Slide
down, sweep the floor. The knife blade
catches something. Thin, taut. A
tripwire connected to a grenade wedged
inside a tin can. If you'd kicked it,
the spoon would have released and you
would have had 4 seconds in a space with
nowhere to run. You cut the wire, you
keep going. The tunnel turns. The knife
hits something soft, a snake. Small
head, banded pattern, a crate. The VC

ceiling, rigged to tripwires. One of the

vertical drop. Sharpened bamboo smeared

if you fall, you grab the walls to catch
yourself and the stakes go through your
hands. You emerge at 0900, 3 hours
underground. Gutierrez pulls you out by

yards away, Webb comes out of a

too low, so he couldn't lift his head.

section this afternoon. You say yes. You
don't know why. You go back in at 1400.

second level junction, scraping, then
silence. Gutierrez squeezes your
shoulder. You drop into the shaft.

listen. 60 seconds, nothing. Then,
faint, the sound of someone shifting
weight. Cloth on clay, the breathing.

aimed forward. You back away 2 ft to the
right. You reach over and click it on.

from the dark, 3 ft to the left of where
you were just lying, a muzzle flash
answers. The shot goes through the space
where your chest was half a second ago.

three times. Silence. You reload. You
crawl forward. He's dead. Young, maybe
19, sitting in a carved alcove cut into
the wall, a kill zone. You were supposed
to crawl past and get shot from behind.

Batten taught you that. You check his
pockets. A photograph of a woman holding
a baby. Nothing useful to intelligence,
but you don't pull out. Not yet. The
fighter was guarding something. Past the
alcove, the tunnel widens into a
chamber. Rice bags stacked against walls
and AK-47 wrapped in oiled cloth and on
a wooden table, documents. Maps of
American patrol routes, lists of names,
a radio with frequencies written on tape
stuck to the housing. You mark
everything. You start dragging what you
can back toward the shaft. By the time
the intelligence officer has the
documents spread across a folding table
on the surface, the engineers are
already lowering C4 into the tunnel. The
ground sags. Dust pours from vents you
didn't even know existed. The section
collapses in on itself. For a few
minutes, you feel something close to
pride. You found the fighter. You found
the intel. You destroyed the tunnel.
That's the job start to finish.
Gutierrez walks over. He's been assigned
to cover a private named Molina who's
going into a new section 300 yards east.
A fresh trapdoor found an hour ago.
Gutierrez gives you a nod and follows
Molina toward the tree line. He doesn't
come back. An hour passes. The comm wire
goes slack. They call down the entrance,
nothing. They tug the wire, it pulls
free. Cut clean. You volunteer to go in.
You find Gutierrez 40 yards from the
entrance. Tripwire grenade. Tin can,
spoon release, rigged at a junction. He
never saw it. The man who held your wire
all morning, who pulled you out by the
forearms, who squeezed your shoulder
before every descent, he's face down in
the clay with his flashlight still on.
The red beam pointing at nothing. No
tunnel rat is ever left underground. You
drag him out by his ankles. That night,
you sit with Batten behind the motor
pool. A kid named Reyes is writing a
letter to his wife, but he keeps
crossing things out. Everything he
writes sounds like a goodbye, and he
doesn't want her to read it that way.

says the tunnels will outlast all of
you. But here's the thing, he's right.

1967,
tunnel rats will pull half a million
documents from a Viet Cong district
headquarters. Maps, codebooks, a plan to
assassinate Defense Secretary McNamara.
It won't matter. Within months, the VC
will move back in, and in January 1968,
the tunnels of Cu Chi will serve as the
staging point for the Tet Offensive
against Saigon. You'll destroy a tunnel
complex on Tuesday, by Friday, it'll be
operational again. The section you
collapse this afternoon, the one
Gutierrez died protecting, it'll be dug
out and reinforced before the month is
over. That's the job. Of roughly 700 men
who did this job during the war, about a
third came out wounded or didn't come
out at all. There was never an official
unit designation, never an official
patch, never a formal training program.
The only recognition was a homemade
patch with a rat holding a pistol and a
flashlight, and a motto in bad Latin,
non gratum anus rodentum, not worth a
rat's ass.

transcript_plaintext:
It is 4:30 in the morning. You are on
Hiryu's flight deck in the dark. The
wind is warm and smells like aviation
fuel. Your hands are slick with it.
You've been hauling aircraft into launch
position for 30 minutes, pushing tail
wheels across the deck with eight other
men. The prop wash from 200 warming
engines is strong enough to knock you
sideways. You are a flight deck crewman
aboard one of four fleet carriers in the
Kido Butai, Japan's first carrier
striking force. Akagi, Kaga, Soryu, and
your ship, Hiryu. The same carriers that
hit Pearl Harbor six months ago. Midway
is a tiny atoll 1,300 miles northwest of
Hawaii. Two islands, one airstrip,
surrounded by open Pacific in every
direction. Japan wants it as a forward
base to threaten Hawaii, but the atoll
is bait. The real prize is what's left
of the American fleet. One more decisive
victory and the Americans will have no
carriers left in the Pacific. The
Americans know you are coming.
Codebreakers at Pearl Harbor cracked the
Japanese naval code weeks before the
battle. They know the target. They know
the date. They know how many ships
you're bringing. Three American carriers
are already in position northeast of the
atoll, waiting. Every man on your flight
deck thinks this is a surprise attack.
It is, just not in the way you think. At
4:30, 108 planes launch. The strike
leader is Lieutenant Joichi Tomonaga
flying off your ship. You watch his
torpedo bomber climb into the pre-dawn
sky and bank south toward Midway. It is
the last time you will see him take off
with a plane that can bring him home. At
7:00, Tomonaga's strike hits Midway. The
atoll burns, but the airfield is still
working and Tomonaga radios back. There
is need for a second attack wave. You
hear the order before you understand it.
Swap the reserve torpedoes for land
bombs, hit Midway again. You go below.
The hangar deck is hot and reeks of
avgas. You and your crew start unjacking
a torpedo from the belly of a Kate
bomber. Four men to lower a 1-ton weapon
onto a hand push dolly, wheel it to the
elevator, send it down, then the bomb
comes up the same way. 25 minutes per
squadron. You are halfway through when
the order changes. Enemy ships sighted.
One appears to be a carrier. New order,
stop. Swap back to torpedoes. The
hangars are a disaster. Bombs halfway
mounted, torpedoes halfway struck below,
weapons on dollies everywhere, lined up
against the bulkheads because there's no
time to put them back in the magazines.
You look at the ordinance stacked around
you, bombs, torpedoes, fuel lines
running above your head, armed aircraft
3 ft away. You know what this is. You
just don't have a word for it yet.
Topside, your admiral, Rear Admiral
Tamon Yamaguchi, signals Vice Admiral
Nagumo on Akagi, "Consider it advisable
to launch attack force immediately. Send
the dive bombers now before the
Americans find you." Nagumo says no.
Full escort, standard doctrine.
Yamaguchi studied at Princeton. He was
the last Japanese naval attaché in
Washington. He is widely considered
Yamamoto's eventual replacement, but he
follows orders for now. At 8:47,
Tomonaga's planes start coming home,
shot up, trailing smoke. The engines
sound wrong, rough, stuttering. You can
smell the burnt oil before the first one
enters the landing pattern. The flight
deck has to be cleared to recover them.
It takes until 9:17. 2 hours of
preparing, canceling, and reversing a
strike, [music] and the hangars are
still full of loose ordinance that never
went back to the magazines. The American
torpedo bombers find you first. You are
refueling a Zero when the anti-aircraft
guns open up. You flatten yourself
against the deck and watch. Three waves
between 9:18 and 10:15, slow, low,
straight at the fleet. The Zeros tear
them apart. The first squadron loses all
15 planes, every one. The second wave
loses 10 of 14. The third, 10 of 12. Not
a single torpedo hits a Japanese ship,
not one. You watch American planes
falling into the sea for nearly an hour,
trailing fire, cartwheeling on impact.
The zeros are chasing the last
stragglers at sea [music] level, and the
sky above the carriers is wide open,
blue and empty. That is the last good
minute of your war. 10:22, a lookout
aboard Kaga screams. You hear it a half
second later. Dots, high, coming down.
American dive bombers, 50 of them,
14,000 ft. There are no zeros up there.
The torpedo attacks pulled every fighter
to the surface, and nobody sent them
back up. 4 minutes, that is how long it
takes. Kaga goes first. Four bombs into
the hangers, one hits the bridge and
kills the captain and most of his staff.
You hear it from Hiryu's deck, a rolling
boom you feel in your teeth, then a
column of black smoke a mile and a half
to starboard. Soryu, three bombs.
Captain Ryusaku Yanagimoto refuses to
leave the bridge. A wrestling champion
is sent to drag him off. He finds the
captain on the signal platform, sword
drawn, singing the national anthem
alone. He cannot bring himself to touch
him. Akagi, one bomb, that's all. It
hits the midship elevator and detonates
in the upper hanger among the ordinance
you and men like you stacked on dollies
2 hours ago because there was no time to
put it away. One bomb, the loose
ordinance does the rest. You are
standing on Hiryu watching three
carriers burn at the same time. A
mechanic named Sato is standing to your
left. He served on Akagi before
transferring to Hiryu last month. He is
watching [music] his old ship die. A
wrench slips from his hand. He does not
pick it up. Three carriers, 4 minutes,
and there's nothing you can do about any
of it. Yamaguchi does not wait. He
launches 18 dive bombers at the
Yorktown. You watch them go and count
them [music] when they come back. 13 do
not. Three bombs hit, she stops dead.
Then he sends Tomonaga, the same
Tomonaga who led the dawn attack. His
port wing fuel tank was punctured over
Midway and cannot be repaired. Ground
crews can only fuel the starboard tank.
He has enough fuel to reach the
Americans. He does not have enough to
come back. He is offered a different
aircraft. He refuses. You are standing
near the tail when the engine starts.
You can smell the exhaust. You can see
him through the canopy. He does not look
at anyone. 10 torpedo bombers, six
zeros. Tomonaga bores in on the Yorktown
from the port quarter. His wing catches
fire. He holds the run, drops his
torpedo, then his plane crashes into the
Pacific. Two torpedoes hit the Yorktown.
She will never sail again. Five bombers
make it back. Two are still flyable. Two
planes. 12 hours ago, your fleet had
248
The dive bombers, the elevator blown
vertical, the hangars a furnace. You
fight fires for hours, smoke so thick
you cannot see your own hands. Sato is
in the chain beside you. He's not spoken
since the morning. At 9:23, the engine
stop. The ship is dead. Late that night,
Yamaguchi assembles the survivors. 800
men on a burning flight deck. The deck
is hot under your feet. The air tastes
like smoke and fuel oil. He and Captain
Tomioka
stand near the bridge. [music]
Kakuta takes responsibility for the loss
of Hiyu. Yamaguchi takes responsibility
for both Hiyu and Soryu. [music] I
command all of you to leave the ship and
continue your loyal service to His
Majesty the Emperor. The crew shouts
banzai three times [music] facing west
toward Tokyo. The flag comes down.
Kimigayo plays one last time. He removes
his cap and hands it to his staff
officer to be delivered to his family.
He sends a final message to Namugo. I
have no words to apologize for what has
happened. [music] I only wish for a
stronger Japanese navy and revenge.
Captain Kaku turns to him. I'm going to
share the fate of the ship, sir. They
share naval biscuits and water. No sake.
They ate biscuits [music] and they
looked at the moon. Let us enjoy the
beauty of the moon, one of them says.
How bright it shines, [music] the other
replies. It must be in its 21st day. It
was. Destroyers come alongside. You
board with the others. You do not look
back for a long time. When you do,
Yamaguchi and Kaku are still standing on
the burning flight deck waving their
caps. The next morning, a torpedo is
fired to scuttle Hiryu. It is not
enough. She stays afloat. A scout plane
photographs her. The elevator is still
standing against the bridge like a
gravestone. She finally sinks bow first
at 9:12. But 70 crewmen sealed below the
waterline never got the order to abandon
ship. 39 of them fought their way
topside [music] and made it into the
ship's cutter moments before she went
under. They drifted for 14 days. On June
19th, the seaplane tender Ballard pulled
35 men out of the Pacific. They became
the only reason the allies ever learned
how Japanese carriers actually worked.
The Battle of Midway killed roughly
3,057
Japanese sailors. It sank all four
carriers. It destroyed 248 aircraft. But
only about 110 of those dead were
pilots. The rest were mechanics, the
armorers, the ordnance handlers, the
flight deck crews, men like you. They
are dead. You are not. When you reach
port, nobody is waiting. The battle is
classified as a victory. You are taken
to a base in southern Japan and told you
cannot leave. You cannot write home. You
cannot tell anyone what happened. The
navy does not want the country to know
that four carriers are gone. Weeks pass.
Then you are sent directly to the front.
No leave, no family visit. The men who
survived Midway are scattered across the
Pacific as fast as the Navy can move
them. Sent to places where nobody will
ask where they came from. You survived
the bombs, you survived the fire, you
survived 14 hours on a dying carrier,
that doesn't mean that you made it out.

treaty. A treaty? That's just a scrap of

major country in Europe was at war, and
everybody thought it would be over by
Christmas.

crush Paris in 6 weeks. Then, turn the

easy. But, Belgium actually fought back.

moved faster, but were just as bloody.

Ottoman flags, bombarded Russian ports.

came up with a plan. Hey, let's attack
the Ottoman Empire right here at

young politician named Winston Churchill
pushed the whole thing. Ottoman forces
held the high ground and pinned the

side lost roughly 250,000
men. Churchill had to resign. Now it's
1916, and the war got a whole lot worse.

lasted 303
days and produced roughly 750,000
total casualties. France rotated about
75% of their entire army through one
single battle. Then, the British
launched their own offensive at the

them missed. British soldiers went over
the top and walked straight into machine
gunfire. First day, July 1st, 1916,
57,000
British casualties, 19,000
dead. The bloodiest day in British
military history. The whole battle
lasted 5 months, cost over a million
casualties, and the front moved about 6
miles. But one good thing came out of

them on the battlefield? No more
questions, please. They were called

and three big things happened that

and in March 1917, revolution toppled

named Lenin seized power and pulled

the big problem for the allies was that

something incredibly stupid. They sent a

if the United States joins the war
against us, how about you invade
America? And if you win, you can have

you want us to invade the United States?
Yes. And you think that's going to work?
Just do it. British code breakers
intercepted the telegram. American
newspapers published it. On April 6th,
1917, the United States declared war on
Germany. And third, the French army
almost broke. After a disastrous attack
that killed 130,000 men in days,
soldiers in about half of all French
divisions refused to attack. They agreed
to keep defending their trenches, but
they would not charge into machine guns
again. The new commander, Pétain, calmed
things down with better food and regular
leave. But American troops were still
months away from arriving in large
numbers. Germany knew it had one last
chance. In March 1918, over 6,000 guns
fired a million shells in 5 hours. Storm
troopers punched through the lines and
advanced 40 miles, the biggest gain
since 1914. But Germany was losing its
best soldiers faster than it could
replace them. By July, the offensive was
dead. Then, it was the Allies' turn. On
August 8th, British, Australian, and
Canadian forces smashed through the
German lines at Amiens and captured

day of the German army." The Kaiser told
him, "The war must end." And it all
collapsed fast. Bulgaria surrendered
September 29th, the Ottoman Empire
October 30th, Austria-Hungary November
3rd. German sailors mutinied. The mutiny
spread across Germany. The Kaiser
abdicated on November 9th and fled to

November 11th, 1918, at the 11th hour of

went silent. The armistice was signed in

28th, 1919, exactly 5 years after the
assassination in Sarajevo. Hey Germany,
this war was your fault. We didn't start
it. Doesn't matter, you're paying for
it. How much? 132 billion gold marks.
And you're losing 13% of your territory
over here, and all your colonies, and
your military gets capped at 100,000
men. No air force, no tanks, no
submarines. Anything else? Yes, you're
not allowed to join with Austria, ever.
This doesn't seem fair. Sign it or we

Empire, the Austro-Hungarian Empire, the

New countries appeared all over the map.

Latvia, and Lithuania up here. The
Middle East was carved up between

cause problems today. A corporal named

Western Front would spend the next 20
years exploiting Germany's anger over
the treaty. French Marshal Foch looked
at the whole thing and said, "This is
not a peace. It is an armistice for 20
years." He was off by 65 days.

transcript_plaintext:
You hear the gas gong before you see the
cloud. Someone is hammering a shell
casing with a rifle butt, screaming one
word over and over. Gas. Gas. The cloud
is already 50 yards out, yellow-green,
drifting slow. You fumble for your
respirator, but your fingers are numb
and the straps are tangled. And the man
next to you, Private Dawson, is still
asleep. You shake him. He doesn't wake
up. You slap him. Nothing. Then you see
it. His eyes are open. He's not asleep.
He's dead.
Shell fragment, sometime in the night.
You didn't even hear it. The cloud is 30
yards out now. You can smell it. Bleach
and something sweet. Phosgene. You
finally get the mask on. The rubber
seals against your face. You breathe
through charcoal and pray the filter
holds. But here's the thing, the gas
attack isn't the worst part of your day.
It's not even close. Let's go back 22
hours and see how you got here. It's
still dark when Sergeant Whitfield's
voice cuts through the cold. Stand to,
every man. Now. You haven't slept, not
really. Maybe two hours in fragments,
curled in a funk hole carved into the
trench wall, wrapped in a greatcoat that
smells like wet wool and something
worse. Your boots haven't been off in
four days. Your feet feel like they
belong to someone else. You climb onto
the fire step and point your rifle
toward the German lines. 300 yards
across no man's land. German soldiers
are doing exactly the same thing,
pointing rifles at you, waiting. This is
the ritual. Dawn and dusk, the two most
likely times for an attack. Both sides
stand ready, staring into the gray. 30
minutes pass. Nothing happens. The sky
turns from black to gray. Whitfield
walks behind you, checking rifles,
checking faces, checking for men who
died in the night. Two men did. Dawson
will make three by tomorrow. Stand down.
The best moment of your day comes from a
stoneware jar stamped SRD.
Officially means Supply Reserve Depot.
Everyone calls it Seldom Reaches
Destination. Corporal Hargreaves pours 2
and 1/2 oz of navy rum into a shell cap.
He hands it to you. It burns going down.
For 30 seconds, you feel almost warm.
Breakfast is bacon when there's bacon
and tea that tastes like petrol. The
water comes in tins that used to hold
motor fuel. Nobody cleaned them
properly. You drink it anyway. Private
Jennings opens a tin of Maconochie stew,
cold, gray. He takes one bite and gags.
"Tastes like a dead horse." "That's
because it is." Hargreaves says. Nobody
laughs. Lieutenant Ashworth walks the
line. Rifles first, then feet. You
unlace your boots for the first time in
days. Your socks are wet. They're always
wet. Your feet are pale, wrinkled, soft
in ways feet shouldn't be soft. The skin
between your toes is starting to crack.
Ashworth moves to Jennings. Jennings
hesitates. Then, he pulls off his boot.
His foot is gray, black at the edges.
The flesh is dying. You can smell it
from 3 ft away. Ashworth writes
something in his notebook. "Report to
the medical officer. You're done."
Jennings nods. His face shows nothing,
but you see his hands shaking as he
laces his boot back up. You watch him
walk down the communication trench
toward the rear, toward England, toward
amputation and a cane and a pension and
a life. And you feel something you're
not supposed to feel. You look down at
your own feet. Still pink, still
functional. And you think about shoving
them into the standing water at the
bottom of the trench, leaving them there
for a few days, letting the rot set in.
You don't do it, but you think about it.
That's the kind of man the trenches turn
you into.
The morning is for work, filling
sandbags, stacking sandbags, shoring up
trench walls, pumping water, cleaning
latrines. You're not allowed to look
over the top. A man in your platoon
raised his head 3 in last week to light
a cigarette. The bullet caught him above
the left eye. He dropped without a
sound. So, you work with your head down.
You fill sandbags. You don't look up. By
noon, there's nothing to do but wait.
Some men write letters. An officer reads
everyone before it's sent, crossing out
anything useful to the enemy. Most
letters say the same thing. I am well.
The food is fine. Don't worry. Some men
play cards, betting cigarettes they
don't have for money they won't spend.
Some men chat. Not conversation,
chatting. Running a candle flame along
shirt seams to kill the lice. You stop
counting the lice weeks ago. Somewhere
past 50, it doesn't matter.
Around 2:00, you hear it. A voice.
Faint. Coming from no man's land.
Someone is alive out there. He's been
calling since noon. English words.
British accent. Could be from a patrol
that got caught last night. Could be
from the shelling 3 days ago. Doesn't
matter how he got there. What matters is
he's 60 yards from your trench, still
breathing, still calling. You could go
get him. Climb over the parapet, crawl
across the mud in broad daylight. Find
him. Drag him back. 10 minutes. Maybe
less. Snipers miss sometimes. Nobody
moves. Whitfield doesn't give the order.
Ashworth doesn't give the order. Nobody
looks at each other. You just sit there,
backs against the sandbags, listening to
a man die by inches. His name is Parish.
You find out later. He was 22. He had a
photograph of a girl in his pocket. He
lived for 9 hours in a shell crater with
his stomach open. Around 4:00, the voice
stops. You tell yourself there was
nothing you could do. You tell yourself
it would have been suicide. You tell
yourself the smart play was to stay put.
You're right about all of it. That
doesn't help.
A private named Cook crawls into your
funk hole. He's shaking. He's been
shaking since the shelling 3 nights ago,
when a direct hit buried four men alive
10 feet from where he was sleeping. He
holds out his hand. There's a pistol in
it. German. Luger. Probably pulled off a
corpse in no man's land. I can't do it
myself, he says. They'll know. They'll
tell my family. You stare at him. Shoot
me in the foot. Make it look like a
sniper. Please. Self-inflicted wounds
are a capital offense. Firing squads.
But accidents happen. Sniper rounds come
from every direction. A man could step
wrong, catch a ricochet, take a bullet
that nobody saw coming. You could do it.
You could shoot him in the foot right
now and he'd be on a stretcher by
nightfall, on a ship by next week. Home
by Christmas. All you have to do is pull
the trigger. You look at Cook. You look
at the pistol. You think about Jennings
walking toward the rear with his rotting
foot. You hand the pistol back. I can't.
Cook doesn't argue. He just nods, crawls
back out. You don't see him again until
after the gas attack. He's one of the
three who don't make it.
After midnight, Hargreaves picks six
men. Wiring party. You climb over the
parapet into no man's land. 300 yd of
mud and shell craters and bodies. Some
weeks old, some months. You can't tell
German from British anymore. Your job is
to repair the wire. Work in silence.
Don't cough. Don't sneeze. German
sentries are 50 yd away. If they hear
you, they send up a flare. If a flare
goes up, you freeze. You don't move. You
don't breathe. A man named Crosby snags
his sleeve on the wire. Tiny sound,
metal on fabric. A flare goes up. You
drop flat, face in the mud. The light is
blinding. You can feel it on your back
like heat. Your heartbeat pounds in your
ears. The flare drifts down. Darkness
returns. Nobody got shot this time. You
crawl back to the trench at 0200. Your
hands are cut to ribbons. You sleep for
90 minutes.
You wake up to screaming. Not artillery,
not gas. Something worse. Close. Inside
the trench. A flare goes up from
somewhere. German flare. Green light.
And in that light, you see them. Six
Germans in your bay, blackened faces, no
rifles, just clubs and knives and
sharpened spades. Trench raiders. They
came over the top while the sentries
were watching the wrong direction. Three
men are already dead. You can see
Corporal Ellis on the duckboards. His
head is wrong, caved in on one side. A
German is standing over him, pulling a
club out of what used to be his face.
You don't think. You grab your rifle. No
time to aim. You fire from the hip. The
shot goes wide, hits sandbag, does
nothing. The German turns, sees you,
starts moving. You try to work the bolt.
Your fingers won't cooperate. Too cold,
too scared. The bolt jams halfway. He's
on you before you can clear it. The club
comes down. You twist. It catches your
shoulder instead of your skull. The pain
is white, electric. Your arm goes dead.
You fall backward into the mud. He's
standing over you now, raising the club
for the second swing, the one that
finishes it.
Then, his chest explodes.
Whitfield, 10 ft away, rifle still
smoking.
The German drops on top of you, dead
weight. You can't move. You can't
breathe. You just lie there under a dead
man while the fighting continues around
you. 90 seconds. That's how long the
raid lasts.
90 seconds, and then they're gone.
Back over the parapet, into no man's
land, like they were never there.
Whitfield pulls the body off you, checks
your shoulder. Dislocated, not broken.
He pops it back in without warning. You
scream. "You're fine," he says. "Get
up." You get up. You look at Ellis. You
look at the three others. You look at
the blood on your hands that isn't
yours. 90 seconds. You survived because
Whitfield was faster than the German.
That's it. That's the only reason you're
alive.
The gas gong wakes you. You're back
where we started fumbling for your mask.
Dawson dead beside you. The yellow green
cloud 30 yards out. You get the mask on.
Breathe through the filter. Your eyes
burn anyway. The seal isn't perfect. It
never is. The cloud passes over. Men who
didn't get their masks on are on the
ground coughing, choking. Phosgene
doesn't kill you right away. It kills
you in 48 hours after your lungs fill
with fluid. Cook is one of them. You
find him slumped against the trench
wall. Respirator still in his hands. He
never got it on. You wonder if he tried.
At 0600 relief arrives. Fresh troops
moving up. Your unit rotates back to
support. Four days in the fire trench.
Four days in support. Four days in
reserve. Then back to the front. You
walk out through the communication
trench. Three quarters of a mile of mud.
Whitfield walks beside you. Four days
off. Clean your rifle. Get some sleep.
You nod. You don't say anything. There's
nothing to say. You'll be back on this
firestep by next week. Same trench. Same
mud. Different corpses.

transcript_plaintext:
You're 34 years old. The letter arrives
in September 1944. Your wife stands in
the doorway of your small farmhouse in
rural Japan. She doesn't cry. She
already cried when you left for China 6
years ago. She cried again when you came
back missing two fingers. Now, she just
folds the paper and sets it on the
kitchen table. Your father says nothing.
He fought the Russians in 1905. He knows
what the letter means. You've already
served. You came home. You have two
children who barely remember you leaving
the first time. None of that matters.
Japan's universal conscription law says
every man between 17 and 40 belongs to
the emperor. You're a recalled
reservist, a number on a list that
someone in Tokyo decided to pull.
They're building a fortress on an island
you've never heard of, Iwo Jima, Sulfur
Island. 8 square miles of volcanic rock,
660 miles south of the Japanese
homeland. The Americans want it as a
landing strip for damaged B-29 bombers.
Your job is to make that capture as
expensive as possible. You board a
transport ship in late 1944. The deck is
crowded with men just like you,
reservists and conscripts heading south
through submarine-infested waters. 1,500
men on other ships never make it.
American submarines are hunting every
convoy in the Pacific. The transport
Nishu Maru goes down with 28 tanks and
900 men from the 26th Tank Regiment. You
make it. That's not necessarily good
news. You step onto the black volcanic
beach of Iwo Jima expecting a military
posting. What you get is a construction
site. Your commanding general is
Tadamichi Kuribayashi, a 53-year-old
cavalryman who studied at Harvard
University. He knows exactly what Japan
is fighting. The United States is the
last country in the world Japan should
fight, he wrote to his wife back in
Tokyo. He also wrote that he won't be
coming home. His orders are simple.
Forget everything the Imperial Army
taught you. Forget beach defense. The
Americans will pulverize anything you
build on the sand. The battles at Saipan
proved that. Tarawa proved that.
Thousands of Japanese soldiers died in
the first hour at both islands. Forget
banzai charges. Kuribayashi calls them
an unnecessary waste of lives. You will
not die gloriously charging into
American machine guns. You will die
slowly, underground, after killing as
many of them as possible. So, you dig.
Every soldier on Iwo Jima is an engineer
now. Three rotating shifts work around
the clock. One shift digs tunnels
through the volcanic rock. One shift
guards the perimeter. One shift trains
with weapons. Then, you rotate. The
volcanic rock is soft enough to cut with
pickaxes. The heat is not. Temperatures
inside the tunnels beneath Mount
Suribachi reach 120°
F.
In the hottest sections near the sulfur
vents, work shifts last 5 minutes before
you rotate out. Your rubber shoes melt
against the ground. Sulfur gas burns
your throat and stings your eyes. You
wear a cloth mask over your face. It
doesn't help. By February 1945, you've
carved 11 miles of tunnels beneath the
island, 30 to 40 ft deep. Some chambers
drop 75 ft below the surface. The main
communications bunker stretches 150 ft
long and 70 ft wide, buried under solid
volcanic rock. The island's black
volcanic ash makes excellent concrete.
You don't know it yet, but in 6 weeks,
American naval shells will hit those
walls directly and do nothing. The
tunnels work exactly as designed. But
here's the thing nobody tells you.
Imperial General Headquarters in Tokyo
has already issued your posthumous
promotion. They did that before the
battle started. This island is not a
fortress. It's your grave. They just
haven't filled it in yet. Starting June
15th, 1944, American bombers appear over
Iwo Jima every single day for 9 months.
70 consecutive days of concentrated
aerial attack. 5,800
tons of bombs dropped on 8 square miles
of volcanic rock. A captured Japanese
soldier later tells American
interrogators the bombing raids were
relatively welcome because the bombs
often missed the island and killed fish
in the surrounding waters that you could
eat. The bombing doesn't stop
construction. During those 70 days, the
number of defensive positions on Iwo
Jima increases from 450 to 730.
You now have 438
artillery pieces hidden in caves and
concrete bunkers. 33 naval guns. 300
anti-aircraft weapons. 69 anti-tank
guns. But you have only 60% of the
ammunition you need. Food stock piled
for maybe 4 months and almost no
drinking water. The island has no
natural fresh water sources. You collect
rainwater in concrete cisterns. You
distill seawater when the equipment
works. One canteen per day, if you're
lucky. Half a canteen, if you're not.
You look at the tunnels stretching
beneath the island. You look at the
artillery pieces pointed at the beaches.
You look at your half-empty canteen. You
start to understand. February 16th,
1945, the American invasion fleet
appears on the horizon. You stand at the
observation slit of your concrete bunker
and watch the ships approaching. You've
never seen so many vessels in your life.
You stop counting somewhere around 100
because there's no point. 5,000
ships. The largest naval invasion force
the Pacific Ocean has ever seen. And
it's heading straight for your 8 square
miles of volcanic rock. Three days of
naval bombardment shake the island.
Kuribayashi orders complete silence.

transcript_plaintext:
Level one, the Santohe, private recruit.
The emperor needs bodies. That's you.
You're 20, standing on a train platform
in Osaka with a paper notice in your
hand. A corporal walks up and punches
you in the face. No warning, no reason.
That's your welcome to the Imperial
Japanese Army. You are the bottom. You
are furniture. The older soldiers don't
learn your name. They call you
isengodin, one sen, five rin. That's the
cost of the postcard that drafted you.
That's what you're worth. You have a
Type 99 rifle, a bayonet longer than
your arm, and a helmet that rusts in the
rain. Your job is simple, obey. Every
morning at 0600, you bow toward the
Imperial Palace and recite 2,700
characters of the Imperial Rescript. If
you stumble, you get hit. If you're slow
at drill, you get hit. If a second-year
soldier is bored, you get hit. They call
it binta. The manga artist Shigeru
Mizuki said he wasn't in the army 2 days
before the beatings began. You last 4
hours. You make 6 yen a month. Your
sister makes 30 in a textile factory.
You're cheaper than she is. You write
your parents that training is going
well. You don't mention the bruises.
Your first deployment is Guadalcanal.
The navy says 3 weeks. The island is
jungle and American Marines. Your supply
ship sinks, then your second ship, then
your third. You eat grass, you eat bark,
you drink from puddles with bodies
floating in them. Of 31,400
men sent here, 19,200
die, most from starvation. Your own army
forgot to feed you, but you survive.
That makes you useful. Level two, the
Jotohe, superior private. Six months
pass. You're promoted. Your pay bumps to
9 yen. Now, you're a second-year
soldier. Now, you do the beating. A new
conscript arrives from Hokkaido. He's
19. He's shaking. You punch him in the
face, just like they punched you. You
don't enjoy it, but you don't stop. This
is the system. Violence flows downward.
Generals slap colonels. Colonels slap
majors. Tojo himself cuffed subordinates
in staff meetings. The anger has to land
somewhere. It lands on the newest
private. How do you move up? You don't
complain. You don't die. Your lieutenant
points at a machine gun nest. You
charge. Three men beside you drop. You
keep running. You make it to the
sandbags. You kill two Americans with
your bayonet. You walk back alone.
That's how.
Level three, the gocho, corporal. You're
23, two stripes. You have 13 men under
you, kids from fishing villages who held
their first rifle last month. Your job
is to keep them alive long enough to be
useful. You teach them to dig, to clean
a weapon in humidity that rots
everything, to die quiet. You make 15
yen a month. Your father made more
selling fish, but your father isn't
getting shot at. Your division ships to
New Guinea. The officers call it
strategic. What they don't tell you is
that 150,000 Japanese soldiers will be
sent here. Only 10,000 will come home.
One regiment lands with 6,151
men. 91 return. No enemy required. Just
malaria, just starvation, just orders
that made no sense. You write your
mother the weather is pleasant. Every
word is a lie. Your stomach hasn't
stopped cramping in 3 weeks.
Level four, the gunso, sergeant. You're
26. You command a platoon 54 men. Your
job is food, ammunition, discipline, and
making sure none of your men surrender.
The Senjin Kun code is clear. January
8th, 1941, War Minister Tojo issued the
order himself. Never live to experience
shame as a prisoner. If one of your men
tries to surrender, you shoot him
yourself. If you try to surrender, your
family loses their rations. Your parents
get shunned. Your sister never marries.
You make 23 yen a month. You're assigned
to Iwo Jima. General Kuribayashi forbids
banzai charges. He wants tunnel warfare.
You dig 18 miles of underground fortress
with hand tools. The sulfur vents make
it 140°.
Men collapse from heat. You drag them
deeper, but here's the catch. Of 21,000
defenders, 20,700
will die. That's 98.9%.
The Americans take 216 prisoners. Most
of them unconscious when captured. You
do the math once, you stop doing the
math.
Level five, the June E, warrant officer.
You're the bridge. Enlisted men below,
officers above. You rose from private.
You know this army from the bottom. You
make 40 yen a month. Your job is
technical. Maybe communications, maybe
artillery maintenance, maybe you're the
senior medic who ran out of morphine six
months ago. You don't lead charges
anymore, but you watch the lieutenants
lead them. Academy boys. 22 years old,
swords raised, dead in a week. You've
outlived 11 platoon leaders. You stopped
learning their names.
The loneliness is different here.
Enlisted men see you as an officer.
Officers see you as enlisted. You eat
alone. You write letters to a wife who
stopped writing back after Saipan fell.
If you survive, you retire as a
forgotten man. If you die, your name
goes on a list nobody reads. Level six,
the Showi, second lieutenant. You
graduated from the Imperial Army
Academy. Four years, eight months of
training. You carry a sword, not because
it's useful, because it marks you as
samurai. You make 70 yen a month. You
have an orderly who polishes your boots.
You eat better than your men. You sleep
in a tent while they sleep in mud, but
your job is to die first. You stand at
the front with your sword raised. You
scream "Tenno Heika Banzai!" and charge
machine guns. The Americans have
water-cooled Brownings, 500 rounds per
minute. Your sword is 3 ft long. Your
life expectancy in combat is measured in
weeks, not months, weeks. The war
ministry knows this. They keep the
academy running at full capacity.
There's always another lieutenant. Level
seven, the Tai I, captain, company
commander, 180 men. Your job is to feed
them, equip them, lead them to victory.
Instead, you watch them disappear.
You're in the Philippines. Supply
convoys get torpedoed by American
submarines. The navy lost the sea lanes
8 months ago, but nobody told
headquarters. Your men haven't eaten in
6 days. They're too weak to hold their
rifles steady. You order foraging
parties. They come back with roots and
frogs. Of 432,000
Japanese soldiers in the Philippines,
255,000
will die, up to 80% from starvation, not
combat. You write metal recommendations
for men who charge tanks. The truth is,
they were too hungry to run in any
direction. You make 122 yen a month. You
haven't spent a single yen in 4 months.
There's nothing to buy. Your own stomach
cramps constantly, but you eat last,
always last. That's the code. Level
eight, the Taisa, colonel. You're 45,
regimental commander, 3,800 men. You
attend briefings in bunkers that smell
like mold. You sign orders that send
battalions into valleys where none
return. You make 310 yen a month. It
sits in a bank in Tokyo you'll probably
never see again. Your job is to execute
strategy, but there is no strategy. You
knew the war was lost after Midway,
after Guadalcanal, after the Marianas,
but you cannot say this. Defeatism is
treason. So, you bow. You salute. You
sign more orders. The Americans are
landing with translators and file
clerks. They're documenting everything.
Who gave which order? Who commanded
which unit during which massacre? War
crimes tribunals are coming. The Germans
are already hanging at Nuremberg. You
have options. A pistol, a sword, a rope
in Colorado, or you testify against the
generals and pray MacArthur shows mercy.
Level nine, the Chujo, lieutenant
general, division commander, 15,000 men.
You answer directly to Imperial General
Headquarters. You receive orders stamped
with the emperor's chrysanthemum seal.
You're on Okinawa, June 22nd, 1945.
The battle is over. American flags fly
over Shuri Castle. 110,000
of your soldiers are dead. You failed.
You put on your dress uniform, white
gloves, all your medals. You face north
toward the Imperial Palace. Your
adjutant hands you a knife. You kneel on
a white sheet so the blood won't stain
the floor. You cut. Your aide fires a
bullet into your skull to end it. He
follows 30 seconds later.
Your last order, Colonel Yahata must
survive. Someone has to tell Tokyo what
happened here. The defeat needs a
witness.
Level 10, the Gensui,
field marshal. This rank doesn't come
from promotion. It comes from the
emperor himself. Only 17 men in history
received it. You are a living symbol of
Imperial power, but symbols don't stop
B-29s. Field Marshal Sugiyama shoots
himself on September 12th. His wife
follows with a knife. Field Marshal Hata
gets 20 years at Sugamo Prison. The
Imperial Japanese Army dissolves. The
flag burns. 2.3 million graves remain.
Most of them dead from starvation,
disease, and orders that made no sense.

samurai. You make 70 yen a month. You
have an orderly who polishes your boots.

in a tent while they sleep in mud, but
your job is to die first. You stand at
the front with your sword raised. You
scream "Tenno Heika Banzai!" and charge
machine guns. The Americans have
water-cooled Brownings, 500 rounds per
minute. Your sword is 3 ft long. Your
life expectancy in combat is measured in
weeks, not months, weeks. The war
ministry knows this. They keep the
academy running at full capacity.

seven, the Tai I, captain, company
commander, 180 men. Your job is to feed
them, equip them, lead them to victory.

submarines. The navy lost the sea lanes

headquarters. Your men haven't eaten in

rifles steady. You order foraging
parties. They come back with roots and
frogs. Of 432,000
Japanese soldiers in the Philippines,
255,000

combat. You write metal recommendations

they were too hungry to run in any
direction. You make 122 yen a month. You
haven't spent a single yen in 4 months.

cramps constantly, but you eat last,
always last. That's the code. Level

regimental commander, 3,800 men. You
attend briefings in bunkers that smell
like mold. You sign orders that send
battalions into valleys where none
return. You make 310 yen a month. It
sits in a bank in Tokyo you'll probably
never see again. Your job is to execute
strategy, but there is no strategy. You
knew the war was lost after Midway,
after Guadalcanal, after the Marianas,

treason. So, you bow. You salute. You
sign more orders. The Americans are
landing with translators and file
clerks. They're documenting everything.

which unit during which massacre? War
crimes tribunals are coming. The Germans
are already hanging at Nuremberg. You
have options. A pistol, a sword, a rope

generals and pray MacArthur shows mercy.

gloves, all your medals. You face north

adjutant hands you a knife. You kneel on

bullet into your skull to end it. He
follows 30 seconds later.

survive. Someone has to tell Tokyo what
happened here. The defeat needs a
witness.

field marshal. This rank doesn't come
from promotion. It comes from the
emperor himself. Only 17 men in history
received it. You are a living symbol of
Imperial power, but symbols don't stop

transcript_plaintext:
Level one. The private.
You're 18. You're eating breakfast when
the letter arrives. Brown envelope, ohms
in the corner.
Your mother reads it twice, then puts
the kettle on because she doesn't know
what else to do. Three weeks later,
you're standing in a barracks with 40
other boys who've never held a rifle.
They shave your head. They hand you a
uniform that doesn't fit. They pay you
two shillings a day, 14 shillings a
week, 36 pounds a year. An American
private earns nearly three times what
you do. You don't complain. Complaining
gets you noticed. Six weeks of basic
training, then 14 more weeks learning to
be infantry. They give you a Lee-Enfield
rifle, a spike bayonet, a steel helmet
that weighs 2 lb, and wool battle dress
that soaks up rain like a sponge. You
learn to dig a slit trench in 20
minutes. You learn to eat bully beef
cold from a tin. You learn that the Bren
gun jams if you don't clean it every
night. Then, they ship you to Normandy.
You're in a rifle company now. 120 men.
You make up 20% of the battalion
strength. You will take 70% of the
casualties. The first time artillery
falls, your bowels turn to water. Nobody
mentions it. Half the platoon did the
same. By August 1944, all seven British
infantry divisions in Normandy have lost
three-quarters of their original men.
The math isn't complicated. In an
infantry rifle company, survival is a
coin flip. You keep your head down. You
watch the man next to you catch shrapnel
in the throat, and 20 minutes later,
you're eating your rations because the
sergeant says you need to eat. You carry
a photograph in your breast pocket. Her
name is Mary or Joan or Dorothy. You
haven't written home in three weeks.
What would you say?
Dear mum, watched a man drown in his own
blood today. Weather's been fine. The
army censors your letters anyway. They
black out anything real.
Level two. Lance corporal. You survived
six months. Someone noticed. Now, you're
second in command of a section. 10 men.
Your pay jumps to three shillings three
pence. A 62% raise for 200% more
responsibility. Your job is the Bren gun
group. Three men, one light machine gun,
500 rounds. When the section attacks,
you provide covering fire while the
rifle group advances. Your hands shake
when you load the magazine. You tell
yourself it's the cold. If the corporal
gets killed, you take command. If the
section gets pinned down because you're
suppressing the wrong position, those
deaths are on you. You're 19 years old.
The promotion came fast. That's because
NCO casualties run high. The Germans
know what a lance corporal looks like.
They know you give orders. In combat,
that makes you a target. You don't wear
anything different, but somehow snipers
find you anyway. Level three. Corporal.
You command the section now. Eight to 10
men. Four shillings a day. You carry a
Sten submachine gun, which marks you as
leadership, which marks you for death.
Some corporals ditch the Sten and carry
a rifle instead. You decide whether
that's cowardice or wisdom. Your mouth
goes dry before every assault. You can't
swallow. You go anyway. You lead the
rifle group forward while the Bren group
covers. You make decisions in seconds
that determine who lives. You write
letters to mothers. Your son died
bravely. You don't mention that he died
screaming or that he died for a hedgerow
you abandoned the next morning. The army
doesn't want those details. Neither do
the mothers. In peacetime, reaching
corporal takes years. In Normandy,
capable men make it in six months
because the capable men ahead of them
are dead. Level four. Sergeant. You're
the platoon sergeant now. Second in
command of 36 men. Six shillings a day.
Three times what a new private earns.
You get access to the sergeants' mess.
Better food, alcohol, a place to sit
that isn't mud. Your wife sends letters.
You read them by torchlight in a slit
trench. She writes about rationing in
the Anderson shelter and whether you'll
be home for Christmas. You write back
about the weather. You never mention the
faces. The platoon commander is a second
lieutenant. He's 21. Fresh from officer
training. Never seen combat. You've been
fighting for two years. He has education
and rank. You have experience and the
respect of the men. If he's smart, he
listens to you. If he's not smart, he's
dead within a week, and you're
commanding the platoon anyway. When the
lieutenant dies, you take over. No
ceremony. No paperwork. Just 36 men
looking at you for orders while mortar
rounds drop. You're the one who keeps
the platoon alive while the army feeds
you replacement lieutenants who last an
average of three weeks. Level five.
Warrant officer. Regimental sergeant
major. The highest rank an enlisted man
can reach. 12 shillings a day. One per
battalion. You hold a royal warrant, not
a commission. On the parade ground, even
officers follow your commands. You've
served through every enlisted rank.
You've buried men you trained. You've
watched boys become soldiers and
soldiers become corpses. The standing
orders say the discipline and good
conduct of the company depend upon your
zeal, ability, and integrity. In
practice, you keep 800 men functioning
while the officers make decisions that
get them killed. Some warrant officers
receive late entry commissions. They
become officers, but the old money
regiments never quite accept them.
You're a temporary gentleman now, which
means you're not really a gentleman at
all. Level six. Second lieutenant.
You're 21. You earn 11 shillings a day.
You command a platoon of 37 men. Most of
them are older than you. Your platoon
sergeant has more combat experience than
you will ever accumulate because you
won't live long enough to accumulate it.
In Normandy, junior infantry officers
have a one in 10 chance of surviving
unscathed. One in 10. The casualty rate
for second lieutenants is 204 per
thousand. Four times the rate for
captains. Six times the rate for
generals. You die at these rates because
you lead from the front. You carry a
pistol instead of a rifle. You read
maps, which makes you stand still.
German snipers are trained to identify
the man giving orders.
Level seven. Captain. You command a
company now. 120 to 150 men. 16
shillings sixpence daily. You've
survived long enough that survival
itself is suspicious. Most of the men
you trained with are dead. By 1944, some
company commanders are 23 years old.
Leading 150 men into combat. Writing
condolence letters by candlelight.
Deciding which platoon takes point
knowing that taking point means taking
casualties. You wanted promotion.
Promotion found you. Now you understand
that every step up is a step deeper into
a machine designed to consume men. Level
eight. Lieutenant colonel. You command a
battalion. 800 men. Four rifle
companies. A headquarters company. A
support company. You know these men by
name. You've trained with them. Eaten
with them. And now, you make decisions
that kill them. In Normandy, a battalion
might lose 30 to 50% of its strength in
days. You don't see them die. You read
reports. Casualty figures. Replacement
requests. But you remember teaching a
corporal to read maps six months ago,
and now his name is on a list, and he's
never going home. At Arnhem, John Frost
held the bridge with 740 men of the
second parachute battalion. Four days
against two SS Panzer divisions. Eight
of nine battalion commanders in the
first airborne were killed or captured.
The division lost 80% of its men.
Montgomery called it 90% successful.
Level nine. Major general. You command a
division. 15,000 men. Your headquarters
sits miles behind the front. You have
staff officers, aides, drivers, a cook.
You sleep in a bed. You eat hot food.
You haven't heard a rifle shot in
months. But you see the casualty reports
every morning. A division in heavy
fighting can lose a thousand men in a
week. You decide which brigade attacks.
You decide when to commit the reserve.
You decide whether to push forward or
consolidate. Every decision trades lives
for ground, ground for time, time for
objectives that someone above you deemed
worth the cost. At Arnhem, the first
airborne division was destroyed waiting
for relief that never came. Major
General Roy Urquhart was cut off from
his headquarters for 36 hours. Much of
it spent hiding in an attic while his
men died around a bridge they couldn't
hold. You wear red tabs on your collar
now. You attend conferences with men who
smile and shake your hand and would take
your command tomorrow if they could.
Churchill sacks generals the way other
men change shirts. You could be next.
You're always next. You tell yourself
someone has to make these decisions. You
tell yourself you're saving lives by
making them well.
Some nights, you almost believe it.
Level 10. Field marshal. You command
armies. Hundreds of thousands of men.
Entire theaters of war. Your decisions
cascade across continents. History will
remember your name. Whether as hero or
butcher, depends on who wins. Montgomery
commanded the Eighth Army at El Alamein.
190,000
men attacking across a 40-mile front. A
barrage from nearly a thousand guns.
13,560
casualties. Churchill said,
"Before Alamein, we never had a victory.
After Alamein, we never had a defeat."
What Churchill didn't mention was that
2,350
of those casualties were dead. These
were the field marshals. They won the
war. They also spent it making decisions
that killed tens of thousands of the men
who trusted them. That's what command
means at the top. You don't carry a
rifle. You carry the weight.
The math is simple. 3 and 1/2 million
men served in the British Army from 1939
to 1945. 569,000
became casualties. Everyone served the
same king. Not everyone paid the same
price. This was the British Army. Not a
brotherhood. A hierarchy, a machine that
processed men into soldiers and soldiers
into statistics.

second in command of a section. 10 men.
Your pay jumps to three shillings three
pence. A 62% raise for 200% more
responsibility. Your job is the Bren gun
group. Three men, one light machine gun,
500 rounds. When the section attacks,
you provide covering fire while the
rifle group advances. Your hands shake
when you load the magazine. You tell
yourself it's the cold. If the corporal
gets killed, you take command. If the
section gets pinned down because you're
suppressing the wrong position, those
deaths are on you. You're 19 years old.
The promotion came fast. That's because
NCO casualties run high. The Germans
know what a lance corporal looks like.
They know you give orders. In combat,
that makes you a target. You don't wear
anything different, but somehow snipers
find you anyway. Level three. Corporal.
You command the section now. Eight to 10
men. Four shillings a day. You carry a
Sten submachine gun, which marks you as
leadership, which marks you for death.
Some corporals ditch the Sten and carry
a rifle instead. You decide whether
that's cowardice or wisdom. Your mouth
goes dry before every assault. You can't
swallow. You go anyway. You lead the
rifle group forward while the Bren group
covers. You make decisions in seconds
that determine who lives. You write
letters to mothers. Your son died
bravely. You don't mention that he died
screaming or that he died for a hedgerow
you abandoned the next morning. The army
doesn't want those details. Neither do
the mothers. In peacetime, reaching
corporal takes years. In Normandy,
capable men make it in six months
because the capable men ahead of them
are dead. Level four. Sergeant. You're
the platoon sergeant now. Second in
command of 36 men. Six shillings a day.
Three times what a new private earns.
You get access to the sergeants' mess.
Better food, alcohol, a place to sit
that isn't mud. Your wife sends letters.
You read them by torchlight in a slit
trench. She writes about rationing in
the Anderson shelter and whether you'll
be home for Christmas. You write back
about the weather. You never mention the
faces. The platoon commander is a second
lieutenant. He's 21. Fresh from officer
training. Never seen combat. You've been
fighting for two years. He has education
and rank. You have experience and the
respect of the men. If he's smart, he
listens to you. If he's not smart, he's
dead within a week, and you're
commanding the platoon anyway. When the
lieutenant dies, you take over. No
ceremony. No paperwork. Just 36 men
looking at you for orders while mortar
rounds drop. You're the one who keeps
the platoon alive while the army feeds
you replacement lieutenants who last an
average of three weeks. Level five.
Warrant officer. Regimental sergeant
major. The highest rank an enlisted man
can reach. 12 shillings a day. One per
battalion. You hold a royal warrant, not
a commission. On the parade ground, even
officers follow your commands. You've
served through every enlisted rank.
You've buried men you trained. You've
watched boys become soldiers and
soldiers become corpses. The standing
orders say the discipline and good
conduct of the company depend upon your
zeal, ability, and integrity. In
practice, you keep 800 men functioning
while the officers make decisions that
get them killed. Some warrant officers
receive late entry commissions. They
become officers, but the old money
regiments never quite accept them.
You're a temporary gentleman now, which
means you're not really a gentleman at
all. Level six. Second lieutenant.
You're 21. You earn 11 shillings a day.
You command a platoon of 37 men. Most of
them are older than you. Your platoon
sergeant has more combat experience than
you will ever accumulate because you
won't live long enough to accumulate it.
In Normandy, junior infantry officers
have a one in 10 chance of surviving
unscathed. One in 10. The casualty rate
for second lieutenants is 204 per
thousand. Four times the rate for
captains. Six times the rate for
generals. You die at these rates because
you lead from the front. You carry a
pistol instead of a rifle. You read
maps, which makes you stand still.
German snipers are trained to identify
the man giving orders.
Level seven. Captain. You command a
company now. 120 to 150 men. 16
shillings sixpence daily. You've
survived long enough that survival
itself is suspicious. Most of the men
you trained with are dead. By 1944, some
company commanders are 23 years old.
Leading 150 men into combat. Writing
condolence letters by candlelight.
Deciding which platoon takes point
knowing that taking point means taking
casualties. You wanted promotion.
Promotion found you. Now you understand
that every step up is a step deeper into
a machine designed to consume men. Level
eight. Lieutenant colonel. You command a
battalion. 800 men. Four rifle
companies. A headquarters company. A
support company. You know these men by
name. You've trained with them. Eaten
with them. And now, you make decisions
that kill them. In Normandy, a battalion
might lose 30 to 50% of its strength in
days. You don't see them die. You read
reports. Casualty figures. Replacement
requests. But you remember teaching a
corporal to read maps six months ago,
and now his name is on a list, and he's
never going home. At Arnhem, John Frost
held the bridge with 740 men of the
second parachute battalion. Four days
against two SS Panzer divisions. Eight
of nine battalion commanders in the
first airborne were killed or captured.
The division lost 80% of its men.
Montgomery called it 90% successful.
Level nine. Major general. You command a
division. 15,000 men. Your headquarters
sits miles behind the front. You have
staff officers, aides, drivers, a cook.
You sleep in a bed. You eat hot food.
You haven't heard a rifle shot in
months. But you see the casualty reports
every morning. A division in heavy
fighting can lose a thousand men in a
week. You decide which brigade attacks.
You decide when to commit the reserve.
You decide whether to push forward or
consolidate. Every decision trades lives
for ground, ground for time, time for
objectives that someone above you deemed
worth the cost. At Arnhem, the first
airborne division was destroyed waiting
for relief that never came. Major
General Roy Urquhart was cut off from
his headquarters for 36 hours. Much of
it spent hiding in an attic while his
men died around a bridge they couldn't
hold. You wear red tabs on your collar
now. You attend conferences with men who
smile and shake your hand and would take
your command tomorrow if they could.
Churchill sacks generals the way other
men change shirts. You could be next.
You're always next. You tell yourself
someone has to make these decisions. You
tell yourself you're saving lives by
making them well.
Some nights, you almost believe it.
Level 10. Field marshal. You command
armies. Hundreds of thousands of men.
Entire theaters of war. Your decisions
cascade across continents. History will
remember your name. Whether as hero or
butcher, depends on who wins. Montgomery
commanded the Eighth Army at El Alamein.
190,000
men attacking across a 40-mile front. A
barrage from nearly a thousand guns.
13,560
casualties. Churchill said,
"Before Alamein, we never had a victory.
After Alamein, we never had a defeat."
What Churchill didn't mention was that
2,350
of those casualties were dead. These
were the field marshals. They won the
war. They also spent it making decisions
that killed tens of thousands of the men
who trusted them. That's what command
means at the top. You don't carry a
rifle. You carry the weight.
The math is simple. 3 and 1/2 million
men served in the British Army from 1939
to 1945. 569,000
became casualties. Everyone served the
same king. Not everyone paid the same
price. This was the British Army. Not a
brotherhood. A hierarchy, a machine that
processed men into soldiers and soldiers
into statistics."}]

transcript_plaintext:
You're 18 years old. The letter arrives
in March 1943.
Your mother cries. Your father says
nothing. He fought in the first war. He
knows what the letter means. You report
to the induction center in Hamburg. They
give you a uniform two sizes too big and
a rifle older than you are. The drill
sergeant says you're going to defend the
fatherland. He doesn't say which front.
The Eastern Front is eating entire
divisions. Stalingrad just fell.
Everyone knows what happens to soldiers
sent east. But you don't get sent east.
You get sent west. You get assigned to
something called the Atlantic Wall.
December 1943. You arrive at a muddy
construction site on the coast of
Normandy, a fishing village called
Colleville-sur-Mer. Your position is
designated resistance nest 62. For the
next 6 months, you pour concrete rated
to withstand 500 kg bombs. You dig
trenches until your hands bleed. Then,
you dig more trenches. You position
beach obstacles along the waterline.
Steel crosses, wooden stakes, concrete
pyramids, all of them angled toward the
sea. All of them designed to rip the
bottoms out of landing craft. The
engineers tell you it's the most
fortified coastline in human history.
They tell you the allies will shatter
themselves against it like waves against
a cliff. They sound very confident. The
veterans from the Eastern Front are also
assigned here. They don't say anything
about the fortifications. They just dig.
By May 1944, your position is finished.
WN 62 sits on a bluff 40 m above the
beach overlooking a natural gap in the
cliffs called the E3 draw. It's one of
only five exits off the entire beach. If
the Americans want to get their tanks
and trucks inland, they have to come
through you. Your garrison is 40 men.
You have two 75-mm guns mounted in
concrete casemates, one 50-mm anti-tank
gun, two 50-mm mortars, six machine gun
positions. Your personal weapon is an MG
42. The MG 42 fires 1,200
rounds per minute, 20 bullets per
second. The barrel overheats after 250
rounds, so you learn to swap barrels in
under 8 seconds. You practice this until
you can do it with your eyes closed. The
Americans have a nickname for your gun.
They call it the bone saw. You don't
know it yet, but in 6 weeks, you're
going to fire that gun so long and so
fast that the barrel will ignite the
grass around your foxhole. You're going
to swap barrels so many times, you'll
lose count somewhere around 15. You're
going to kill more men in 9 hours than
most soldiers kill in an entire war. But
that's later. Right now, you're just a
kid cleaning his gun and playing cards
and waiting for an invasion that might
never come. June 5th, 1944. A storm is
hammering the coast. Rain is coming
sideways. Your commanding officer,
Lieutenant Bernhard Frerking, says
everyone can relax. Maybe get some
sleep. The Allies aren't stupid enough
to cross the channel in a storm. You go
to bed at 2300 hours. At 0030 hours, the
air-raid sirens drag you out of sleep.
Bombers. You can hear hundreds of them
somewhere above the clouds. The ground
starts shaking. You run to your
position, heart pounding, and you wait
for the bombs to find you. They don't.
The clouds are too thick. The rain is
too heavy. The bombardiers can't see
their targets. They drop their payloads
3 km inland, blowing up empty fields and
confused cows. Your bunker doesn't take
a single hit. You don't realize it yet,
but this is the luckiest moment of your
life. 448
B-24 bombers just missed you by
accident. At 0400 hours, the clouds
break just enough to see the horizon.
And that's when you see them. Ships.
You've never seen so many ships. You
stop counting at 5,000 because there's
no point. They stretch from one edge of
the horizon to the other. Battleships,
cruisers, destroyers, troop transports,
the largest naval invasion force ever
assembled in human history, and it's
heading straight for your 40-man
outpost. Your radio man, Private
Wornicke, is screaming into his
transmitter. "5,000 ships heading
straight for us. Send reinforcements.
Send the Luftwaffe. Send anyone." The
response comes back scratchy and
confused. Rommel is in Germany for his
wife's birthday. The Fuhrer is asleep,
and no one is authorized to wake him.
The 21st Panzer Division is on standby,
but no one has given the order to move.
You look at the ships. You look at your
40 men. You look at the empty sky where
the Luftwaffe is supposed to be. At 6:30
hours, the first landing craft hit the
water. They're 450 m out. You can see
some of the boats swamping, men spilling
into the freezing water, drowning before
they ever reach the sand. Lieutenant
Furking gives the order. "Wait. Let them
get closer. Wait until they drop the
ramps. Wait until they're in knee-deep
water where they can't run, can't hide,
can't do anything but die." They drop
the ramps. The Americans pour out.
They're loaded down with 60 lb of gear.
They're struggling through the surf.
They can't run. They can barely walk.
Furking gives the order. You pull the
trigger. The first burst kills six men.
They don't fall dramatically like in the
movies. They just stop moving. The ones
behind them trip over the bodies. The
second burst kills four more. You're not
aiming at individuals. You're not even
aiming at soldiers. You're aiming at a
mass, a wave of human bodies that keeps
coming no matter how many you cut down.
The beach fills with the dead. The
living hide behind the dead. They bunch
up behind the steel obstacles, the ones
you positioned 6 months ago. They do
exactly what the obstacles were designed
to make them do. They make themselves
easy targets. Your loader is feeding
belts as fast as he can. Every 250
rounds, you swap barrels. You throw the
spent ones into the mud where they hiss
and steam. The gun is so hot you can
smell the paint burning off. One of the
other gunners in your position, a
corporal named Heinrich Severloh, will
later claim he fired 12,000 machine gun
rounds that day. Plus 400 rifle bullets
when the machine gun jammed. Historians
will call that number implausible. The
Americans will call him the beast of
Omaha Beach. You're not counting rounds.
You're not counting kills. You're just
pulling the trigger until the belt runs
out. This is what the Atlantic Wall was
built for. This is working exactly as
designed. But something is wrong. By
0800 hours, you look up at the sky. It's
empty. Where is the Luftwaffe? You were
promised air support. Thousands of
planes. Not a single German aircraft
appears over Normandy on June 6th, 1944.
The Luftwaffe has been shattered in a
thousand dogfights over the past year.
Nobody told you. You radio for
reinforcements. The 21st Panzer Division
should be counter-attacking by now.
Nobody will come until 1430 hours. And
when they finally move, they'll be sent
to fight the British 15 km away. You're
on your own. By noon, you're running low
on ammunition. You fired 8,000 rounds,
maybe 10,000. Your hands are shaking
from the recoil. The American destroyers
have moved in close, within a thousand
meters of the beach, and they're firing
directly into your position. One shell
hits 10 meters from your foxhole. The
pressure wave slams you against the
concrete wall and you taste blood.
Lieutenant Furking is on the radio,
begging for ammunition resupply. The
answer is there is no ammunition. There
is no resupply. There is nothing coming.
At 1500 hours, you load your last belt.
It's all tracers. They work fine for
killing, but every round shows the
Americans exactly where you are. Within
20 minutes, every gun on the beach is
focused on your position. Ferking takes
a shell fragment to the neck. He bleeds
out in the trench, still holding the
radio handset, still waiting for the
reinforcements that were never coming.
At 1530, the order comes. Retreat. Fall
back to the secondary position. There is
no secondary position. There is no
organized retreat. You crawl out the
back of WN 62 with three other men. Of
your original 40, 18 are dead. The rest
are scattered across the Normandy
countryside, running from an invasion
they were told was impossible. You make
it 200 m before the Americans find you.
They're not gentle. One of them hits you
with a rifle butt. You go down hard. You
expect to be shot. Instead, they put a
zip tie around your wrists and march you
back to the beach. The beach doesn't
look like a killing field anymore. It
looks like a city being constructed.
Trucks, tanks, cranes, thousands of men
pouring ashore like they own the place,
because they do now. You look at the
bodies still floating in the surf. You
did that. You and your MG 42 and your 6
months of preparation. And it didn't
matter. Not even a little. They put you
on a transport ship. You expect
starvation. You expect beatings. What
you get is sausage, mashed potatoes,
white bread, and coffee. The American
guards give you cigarettes. One of them
even offers you chocolate. You end up in
Kansas, a place called Camp Concordia.
The prisoners call it Fritz Ritz. Ice
cream, Coca-Cola, 80 cents a day for
work details. You try not to think about
the beach. You try not to count the
bodies. May 1945, the war ends. They
ship you back to Germany, what's left of
it. Your hometown is rubble. Your father
never came home from the Eastern Front.
Trials are happening. Nuremberg. You're
not a war criminal, you were a conscript
who followed orders. But a man
approaches you in the winter of 1946. He
knows your name. He knows you can
process paperwork. There are Germans who
need to disappear, he says, "Good
Germans." You don't ask what they did.
You process the Red Cross travel
documents. Germans become Argentines.
Austrians become Brazilians. The
paperwork goes through Rome, then Genoa,
then Buenos Aires. You process 847
documents in 18 months. You get paid in
cash. You don't ask questions. In 1950,
you process your own documents. You
become someone else. Buenos Aires. A
small apartment. A job keeping books for
a shipping company. For 34 years, you
live quietly. You change your name
twice. Every time there's a knock at the
door, you stop breathing. The Israelis
found Eichmann in 1960. He was living 12
blocks from your first apartment. They
drugged him and flew him to Jerusalem in
a cargo hold. That was too close. You
move to São Paulo. October 1984. There's
a knock at your door. Two men. They know
your real name. They know about WN62.
They know about the 847 documents. You
don't answer their questions. You can't.
The men you helped disappear, some of
them are still alive. Some of them have
friends in dark places. The men leave.
They say they'll be back. Three days
later, you're found in your apartment.
Heart failure. Natural causes. That's
what the death certificate says. but the
coffee cup on your table has residue the
coroner doesn't recognize. You were a
number on a conscription list in 1943, a
number on a machine gun position in
1944, and now you're a number on a
coroner's report in Brazil. Nobody comes
to your funeral. There are no records
connecting your fake name to your real
one. That was the whole point. The war
never ended for you. It just moved to a
different column on someone else's list.
